1.2.16.1
Safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity are the necessary safety
precautions to know to prevent excessive exposure to radioactivity, which can cause serious
injury or damage to the environment.
Always use two radiation detectors to measure the level of induced radioactivity. Only use
radiation detectors that have an applicable calibration certificate. The period of time since the
last calibration date must be less than 12 months. Do not use the radiation detectors if the period
of time since the last calibration date is more than 12 months.
WARNING 1.23
Do not move radioactive material (by air, sea, or land) unless you obey the applicable laws and
regulations for induced radioactivity and disposal of radioactive material of the jurisdictions
through which the movement occurs. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury
and damage to the environment.
1.2.16.2
Safety precautions for handling parts with induced radioactivity
The handling of parts with induced radioactivity must comply with the laws and regulations of the
jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed. The safe levels of radiation applicable in the UK
do not apply in all jurisdictions. The permitted level of radioactivity must always be as low as
reasonably achievable (ALARA). This level may vary depending on local rules, therefore the safe
working levels from the applicable local rules must be considered as the acceptable working limit.
If there are no safe levels available for a jurisdiction, use the UK value as a guideline, which is a
maximum of 150 cps at the surface for a maximum duration of 72 minutes. The following table
shows the conversion from this value to other units.

Glossary of terms
Table 3.3
Glossary of terms
Term
Definition
Autotrack function
The autotrack function automatically moves the diaphragms or

Cal block
The Cal block contains the item and part values that, when
loaded, configure the linear accelerator for a given energy.
Clinical Mode
In Clinical Mode, Clinical Users use the linear accelerator and its
accessories for the radiation therapy treatment that a licensed
medical practitioner prescribes.
Gating
Gating is the procedure by which an external system or manual
task pauses and starts the radiation delivery as a result of
information received relating to the treatment position of the
patient.
Interdigitation
Interdigitation is an overlap of the opposite adjacent leaves of a
multileaf collimator.
Service life
Service life is the length of time that the regular servicing and
repair procedures can keep the machine in operation.
Service Mode
In Service Mode, Service Users do the necessary maintenance
tasks and calibration of the equipment.

4.1.3
Integrity™ R4.x treatment control system (TCS)
Integrity™ R4.x provides the user interface for the treatment control system. It is part of the
consolidated computing platform (CCP) and runs as a virtual machine on the Enterprise Server.
The Enterprise Server is installed in the treatment control cabinet (TCC). The TCC is normally
located in either the treatment suite control room or a server room.
Refer to the EMLA Service User Guide for: Integrity with the Consolidated Computing Platform
(CCP) for information on fault finding for Integrity™ R4.x and the TCC.
The linear accelerator has two modes of operation, delivering either an X-ray beam or an electron
beam. For each mode, the beam shape is changed through the BLD. For a full description, refer to
the EMLA Instructions for Use Volume 1 manual.

LED rocker switch
The LED ON/OFF switch is useful in two ways:
•
You can switch off the LEDs before working on the BLD to avoid any danger from
UV radiation. This is useful if you are removing the crosswire screen.
•
The LED rocker switch does not power off the projector cooling fan, so it can be
used to cool down the projector. Power off the LEDs and wait at least five minutes
for the projector to cool down before you remove the projector for maintenance
work.

6.1
Safety precautions for BLD maintenance
6.1.1
Making the linear accelerator safe for Agility™ BLD maintenance
WARNING 6.1
Do not do work on the Agility™ beam limiting device unless the gantry is at 0° or 180°. Gravity
can cause the leaves, diaphragms and DLGs to move. If you ignore this warning, it can cause
fatal injury.
1 
Rotate the gantry to 180°.
2 
Rotate the Agility™ BLD to 0°.
This is necessary to remove the inner covers.
3 
Set the treatment table at 0° and the column at 90°.
4 
At the interface cabinet, switch off the circuit breaker CB7 (ICCA).
This will keep the Leaf Limits (40×40) shape.
WARNING 6.2
Do not remove the BLD unless you fit the gantry locking straps and rear support post. The
gantry can become unbalanced. If you ignore this warning, parts that move can cause fatal
injury.
WARNING 6.3
Do not lift the Agility™ BLD unless you use a suitable hoist and fit the shackles and slings
provided. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury.
5 
If you remove the Agility™ BLD, do the steps that follow:
a
Install the bolts to attach a locking bar at each end of the gantry drum to:.
‒
The center of the support wheel
‒
The attachment point on the outer surface of the gantry drum.
b
At the gun end of the gantry arm, install the bolts to attach the rear support bar to:
‒
The support bracket
‒
The nut at the attachment point in the site floor.
6

WARNING 6.54

bank assembly. The result can be incorrect radiation delivery and other malfunctions. If you
ignore this warning, it can cause fatal injury and clinical mistreatment.

Log file Sorting
This lets you put the log files in for machine state changes in sequence (for example, suspends,
interrupts, and terminated treatments). This lets you find a problem more easily.
Date Filter
It is possible to set a filter to show only the log files that were saved between two dates. Be
careful when you type the date. Elekta recommends that you use a three letter abbreviation for
the month, for example, ‘10 Nov 11’. Also, Elekta recommends that you set filters for dates,
because some time is necessary for 999 log files to load (the maximum available).
Other Information
You can look at the calibration files, energy calibration files, linac terminations, and HT Hours/Life
Dose. The energy calibration files show the saved values for a given energy. The calibration files
do not give much information for the field engineer. The Linac Terminations filter shows all the
log files for suspends and terminated treatments. HT Hours/Life Dose gives information on the
dose delivered during the life of the machine.
Note:
When there are 999 log files, some time is necessary before the system can show the terminated
treatments only.
MLC Log files
The MLC log files are saved with the log files for the linear accelerator. The Log File Format is
different to that of the linear accelerator.
Note:
There are always entries in the log files with RECOV at the end. These show general errors that
cleared after two or three tries.

when the leaves move against gravity.

In the Deliver Quick Beam window, set the Radiation Type and Energy.
5 
Click on the MLC icon then click on the Display Shape Codes icon.

Load the Interdigitate Full Evens shape.
7 
Monitor the image and make sure that all the leaves move to the correct position.

Click on the Service Graphing icon.
9 
Select Files.
10 
In the Manage configurations field, select Leaf 40 position v leaf motor currents.

Click Load.
All Leaves part 206 (Motor Current) against Leaf Y2 41 item 2420 part 129 (Scaled Actual)

12 
Click Begin Acquire.

Select the Interdigitate Full Odd shape.
14 
Click Load. Wait for the leaves to stop moving.
15 
Click End Acquire.
16 
Make a note of the leaves that have a maximum value more than the threshold within the

identify the leaves on the graph.

These tests checks the current limit circuitry and potentiometer readings at outer end stops to
ensure required travel range could be achieved.
8.12.1
Test diaphragm limits at outer end stops
Set diaphragm motor current limit (700mA), 25% demands and direction: message 0x211 {-30,
60,-30, 60}. Send 1 byte diaphragm motor Enable message 0x210 {01 101 101}.
Wait for 20 seconds or until both diaphragms reach the end stops. Monitor messages 0x215 and
0x216 for coarse and check potentiometer readings until they stop changing by more than 30.
Then read message 0x213 for current limit of more than 20 ADC units.

1.1
Important safety instructions
It is important to install, operate, maintain, and dispose of the equipment according to the
information in the product documentation, and in compliance with local regulations. For the
safety of the users and the patients, before a user operates or works on the equipment, they
must read, understand, and obey all:
•
Warnings, cautions, instructions, and notes in this document and the related
documents.
•
Safety instructions, emergency procedures, and information in this document and the
related documents.
•
Warnings, cautions, and safety markings on the equipment and the accessories of the
equipment.
If you have local work instructions for the equipment, then Elekta recommends that you include
the warnings, cautions, and notes from this document in your local work instructions.
1.1.1
Conventions for warnings, cautions, and notes
The conventions give information about the class and the level of the risk in the warnings and
cautions, and the content of notes.
WARNING 1.1
A warning is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of fatal or serious
injury, injury, or clinical mistreatment, if you do not obey the instructions.
CAUTION 1.1
A caution is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of damage to the
equipment, data, or the environment, if you do not obey the instructions.
Note:
A note gives more information about a related text.
1.1.2
Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can
keep the equipment safe to operate.
WARNING 1.2
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each
week of the year. If the equipment is used more frequently than this, the frequency of the
planned maintenance must increase accordingly and the extended life checks must also be
brought forward accordingly.

1.2.16.1
Safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity are the necessary safety
precautions to know to prevent excessive exposure to radioactivity, which can cause serious
injury or damage to the environment.
Always use two radiation detectors to measure the level of induced radioactivity. Only use
radiation detectors that have an applicable calibration certificate. The period of time since the
last calibration date must be less than 12 months. Do not use the radiation detectors if the period
of time since the last calibration date is more than 12 months.
WARNING 1.23
Do not move radioactive material (by air, sea, or land) unless you obey the applicable laws and
regulations for induced radioactivity and disposal of radioactive material of the jurisdictions
through which the movement occurs. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury
and damage to the environment.
1.2.16.2
Safety precautions for handling parts with induced radioactivity
The handling of parts with induced radioactivity must comply with the laws and regulations of the
jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed. The safe levels of radiation applicable in the UK
do not apply in all jurisdictions. The permitted level of radioactivity must always be as low as
reasonably achievable (ALARA). This level may vary depending on local rules, therefore the safe
working levels from the applicable local rules must be considered as the acceptable working limit.
If there are no safe levels available for a jurisdiction, use the UK value as a guideline, which is a
maximum of 150 cps at the surface for a maximum duration of 72 minutes. The following table
shows the conversion from this value to other units.

The corrective maintenance manual (CMM) helps service engineers troubleshoot, repair and
maintain the systems, subsystems and components of the linear accelerator. The target audience
is qualified service engineers. These may be engineers employed directly by Elekta, qualified
representatives of Elekta or qualified representatives of Elekta's customers.
The manual provides:
•
A description of the system or sub-system in question.
•
A troubleshooting section to identify the problem areas.
•
A set of detailed procedures used to replace FRUs (field replaceable units).
•
A section on how to return the device to work.
If you find any mistakes in this document, or identify areas for improvement, please raise a CLM
(customer lifecycle management) case and assign it to the relevant queue.

4.1
Cover sets for the Elekta linear accelerator
All Elekta linear accelerators are installed with a set of covers, which give:
•
Protection to patients and users from hazardous parts and conditions in the gantry arm
and beam limiting device (BLD).
•
Protection against damage during treatment to the parts of the linear accelerator in
the treatment room.
•
A comfortable environment for patients during treatment.
The gantry arm and BLD of the linear accelerator have covers installed around their structures.
There are no covers on the openings for the treatment field.
Some covers attach to posts of the frame installed between the treatment room and the
equipment room. Patients and users in the treatment room cannot see the internal structure of
the linear accelerator.
In most conditions, the covers for the linear accelerator do not make a full partition wall between
the treatment room and the equipment room. It is usual to add more panels to extend the wall
across the full width of the treatment room in the A-B direction. These panels usually include one
or two access doors to the equipment room.
Different cover sets have different assemblies and are different colors.
The available cover sets are shown in Figure 4.1, Figure 4.2 and Figure 4.3.

Description of the inner arm cover
These systems are installed with one inner arm cover on the bottom surface of the gantry arm to

These systems have one outer arm cover installed on the top section of the gantry arm. Two
brackets and four standoff nuts at the G-end attach the outer arm cover to the gantry arm.

Description of the gantry drum cover
These systems have a circular gantry drum cover. Six screws and eight fasteners attach the gantry
drum cover directly to the gantry drum.
A gantry scale assembly attaches to the center hole in the gantry cover. There is a specified shape
cut in the gantry cover for the iViewGT™ imaging system.
4.2.5
Description of the gantry scale
The gantry scale is installed around the hole in the center of the gantry cover. Eight button fixings
go through the holes in the gantry cover to hold the gantry scale in position.

The cover set of the Agility™, MLCi2™ and Beam Modulator BLDs have two semicircular covers,
one on the left side and one on the right side of the BLD.
The MLCi2™ BLD cover has an opening on the side for the BLD control unit. On the MLCi2™, a
small rubber panel gives protection to the openings for the BLD control units. This rubber panel is
part of the BLD cover. On the Beam Modulator™, the BLD control unit does not have a protective
rubber panel.
All the BLD covers have a semicircular scale which, when put together, gives a 360° rotation scale
for the BLD. The two panels are not the same, because the scale of the right panel is different to
that of the left panel.
All three BLD covers are not connected to and have no contact with the touchguard ring.
4.3.2
Description of the inner arm covers
These systems have two inner arm covers. One inner arm cover is installed on the left side of the
gantry arm, and one on the right side. The shape of the covers is a mirror image of each other.
The left inner arm cover has a pointer on the BLD scale.
Screws attach each inner arm cover to the outer arm cover. Self-adhesive seals attach the front
and center of each inner arm cover to each other.
4.3.3
Description of the outer arm covers
These systems have one outer arm installed on the top section of the gantry arm. Two brackets
and four nuts attach the G-end of the outer arm cover to the gantry arm.
4.3.4
Description of the gantry drum cover
These systems have a circular gantry drum cover. Screws attach the gantry drum cover directly to
the gantry drum.
A gantry scale assembly attaches to the center hole in the gantry cover. The other end of the
cover has a shape cut in it for the iViewGT™ detector arm and an XVI imaging system.
4.3.5
Description of the ring covers of the gantry drum
These systems have two semicircular ring covers. One ring cover installs on the left side of the
gantry drum cover, and one on the right side. Four screws attach the ring covers to the gantry
drum. The ring covers do not go across the full 360° range of the gantry drum.
One end of each ring cover has a shape cut in it for the gantry arm. The other end of the ring
cover has a shape cut in it for the iViewGT™ detector arm.

4.3.6
Description of the center disc
The center disc is installed across the hole in the center of the gantry drum cover. Eight screws
install through the holes in the gantry drum cover to hold the center disc in position.
The center disc can have an optional gantry scale.
4.3.7
Description of the lower quadrant fascia panels
Four screws and a packing piece attach the left and right lower quadrant fascia panels together.
Screws attach the fascia panels to the fascia support posts between the treatment room and the
equipment room.
Because the fascia panels are large and flexible, they can bend during installation. Velcro® pads
are installed at the center of each panel to help prevent this.
4.3.8
Description of the upper quadrant fascia panels
Four screws and a packing piece attach the left and right upper quadrant fascia panels together.
Screws attach the panels to the fascia support posts between the treatment room and the
equipment room.
4.3.9
Description of the treatment room monitors
These systems have two TRMs, one in each upper quadrant fascia panel. The TRMs attach to a
bracket on the fascia support posts between the treatment room and the equipment room. They
are not attached to the upper quadrant fascia panels.
The SVGA cable from the TCC connects to the TRM behind the partition wall. Some earlier
configurations have an isolation transformer installed on the bracket which is the power supply
for the TRMs.
4.3.10
Description of TRM bezels and handset rails
Each TRM has a bezel around the front of the TRM. The bezel attaches to the upper fascia
quadrant panel. A bracket attached to the bezels supplies an installation point for the HHC
receiver unit.
The handset rails for the HHCs attach to the TRM bezels. The HHC cable, and the ground (earth)
cable of the handset rail go through the holes in the bezel. The HHC cable connects to the HHC
receiver unit. The ground (earth) cable connects to the bracket of the bezel.
If the linear accelerator is installed in a smaller width treatment room, the cover set does not
have sufficient space for TRMs and HHCs. Therefore, the TRMs bezels and handset rails are not
used.
4.3.11
Description of the narrow covers
The narrow covers have a smaller width than the standard cover set. It is almost the same as the
standard cover set but does not have sufficient space for TRMs and HHCs. Therefore, the upper
quadrant fascia panels do not have the holes for TRMs, bezels or handset rails.

When the electrical supply is switched on to the linear accelerator, the LEDs in the center disc
come on. When the system is switched off, the LEDs go off.
The LEDs in the center disc is also controlled by the HHC.
4.4.6
Description of the half fascia panels
Four screws and shims attach the left and right half fascia panels together. Screws attach the
fascia panels to the fascia support posts between the treatment room and the equipment room.
Because the fascia panels are large and flexible, they can bend during installation.

Description of the treatment room monitors

attach to a bracket on the fascia support posts between the treatment room and the equipment

The SVGA cable from the TCC connects to the TRM behind the partition wall. Some earlier
configurations have an isolation transformer installed on the bracket which is the power supply
for the TRMs.
4.4.8
Description of handset rails

the handset rail go through the holes in the cover panel. The HHC cable connects to the HHC
receiver unit. The ground cable connects to the bracket on the rear panel.

WARNING 6.12

The covers on the equipment prevent access to high voltage parts, and parts that move. After you

1 
Rotate the gantry to 0°.
2 
Put the front surface of the left and right upper quadrant fascia panels on a clean, flat

the top and bottom.

–
An equal clearance at the bottom and the top of the panels
–
A clearance of 4 mm between the gantry drum ring cover, and the lower quadrant
fascia panel.

support post.

remove the covers, there is a risk of high voltage shock or injury from parts that move. Always

1.1
Document scope
The corrective maintenance manual (CMM) helps service engineers troubleshoot, repair and
maintain the systems, subsystems and components of the linear accelerator. The target audience
is qualified service engineers. These may be engineers employed directly by Elekta, qualified
representatives of Elekta or qualified representatives of Elekta's customers.
The manual provides:
•
A description of the system or sub-system in question.
•
A troubleshooting section to identify the problem areas.
•
A set of detailed procedures used to replace FRUs (field replaceable units).
•
A section on how to return the device to work.
If you find any mistakes in this document, or identify areas for improvement, please raise a CLM
(customer lifecycle management) case and assign it to the relevant queue.

The role of Radiation Therapists, also referred to as Radiotherapists,
Radiation Treatment Technicians or Therapeutic/Therapy radiographers, may

However, their primary roles and obligations are expected to be similar among
different regions and sites.
Note: Radiation Therapists are trained on all aspects of system operation, but
not trained on installation, calibration or service maintenance.
Note: Radiation Therapists who work at the site when the system is installed
will be trained by an Elekta trainer. After the system is introduced, Elekta
authorized trainers, or experienced Radiation Therapists who are already
trained on the equipment, can train Radiation Therapists who are new to
the equipment.

1.4
Glossary of terms
Table 1.3
Glossary of terms
Term
Definition
Autotrack function
The autotrack function automatically moves the diaphragms or
leaves to their prescribed position.
Cal block
The Cal block contains the item and part values that, when
loaded, configure the linear accelerator for a given energy.
Clinical Mode
In Clinical Mode, Clinical Users use the linear accelerator and its
accessories for the radiation therapy treatment that a licensed
medical practitioner prescribes.
Gating
Gating is the procedure by which an external system or manual
task pauses and starts the radiation delivery as a result of
information received relating to the treatment position of the
patient.
Interdigitation
Interdigitation is an overlap of the opposite adjacent leaves of a
multileaf collimator.
Service life
Service life is the length of time that the regular servicing and
repair procedures can keep the machine in operation.
Service Mode
In Service Mode, Service Users do the necessary maintenance
tasks and calibration of the equipment.

2.1
Important safety instructions
It is important to install, operate, maintain, and dispose of the equipment according to the
information in the product documentation, and in compliance with local regulations. For the
safety of the users and the patients, before a user operates or works on the equipment, they
must read, understand, and obey all:
•
Warnings, cautions, instructions, and notes in this document and the related
documents.
•
Safety instructions, emergency procedures, and information in this document and the
related documents.
•
Warnings, cautions, and safety markings on the equipment and the accessories of the
equipment.
If you have local work instructions for the equipment, then Elekta recommends that you include
the warnings, cautions, and notes from this document in your local work instructions.
2.1.1
Conventions for warnings, cautions, and notes
The conventions give information about the class and the level of the risk in the warnings and
cautions, and the content of notes.
WARNING 2.1
A warning is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of fatal or serious
injury, injury, or clinical mistreatment, if you do not obey the instructions.
CAUTION 2.1
A caution is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of damage to the
equipment, data, or the environment, if you do not obey the instructions.
Note:
A note gives more information about a related text.
2.1.2
Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can
keep the equipment safe to operate.
WARNING 2.2
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days
each week of the year. If the equipment is used more frequently than this, the frequency of
the planned maintenance must increase accordingly and the extended life checks must also be
brought forward accordingly.

Safety precautions
2.2.1
Safety precautions for the compatibility of the equipment
WARNING 2.3
Do not use parts, accessories, or other equipment, without approval by Elekta of their
compatibility. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury and damage to the
equipment.
Only operate the equipment with Elekta supplied or approved, compatible equipment or parts.
Accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by or do not have the approval of
Elekta can cause an incorrect treatment delivery. They can also have an effect on the performance
of the electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), which can increase the emissions or decrease the
immunity of the equipment.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of other equipment or parts.
2.2.2
Safety precautions for the electromagnetic compatibility
The design and manufacture of Elekta products is in compliance with applicable EMC standards.
The intended result of the standards is to minimize the risk of electromagnetic interference
by RF devices. The type of device and the distance to the equipment has an effect on the
intensity of the electromagnetic interference. The equipment includes the linear accelerator and
accessories, the control cabinets, the computers in the control room, and equipment from other
manufacturer.

It is necessary to have special precautions for EMC emissions. Elekta recommends that you obey
these precautions when you use RF devices near the equipment.
•
Do not use RF devices unless they are in compliance with international standards for
electromagnetic compatibility, for example, the CE or FCC mark.
•
Do not use a two-way emergency radio in the treatment room or the control room.
Only use an emergency radio if there is an emergency.
•
Do not use cellular telephones, or other devices with cellular modems near the
equipment. The Instructions for Use contains information on the minimum safe
distance of these devices from the equipment.
•
When you use a device that is enabled for wireless operation, it must be a minimum of
10 cm from the equipment.
•
Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID) readers, when activated to do a scan of a RFID
tag, must be a minimum of one meter from the equipment.
Note:
The RFID systems that Elekta supply use lower power levels. You can safely use these RFID systems
when you obey the procedures in the Instructions for Use for the product.
The system must be installed, put into service, and maintained in compliance with the EMC
information in the Instructions for Use.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of parts and equipment.
WARNING 2.4
Do not put portable or mobile radio frequency (RF) communication devices near to the
equipment. The emissions from such RF devices can be more than the EMC standards, and
can have unwanted effects on the equipment operation. If you ignore this warning, the RF
emissions can cause the equipment to have a malfunction. A malfunction can cause fatal injury,
clinical mistreatment, or damage to the equipment.
WARNING 2.5
Do not use accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by Elekta. They can
have an effect on the EMC performance, which can increase EMC emissions or decrease the
immunity to RF interference of the equipment. If you ignore this warning, incorrect radiation
delivery and other malfunctions can occur, which can cause fatal injury or clinical mistreatment.

Safety precaution for the removal of parts from the radiation head
WARNING 2.21
Do not touch the flight tube, bending magnet, or other parts near to them until a check for
induced radioactivity is completed. Excessive exposure to radioactivity is dangerous. If you
ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.
After the operation of the linear accelerator at high energy, the parts in the radiation head
can become radioactive and a radiation hazard. Before you do work on, or remove parts
from the radiation head, use a calibrated radiation detector to measure the level of induced
radioactivity. Use the applicable safety procedures when you remove radioactive parts and
material. The maximum dose rate for the safe removal of radioactive parts and material is 50
µSv/hr (microsievert per hour). Do not remove the radioactive parts and material from the
treatment room before they are correctly prepared for safe removal.

decommissioning
WARNING 2.22
Do not do work, or make modifications to the equipment without the correct training and
authority. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury, clinical mistreatment, and
damage to the equipment.
Only do work on, or make modifications to, the equipment if you are an Elekta approved
person with the applicable authority. Such work must use best practice and obey the laws and
regulations in the jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed.
Modifications or work that does not have approval by Elekta, and is not done by an Elekta
approved person with the correct authority, can cause:
•
Fatal injury
•
Incorrect radiation delivery
•
Malfunction of the equipment
•
Damage to the equipment
•
The warranty to be canceled.

The safety precautions for work in areas of induced radioactivity are the precautions to prevent
an excessive exposure to, and serious injury from, induced radioactivity.
When you operate or do work on the equipment, Elekta recommends that you use the applicable
radiation protection functions, devices, systems, procedures, and accessories. Always obey
the applicable laws and regulations for induced radioactivity for the jurisdiction in which the
equipment is installed.
The safety precautions are applicable to:
•
Maintenance, modifications, and decommissioning
•
Measurement of the induced radioactivity
•
Removal and movement of parts with induced radioactivity.

2.2.16.1
Safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity are the necessary safety
precautions to know to prevent excessive exposure to radioactivity, which can cause serious
injury or damage to the environment.
Always use two radiation detectors to measure the level of induced radioactivity. Only use
radiation detectors that have an applicable calibration certificate. The period of time since the
last calibration date must be less than 12 months. Do not use the radiation detectors if the period
of time since the last calibration date is more than 12 months.
WARNING 2.23
Do not move radioactive material (by air, sea, or land) unless you obey the applicable laws and
regulations for induced radioactivity and disposal of radioactive material of the jurisdictions
through which the movement occurs. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury
and damage to the environment.
2.2.16.2
Safety precautions for handling parts with induced radioactivity
The handling of parts with induced radioactivity must comply with the laws and regulations of
the jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed. The safe levels of radiation applicable in the
UK do not apply in all jurisdictions. The permitted level of radioactivity must always be as low as
reasonably achievable (ALARA). This level may vary depending on local rules, therefore the safe
working levels from the applicable local rules must be considered as the acceptable working limit.
If there are no safe levels available for a jurisdiction, use the UK value as a guideline, which is a
maximum of 150 cps at the surface for a maximum duration of 72 minutes. The following table
shows the conversion from this value to other units.

4.1
Description of the dosimetry system
The dosimetry system of the linear accelerator has dual circuits (see Figure 4.1) which control and
monitor the:
•
Radiation dose
•
Ambient temperature and atmospheric pressure.

Figure 4.1
Block diagram of the dosimetry system
During the treatment, the dual circuits measure these parameters and send signals to the control
processor of the TCS. The control processor compares the two signals to make sure that the
indications are in the permitted limits.
If a fault or error occurs, the dosimetry system has a number of safety interlocks. The interlocks
operate to prevent the delivery of radiation.
Refer to the dosimetry system diagrams in the Elekta Medical Linear Accelerator System Diagrams
manual for more information.
4.2
Description of dose monitoring and control
An ionization chamber (ion chamber), which is in the path of the radiation beam, senses the
radiation. The ion chamber monitors the radiation dose and gives servo control of the electron
beam in the linear accelerator waveguide. The ion chamber has a number of plates.
•
Two plates send the dose monitoring signals to the two dosimetry channels (DOS-A
and DOS-B).
•
A third set of plates send the dose monitoring signals to the TCS for the servo control
of the energy and symmetry.
The radiation and the output currents from the ion chamber are pulse currents. The pulses are
put together on two dosimetry PCBs. The TCS reads the pulse count during treatment when the
pulses are at a calibrated threshold. A threshold is set for each energy level because the output of
the ion chamber does not increase linearly as the energy increases.
Before a treatment starts, the TCS supplies the dosimetry PCBs with an energy calibration value.
The calibration value is defined as 1/64 of a monitor unit (MU) and is known as the dose_ref.
For each 64 counts, the dosimetry PCBs send a 1 MU signal to the TCS. The TCS sends an
acknowledged signal to the dosimetry PCBs each time it receives a 1 MU signal.

4.2.1
Description of single and multiple dose treatments
A patient treatment can have one dose, or multiple doses, of radiation. For multiple dose
treatments, each segment of the prescription can have different qualities. For example, a
segment can be delivered at a different energy, or from a different gantry angle. Therefore each
dosimetry PCB has two counters that measure the delivered dose:
•
The Segment dose counter is loaded with the segment dose value at the start of a
beam (dose period). The segment dose counter records the delivered dose in each
segment of a multiple dose treatment.
•
The Total dose counter is loaded with the total dose value at the start of the
treatment. The total dose counter records the total dose for a treatment.
The two dosimetry PCBs record the total dose and the segment dose for each treatment. The TCS
continuously monitors and measures the pulse counts on the PCBs.
When the segment dose counter is at zero, the dosimetry PCB sends a segment dose complete
signal to the TCS. The TCS sends a signal which causes the radiation to pause until the next
segment is loaded. After the total dose is delivered, the TCS stops the radiation. At the end of a
treatment, the total dose will equal the sum of the segment doses.
4.3
Description of the HT and PRF interlocks
The dosimetry PCBs have a number of internal circuits that monitor the dose rate, voltages and
system bus activity. The dosimetry PCBs also monitor the external condition of the:
•
-320 V voltage
•
Ion chamber leakage current
•
1 MU handshake with the TCS.
The dosimetry PCB has four monitor circuits that remove power to the HT relay if they operate.
During treatment, the dosimetry PCB controls the PRF interlock circuit through a SEGMENT DOSE
COMPLETE signal.

4.4
Description of the backup dose count
The dosimetry system has an LCD module installed in the TCC. The LCD module counts the 1 MU
pulses from the DOS-A PCB independently. An LCD display shows the measured dose count value.
The LCD module has battery backup. Therefore if a mains power supply failure occurs, the LCD
module records the backup dose count. The LCD display continues to show this value. Software
item i448 also records the backup dose count.
Refer to the Corrective Maintenance Manual - Technical Reference for the linear accelerator for
more information about the software items.

4.5
Description of the temperature and pressure monitor
circuits of the dosimetry system
The dual temperature and pressure circuits monitor the temperature at the BLD and the local
atmospheric pressure. The sensors are installed as follows:
•
The pressure sensors are installed on the DPT and SIB PCBs.
•
The two temperature sensors are installed on one of the arms to which the ion
chamber attaches in the collimator assembly.
The system sends the temperature and pressure data to the TCS through the SCC and AI12 PCBs.
Treatment is not permitted if there is a difference between the dual circuits. If there is a drift in
temperature or pressure during treatment, radiation stops. The temperature and pressure values
correct the dose_ref levels for changes in ambient atmospheric conditions.
4.6
Description of the -320 V PSU system
An auxiliary PSU in the RHCA (Area 12) supplies a -320 V polarized voltage to the ion chamber.
A coaxial cable supplies the polarized voltage from the auxiliary PSU to the ion chamber. The
dosimetry PCBs continuously monitor the polarized voltage, and an interlock terminates the
delivery of treatment if the polarized voltage is more than or less than the defined limits.
4.7
Description of the dosimetry software control
The functions of the dose integrator, are on the second dosimetry PCB for safety. The TCS
also keeps a total of delivered MU and calculates the dose rate. The software controls the
synchronization of the dose measurements. If the dose measurements are not in synchronization,
the radiation stops.
The PLAs on the dosimetry PCBs hold some of the dosimetry control program. This is known as
the control firmware. The firmware gives three basic conditions for the dosimetry PCBs:
•
Idle
•
Wait Acknowledge
•
Radiation Off.
A 1 MU pulse or a software reset gives the condition of the PCB. At the end of a successful
treatment, the dosimetry PCBs are in the Radiation Off condition.
The TCS reads each counter load operation as it completes, to make sure that the operation was
successful. When the command sequence is completed, before the start of the treatment, the
software examines the status of the dosimetry PCBs.
During treatment, the software monitors the operation of the two dosimetry PCBs, and does a
check of the values that follow:
•
Total dose count
•
Segment dose counter
•
Calibration monitor
•
Status bits.
•
The software calculates the timing and calibration differences between the two PCBs.
Treatment stops if the PCB values are different by more than a preset quantity.

4.7.4
Description of the time critical software of the dosimetry system
During treatment, some parts of the control software send signals to the TCS as they occur. The
TCS uses these signals to control the software operations.
An integrator makes the 1 MU pulses which decreases the count of the total dose counter. The
system also sends these pulses through status bit 0, as COUNT pulses, to the TCS. This updates
the value displayed on the software dose counter.
Each 1 MU pulse sets the PCB firmware condition from IDLE to WAIT ACKNOWLEDGE. It goes
back to the IDLE condition when it receives a COUNT ACKNOWLEDGED signal (WR17H) from the
TCS. If a second 1 MU pulse occurs before the COUNT ACKNOWLEDGED signal, the firmware
changes the condition to TREATMENT TERMINATE. This gives the error signal COUNT NOT
ACKNOWLEDGED.
During treatment, the TCS reads the segment dose counter to do a check of the dose rate. The
dose rate value goes to the TCS for display during treatment.

4.8.2.1
Operation of system dose measurement
The dosimetry PCB changes the current from the ion chamber to a voltage and then a digital
value. The PCB reads a sample of the current of a typical radiation pulse approximately 200 times.
This gives an input with a very large, linear, dynamic range.
The radiation is in pulses as is the current from the ion chamber. The digital signal processor (DSP)
uses this to accurately calculate the value of the input when there is no radiation. The DSP then
subtracts this background value from the signal. This adjusts for electronic offsets and leakage
current. If the system increases to the adjustment limit, a status bit is set to prevent the operation
of the linear accelerator. You can view the status on the Dosimetry service page of the TCS.
With electronic offset leakage adjustment, only signals from the radiation pulse go through the
input step. The values from the digital input collect until they increase to the calibration value of
1/64 MU.
When the system increases to the calibration value, the DSP decreases the segment and the
beam counters and sets the input accumulator to a value of zero. The control system does not
read the lower bits of the beam counter. This keeps the current 1 MU resolution. Because the
same signals are used to decrease the two counters, the counter keeps the count as multiple
segments are delivered.
4.8.2.2
Operation of the FPGA control
The dosimetry PCB has a field programmable gate array (FPGA) IC19. This controls the DOS PCB
and also gives the dose measurement. At power up a PROM (IC26) programs the FPGA. When the
program load is successful, LED1 comes on and a CONFIG_DONE signal is applied to the HT relay
output.
The FPGA interfaces with the system bus to send the dose measurements and receive dose
controls. The FPGA also interfaces with all the DOS PCB operations. It has a 20 MHz clock and has
a watchdog timer on the 3.3 V supply rail.
The FPGA also has a check circuit. This looks at the dose count output and makes sure that the
FPGA measures and acknowledges that the dose is the equivalent to the received dose.
The FPGA has a program interface (PL7) and a standard JTAG test connector (PL6).
4.8.2.3
Operation of the DOS PCB receiver
The dose signal from the ion chamber is a number of pulses of approximately 100 µs in width.
On the DOS-A PCB the signal is terminated with a 150 kW resistor. On the DOS-B PCB the signal is
terminated with a 50 kW resistor in parallel with a 1 nF capacitor. This gives an equivalent pulse
height and shape for the two channels.
IC9 is an amplifier which increases and inverts the terminated signal. The signal is input to an
analog-to-digital converter (ADC) IC27. During the change of the signal, IC5 and IC14 add a DC
offset. This has three functions:

The field programmable gate array (FPGA) has a dose integrator

Segment dose
measurement
At the start of a beam (dose period), the segment dose counter is
loaded with a segment dose value. For each count from the dose
integrator the counter decreases. When the count value decreases
to 0, the treatment is terminated until the next segment. The output
of the segment dose counter, signal SEGMENT_DOS_COMPLETE, is
set high (logic 1).
Total dose measurement
At the start of a treatment, the total dose counter is loaded with
a total dose value. The counter is then decreased by one for each
count from the dose integrator. Therefore it is necessary to have 64
segment counts before the value of the total dose counter changes
by one.
The total dose counter gives each of the 64 counts as a MU
output. At this point the output of the total dose counter, signal
SEG_DOSE_COUNT, is set low (logic 0).

Description of the dose pulse transmitter PCB
The dosimetry system has one DPT PCB that monitors the dose information directly from the
DOS-A PCB in the RHCA. The DPT PCB communicates with the iViewGT™ control cabinet through
an RS232 or RS422 serial link. The DPT PCB is installed in the RHCA.
The DPT PCB sends signals to and receives signals from the iViewGT™ control cabinet (see Figure
4.11). The primary functions of the DPT PCB are:
•
Send and receive the dose information to and from the iViewGT™ control cabinet.
•
Sense when the dose rate increases to a preset limit, to transmit a start byte.
•
Sense when the dose increases to a preset limit, to transmit a stop byte.
•
Sense when the dose rate decreases to a fixed lower limit, to transmit a beam end
byte.
•
Send a status byte if the PCB receives a diagnostics code from the iViewGT™ control
cabinet.
•
Supply a self-test sequence if the PCB receives a self-test command from the iViewGT™
control cabinet.
•
Measure and transmit the atmospheric pressure to the TCS.

A quad dual-in-line switch (SW1) on the PCB lets you configure the baud

The PROM (IC8) holds the configuration data of the PLD. The PROM

Input amplifiers
The SIB PCB has six input plate signals:
•
Two from the 2T plates of the ion chamber
•
Two from the 2R plates of the ion chamber
•
One from the inner hump plate, which monitors the level of
the energy in the center of the chamber
•
One from the outer hump plate which monitors the level of
the energy level in the outer parts of the chamber.
The plate signals are very high impedance current sources which give
tear-drop shape current pulses of approximately 150 µs. An amplifier
receives each input plate signal. The amplifier changes the current
source into a low impedance voltage.
Digitizers
Each of the low impedance voltages from the input amplifiers is
digitized to supply a 12-bit digital word. The rate is controlled at 1 µs by
the CLOCK output from the oscillator.
Oscillator
Oscillator OSC1 is a 20 MHz CMOS clock that times the SIB functions.
Error correction
The error correction part of the FPGA receives the six digital data
streams (6 × 20 Mbits/second). The FPGA has a function that gives
an accurate sum of the input plate signals during each pulse. DC offset
errors, from a number of sources, have an effect on each plate signal.
Rectifier Description
The PPG PCB sends a BLANK synchronization signal to the SIB PCB as
a 1.25 MHz carrier that continues for 220 µs in all energy pulses. The
energy pulse operates through a range of 400 Hz (each 2.5 ms) to 6 Hz
(each 166 ms). The BLANK pulse starts to time the FPGA accumulations.
Digital-to-analog
converter
The digital data from the FPGA is sent in sequence to six of 12 DACs in
one IC (IC11). These give a current output in scale with the plate charge
digital word.
FPGA
The outputs from the DACs are supplied to the FPGA and then put on
the system bus (D0 to D16) through buffers.
Gun amplifiers
The X-ray gun servo system keeps the correct machine energy. The gun
amplifiers make small adjustments to the nominal gun current if there
are changes in magnetron power and frequency.
The X-ray flattening filter gives a flat X-ray field at the correct energy
setting. If the energy changes because of offsets or other changes in the
system, the X-ray field cannot stay flat:

4.8.5
Description of the liquid crystal displays and printed circuit board
The LCD PCB displays the dose count and the control and communication status of the dosimetry
system. A 4-digit LCD displays the dose count. Six LEDs show the status of the control and
communications system.
The LCD PCB is installed on the front panel of the TCC (Area 92). The user can easily see the LCD
and the LEDs.
The LCD PCB has a battery which supplies power to the dose count display if the primary
electrical supply goes off. The power failure circuit charges the battery.
The LCD PCB receives the dose information as one pulse for each MU. A 16-bit counter reads and
changes the count to operate four 7-segment displays. If there is a power failure, the last count
is latched into the converter. Before the display can be updated, it is necessary to reset the the
latch. The LCD PCB sends status signals to the TCS if the battery and oscillator are serviceable, and
the dose count is latched. The TCS can read the dose count in two bytes in time.
A 70 Hz waveform modulates the drive to the displays.
The LCD PCB is connected to the LIB.
The control sequence that the LCD PCB does at the start of each treatment is as follows:
•
The TCS reads and does a check of the LCD counter against the dose for the previous
treatment.
•
The BATTERY TEST signal is set low. After 80 ms the TCS does a check of the BATTERY
OK (board status) signal to make sure that it is low.
•
The TCS does a check of the status to make sure that the OSCILLATOR OK and the
COUNT LATCHED signals are set high.
•
The RESET DOSE READOUT signal is set low. After 5 ms, the TCS checks to make sure
that the OSCILLATOR OK is high and the COUNT LATCHED signal is low.
•
The TCS does a check of the dose counter to make sure that it is at a value of zero.

Description of the temperature and pressure subsystem
Refer to the Elekta Medical Linear Accelerator System Diagrams for more information.
The temperature and pressure subsystem has dual circuits that measure the local atmospheric
pressure and temperature at the Beam Limiting Device (see Figure 4.14). Pressure and
temperature sensors give the data inputs for the temperature and pressure subsystem. A
pressure sensor on each of the DPT and SIB PCBs give the atmospheric pressure input. Two
temperature sensors on the collimator assembly give the temperature inputs.

The SCC-A and SCC-B PCBs supply a 10 V reference voltage to the two temperature sensors.
The sensors decrease the voltage to 0 V through resistors on the SIB PCB and the DPT PCB. The
temperature signals go through the SCC and AI12 PCBs to software items i224 and i226.
The DPT and SIB PCBs energize the pressure sensors. The pressure signals go through the SCC/
AI12 PCBs and are applied to software items i558 and i559.
The TCS receives the temperature and pressure data through the SCC and AI12 PCB pairs.
Treatment is not permitted if there is a difference between the temperature or pressure circuits.
During treatment, the delivery of radiation stops if there is a drift in the temperature or pressure
circuit.

In Clinical mode, a dosimetry system error shows as a low dose (i665 Low Dose Rate), dose

•
A movement in the dosimetry output
•
Dosimetry channel leakage
•
Ion chamber signals that are not stable
•
Incorrect operation of the servo system

No ion chamber signal.

6.1
Replacing the DOS-A and DOS-B PCBs
WARNING 6.1
Record the part numbers of the replacement parts when you replace a part. Do the applicable
test, set up, and calibration procedures for the replacement parts before clinical operation. If
you ignore this warning, you can cause clinical mistreatment.
WARNING 6.2
Do not do work on the linear accelerator before you isolate the electrical supply to the work
area at the interface cabinet. You can get a high voltage electric shock. If you ignore this
warning, you can cause fatal injury.
CAUTION 6.1
Do not touch the PCBs and other electronic parts unless you wear a grounded antistatic wrist
strap. If you ignore this caution, you can cause damage to the equipment.
1 
Disconnect the electrical supply to the RHCA.
2 
At the RHCA (AREA 12), remove the RF EMC screen that gives the control area protection.
3 
Remove the screws and nuts that attach the bar, and remove the bar.
4 
Put on an antistatic wrist strap.

7.7
Calibrating the dose rate monitor
7.7.1
Calibrating the low dose rate monitor
The linear accelerator has a dose interlock that collects differences between the actual dose rate
and the selected dose rate. The actual dose rate must be in a defined range of the selected dose
rate or the related dose rate interlock stops the beam. Therefore, the accurate setting of the
nominal dose rate for each energy is very important.
The low dose rate monitor records the actual dose rate delivered. The stability timer, Item 665
Part 135 (the units are in 125 ms), lets the dose rate become stable before the low dose rate
monitor starts to record. You can adjust this function for a slow beam start.
Note:
For Fast Tuning Magnetrons, the limit of the stability timer is 2.5 seconds (20 units). For Non-Fast
Tuning Magnetrons, the limit of the stability timer is 5.0 seconds (40 units).
If the actual dose rate is less than 75% of the selected dose rate, the system records the
difference. If the difference is 10 MU or more, the beam stops. This can occur on a linear
accelerator with a slow start. If a slow start occurs, the low dose rate monitor can record before it
increases to the selected dose.
Note:
When a new beam loads, the difference is set to zero.

1.1
Important safety instructions
It is important to install, operate, maintain, and dispose of the equipment according to the
information in the product documentation, and in compliance with local regulations. For the
safety of the users and the patients, before a user operates or works on the equipment, they
must read, understand, and obey all:
•
Warnings, cautions, instructions, and notes in this document and the related
documents.
•
Safety instructions, emergency procedures, and information in this document and the
related documents.
•
Warnings, cautions, and safety markings on the equipment and the accessories of the
equipment.
If you have local work instructions for the equipment, then Elekta recommends that you include
the warnings, cautions, and notes from this document in your local work instructions.
1.1.1
Conventions for warnings, cautions, and notes
The conventions give information about the class and the level of the risk in the warnings and
cautions, and the content of notes.
WARNING 1.1
A warning is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of fatal or serious
injury, injury, or clinical mistreatment, if you do not obey the instructions.
CAUTION 1.1
A caution is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of damage to the
equipment, data, or the environment, if you do not obey the instructions.
Note:
A note gives more information about a related text.
1.1.2
Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can
keep the equipment safe to operate.
WARNING 1.2
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each
week of the year. If the equipment is used more frequently than this, the frequency of the
planned maintenance must increase accordingly and the extended life checks must also be
brought forward accordingly.

1.2.1
Safety precautions for the compatibility of the equipment
WARNING 1.3
Do not use parts, accessories, or other equipment, without approval by Elekta of their
compatibility. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury and damage to the
equipment.
Only operate the equipment with Elekta supplied or approved, compatible equipment or parts.

immunity of the equipment.

1.2.2

The design and manufacture of Elekta products is in compliance with applicable EMC standards.
The intended result of the standards is to minimize the risk of electromagnetic interference by RF
devices. The type of device and the distance to the equipment has an effect on the intensity of
the electromagnetic interference. The equipment includes the linear accelerator and accessories,
the control cabinets, the computers in the control room, and equipment from other
manufacturer.

It is necessary to have special precautions for EMC emissions. Elekta recommends that you obey
these precautions when you use RF devices near the equipment.
•
Do not use RF devices unless they are in compliance with international standards for
electromagnetic compatibility, for example, the CE or FCC mark.
•
Do not use a two-way emergency radio in the treatment room or the control room.
Only use an emergency radio if there is an emergency.
•
Do not use cellular telephones, or other devices with cellular modems near the
equipment. The Instructions for Use contains information on the minimum safe
distance of these devices from the equipment.
•
When you use a device that is enabled for wireless operation, it must be a minimum of
10 cm from the equipment.
•
Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID) readers, when activated to do a scan of a RFID
tag, must be a minimum of one meter from the equipment.
Note:
The RFID systems that Elekta supply use lower power levels. You can safely use these RFID systems
when you obey the procedures in the Instructions for Use for the product.
The system must be installed, put into service, and maintained in compliance with the EMC
information in the Instructions for Use.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of parts and equipment.
WARNING 1.4
Do not put portable or mobile radio frequency (RF) communication devices near to the
equipment. The emissions from such RF devices can be more than the EMC standards, and can
have unwanted effects on the equipment operation. If you ignore this warning, the RF
emissions can cause the equipment to have a malfunction. A malfunction can cause fatal injury,
clinical mistreatment, or damage to the equipment.
WARNING 1.5
Do not use accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by Elekta. They can have
an effect on the EMC performance, which can increase EMC emissions or decrease the
immunity to RF interference of the equipment. If you ignore this warning, incorrect radiation
delivery and other malfunctions can occur, which can cause fatal injury or clinical mistreatment.

If there is damage to the covers or screen of the BLD, switch off the linear accelerator and contact
the Elekta representative.

Safety precautions for work with high temperatures on the BLD

Do not touch the connector found in the accessory ring on the BLD. If you ignore this warning,
you can cause injury.

1.2.14
Safety precaution for the removal of parts from the radiation head
WARNING 1.21
Do not touch the flight tube, bending magnet, or other parts near to them until a check for
induced radioactivity is completed. Excessive exposure to radioactivity is dangerous. If you
ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.
After the operation of the linear accelerator at high energy, the parts in the radiation head can
become radioactive and a radiation hazard. Before you do work on, or remove parts from the
radiation head, use a calibrated radiation detector to measure the level of induced radioactivity.
Use the applicable safety procedures when you remove radioactive parts and material. The
maximum dose rate for the safe removal of radioactive parts and material is 50 µSv/hr
(microsievert per hour). Do not remove the radioactive parts and material from the treatment
room before they are correctly prepared for safe removal.
1.2.15
Safety precautions for maintenance, modification, and
decommissioning
WARNING 1.22
Do not do work, or make modifications to the equipment without the correct training and
authority. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury, clinical mistreatment, and
damage to the equipment.
Only do work on, or make modifications to, the equipment if you are an Elekta approved person
with the applicable authority. Such work must use best practice and obey the laws and
regulations in the jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed.
Modifications or work that does not have approval by Elekta, and is not done by an Elekta
approved person with the correct authority, can cause:
•
Fatal injury
•
Incorrect radiation delivery
•
Malfunction of the equipment
•
Damage to the equipment
•
The warranty to be canceled.
1.2.16
Safety precautions for work in areas of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for work in areas of induced radioactivity are the precautions to prevent
an excessive exposure to, and serious injury from, induced radioactivity.
When you operate or do work on the equipment, Elekta recommends that you use the applicable
radiation protection functions, devices, systems, procedures, and accessories. Always obey the
applicable laws and regulations for induced radioactivity for the jurisdiction in which the
equipment is installed.
The safety precautions are applicable to:
•
Maintenance, modifications, and decommissioning
•
Measurement of the induced radioactivity
•
Removal and movement of parts with induced radioactivity.

1.2.16.1
Safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity are the necessary safety
precautions to know to prevent excessive exposure to radioactivity, which can cause serious
injury or damage to the environment.
Always use two radiation detectors to measure the level of induced radioactivity. Only use
radiation detectors that have an applicable calibration certificate. The period of time since the
last calibration date must be less than 12 months. Do not use the radiation detectors if the period
of time since the last calibration date is more than 12 months.
WARNING 1.23
Do not move radioactive material (by air, sea, or land) unless you obey the applicable laws and
regulations for induced radioactivity and disposal of radioactive material of the jurisdictions
through which the movement occurs. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury
and damage to the environment.
1.2.16.2
Safety precautions for handling parts with induced radioactivity
The handling of parts with induced radioactivity must comply with the laws and regulations of the
jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed. The safe levels of radiation applicable in the UK
do not apply in all jurisdictions. The permitted level of radioactivity must always be as low as
reasonably achievable (ALARA). This level may vary depending on local rules, therefore the safe
working levels from the applicable local rules must be considered as the acceptable working limit.
If there are no safe levels available for a jurisdiction, use the UK value as a guideline, which is a
maximum of 150 cps at the surface for a maximum duration of 72 minutes. The following table
shows the conversion from this value to other units.

2.1.3
Disposal of the equipment
End of life (EOL) disposal is the procedure to disassemble, remove, and discard the equipment, in
full or in parts, to a condition where it is not possible to operate the equipment for its intended
use.
Only a Qualified Expert (QE) and an approved facility with an applicable license, may remove and
discard the equipment and recycle the material.
A full description of disposal requirements is detailed in a separate document Product Disposal
Information. This document is available on request from Elekta.
The customer owns the data on the storage media. If there are any data storage media such as
HDDs, remove them from the device and hand them to the customer for disposal. If the customer
entrusts the disposal team to dispose of the data, the data must be destroyed in accordance with
relevant cybersecurity regulations.

2.3.1
Precautions for work with electrostatic discharge sensitive devices
The precautions to prevent an electrostatic discharge (ESD) during work with ESD sensitive
devices.
CAUTION 2.1
Do not touch the PCBs and other electronic parts unless you wear a grounded antistatic wrist
strap. If you ignore this caution, you can cause damage to the equipment.
CAUTION 2.2
Do not touch the parts identified with the ESD caution label. Always obey the ESD precautions
during work on these parts. If you ignore this caution, you can cause damage to the equipment.
Semiconductor devices, integrated circuits, and the parts that contain them, are ESD sensitive
devices. These devices are electrostatic discharge sensitive (ESDS) devices. ESD can cause damage
to these devices and cause them to have a malfunction immediately or some time after the
electrostatic discharge. To prevent the ESD damage to these devices, always wear a grounded
antistatic wrist strap, and obey the applicable ESD precautions and procedures.
Elekta recommends that all users receive the training about ESD. The training must include the
ESD caution label and these ESD precautions.

3.1
Document scope
The corrective maintenance manual (CMM) helps service engineers troubleshoot, repair and
maintain the systems, subsystems and components of the linear accelerator. The target audience
is qualified service engineers. These may be engineers employed directly by Elekta, qualified
representatives of Elekta or qualified representatives of Elekta's customers.
The manual provides:
•
A description of the system or sub-system in question.
•
A troubleshooting section to identify the problem areas.
•
A set of detailed procedures used to replace FRUs (field replaceable units).
•
A section on how to return the device to work.
If you find any mistakes in this document, or identify areas for improvement, please raise a CLM
(customer lifecycle management) case and assign it to the relevant queue.

4.1
Overview of the HT and RF systems
This is an overview of the HT and RF systems that the linear accelerator uses to make the radiation
beam.
The primary function of a linear accelerator is to make a radiation beam of high-energy electrons
or X-rays (photons). The high tension (HT) and radio frequency (RF) systems of the linear
accelerators operate together to make the radiation beam.
The HT system makes stable, high-voltage pulses. In the RF system, the HT pulses make the
traveling RF wave which moves the electrons through a waveguide and into the beam limiting
device (BLD).
The high-voltage pulses from the HT system, energize a modulator which makes the traveling RF
wave. A magnetron in the modulator supplies a RF power input to the waveguide and therefore
makes the traveling RF wave. The HT pulses energize an electron gun which puts electrons into
the waveguide where they are moved by the RF wave. The beam physics system controls the
speed increase and the path of the electron beam.
If there are changes in the current supply to the magnetron changes, it causes the frequency and
amplitude of the RF to become less stable. The magnetron only uses a pulse for micro-seconds.
The modulator develops the high-voltage pulse.
The RF system has two basic configurations:
•
RF feedback - linear accelerators with higher energies of 20 MeV/MV use the
remaining RF energy as feedback to increase the energy in the waveguide (see Figure
4.1).
•
Without RF feedback - linear accelerators with a maximum energy of 18 MeV/MV
supply the remaining RF energy directly to the RF load (see Figure 4.2).

4.1.2
Description of the charge cycle of the high tension system
This is a description of the charge cycle of the HT system.
A switch controls a transformer which gives the storage for the supplied high tension (HT) power.
Darlington pair transistors supply this switch for linear accelerators from 105361 to 151574.
Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistors supply this switch for linear accelerators from 151575.
When the switches are off, the energy held in the charge transformer is transferred to the pulse
forming network (PFN). This stays charged until the thyratron starts.
When the thyratron starts, the energy held in the PFN is discharged through the pulse
transformer. The waveform made is a negative pulse of approximately 3 µs. This pulse goes to the
cathode of the magnetron and the cathode of the electron gun. This causes the emissions of
electrons in the two devices immediately.
When the linear accelerator operates in high energy mode, two charge cycles occur before the
PFN is discharged. The two charges make a total charge of approximately 40 joules.
4.1.3
Description of the magnetron RF power supply
This is a description of how the magneton supplies the RF power for the digital accelerator.
The magnetron is installed in area 30 and makes the radio frequency (RF) power. The magnetron
has a cathode which is installed in the center of an anode block. The anode block has a number of
resonant cavities and is connected to ground (earth). An electromagnet is around the anode and
cathode.
The high tension (HT) system increases the temperature of the cathode and also supplies a pulse
to the cathode which causes the emission of electrons. The voltage between the anode and the
cathode causes a large electric field. This electric field increases the speed of the electrons in the
direction of the anode. This makes an “electron cloud”, which increases and oscillates in the
anode at the resonant frequency of the magnetron, which aligns to that of the waveguide system.
The effect of the resonant cavities of the anode change the energy of the accelerating electrons
to RF energy. A slot in the anode supplies the RF power from the magnetron to the waveguide
system.
An automatic frequency control (AFC) system keeps the accurate control of the resonant
frequency of the magnetron. It does this by the adjustment of the dimensions of the cavities. This
is known as magnetron tuning.
The small adjustment of the current to the magnetron magnet controls the intensity of the
magnetic field around the magnetron.
The power supply that increases the temperature of the cathode, has a small adjustment to keep
the cathode at the correct temperature. This stops the temperature increase that can occur when
some of the electrons go back to the cathode.
4.1.3.1
Description of automatic frequency control
This is a description of the AFC system which tunes the magnetron frequency.
The AFC system is a RF phase error detector that tunes the resonant frequency of the magnetron.
The AFC system compares the phase of the source RF with a RF sample from the middle of the
waveguide. To compare the two phases, the AFC system reads sample from the middle of the
waveguide after approximately 350 ns. Therefore, if the temperature changes in the magnetron
and the waveguide, the phase of the RF waves stays constant.

4.1.4
Description of the electron gun - electron generation
This is a description of the electron gun.
The source of electrons is the electron gun. The cathode releases the electrons when it gets a
pulse from the HT system.
The anode of the electron gun makes the electrons focus into a small beam. The electrons then
go through a hole in the anode into the accelerating waveguide.
The filament of the cathode has a heater. Therefore a small adjustment of the power supply to
the filament heater controls the amplitude of the electron gun output (the beam current).
4.1.5
Description of the particle acceleration
This is a description of the particle acceleration of the digital accelerator.
The waveguide increases the velocity of the electrons from their input energy of 38 kV to 52 kV to
their last energy of 4 MeV to 25 MeV.
Electron energy comes from the electromagnetic fields caused as RF waves in the linear
accelerator. The electrons travel with the RF waves, and they acquire energy continuously from
the axial electric field part of the waves.
4.1.6
Description of the RF feedback system
This is a description of the RF feedback system which maximizes the energy supply to the
waveguide in high power linear accelerators.
The current of the electron beam changes as the energy that is necessary changes. In the Electron
mode, the current is in mA. The X-ray mode has higher currents. Therefore, in X-ray mode, a small
quantity of RF power stays in the waves at the waveguide output. In Electron mode, a large
quantity of RF power stays in the waves at the waveguide output.
In high power machines, the RF system has a feedback system that stays at the waveguide output
again. The directional coupler collects the remaining RF power together and applies it near the
input of the waveguide system. This supply mixes with the RF input to the magnetron which
increases the power flux into the linear accelerator.
4.1.6.1
Description of the remaining RF phase control
This is a description of the remaining RF phase control.
A high power phase (HP) shifter, in the feedback waveguide loop, sets the correct phase of the
remaining RF power to be mixed. The correct frequency of the magnetron output and the correct
setting of the phase shifter are set automatically in software when the mode of operation is
selected. In low power machines, the RF load absorbs the unwanted RF power.
4.1.7
Description of the gas and vacuum separation
This is a description of the gas and vacuum separation.
The rectangular waveguide system (which includes the isolator, the directional coupler, and the
phase shifter) is filled with dielectric gas (SF6) at low pressure (0.8 bar). This is isolated from the
high vacuum accelerator waveguide by two waveguide windows in the input and the output
rectangular waveguide supplies.

4.1.8
Description of the electric field mode transformation
This is a description of the electric field mode transformation.
The input mode transformer and the output mode transformer are side wall couplers that
connect the rectangular waveguide to the waveguide.
The transformers let the full flow of RF power with negligible reflection. The RF field is changed
from transverse electric (TE) to axial electric at the input, and the other way around at the output.
The electric and magnetic fields are at right angles to each other therefore, magnetically, the
change is from axial magnetic at the input to transverse magnetic (TM) at the output.
4.1.9
Description of the high energy beams
This is a description of the high energy beams.
The selection of a high energy treatment decreases the pulse repetition frequency (PRF) by half.
The charge cycle continues at the same rate, therefore in high energy mode, there are two charge
cycles for each discharge cycle. This increases the PFN voltage from 14 kV to 19 kV.
4.1.10
Description of the protection against reverse voltage
This is a description of the protection against reverse voltage.
If the discharge cycle does not agree, this causes an opposite voltage across the pulse forming
network (PFN). A diode and a number of resistors send the opposite voltage to earth. A voltage is
developed across the last resistor in the array, and this voltage supplied to a diode pump. A
comparator then compares the pump voltage to a level set by the comparator. When the
comparator senses six pulses in sequence, it will release.
The output from the comparator prevent the charge enable signals and stop the charge of the
PFN. The inhibit is for 1.5 seconds and is known as the reverse diode overload.
4.1.11
Description of the HT PSU
This is a description of the HT PSU which supplies power to the RF system.
The high tension (HT) power supply unit (PSU) is a switched mode type. A software HT drive pulse
controls the power to the radio frequency (RF) system.
The HT PSU has two modes of operation:
Low energy
In the low energy mode, the power supply supplies one pulse
charge of approximately 20 joules to the pulse forming network
(PFN).
High energy
In the high energy mode, the power supply supplies two
charges in sequence of approximately 20 joules. This gives a
total charge of approximately 40 joules.
An analog signal Item 330 controls the level of the energy. This shows the rate of the charge.
The HT PSU operates at the same pulse repetition rate as the magnetron. A pulse of
approximately 2.4 ms starts the charge before the magnetron pulse occurs.
