4.2
Description of the RF system
This is a description of the RF system.
The RF system moves the RF power from the magnetron through the waveguide to the BLD.
The system contains the magnetron, the electron gun, and a waveguide assembly. The waveguide
increases the velocity of the electrons from their input energy to their last energy.
4.2.1
Description of the waveguide assembly
4.2.1.1
Description of the input part of the waveguide
This is a description of the input part of the waveguide of the digital accelerator.
The RF wave from the magnetron goes through a section of rectangular waveguide before it goes
into the accelerating waveguide. The rectangular waveguide section has a RF isolator, which stops
the accumulation of the standing waves. In linear accelerators with RF feedback, the rectangular
section also has a sidewall coupler, which sends part of the RF that is not used, to the moving
wave.
A section of flexible waveguide connects the rectangular section to a RF input window that keeps
the gas filled rectangular waveguide from the evacuated accelerating waveguide.
4.2.1.2
Description of the accelerating waveguide
This is a description of the part of the waveguide that accelerates the electrons.
This part of the waveguide has two sections that are in a cylinder shape. These are connected at
the center. A mode transformer is at each end of the waveguide. Each of the waveguide sections
has a number of tuned resonant cavities. These cavities, together with a strong magnetic field,
adds the necessary velocity to the electrons.
The waveguide is an evacuated vacuum to prevent the blockage or the travel of the electrons by
collisions with the gas molecules. The vacuum is sealed at the two mode transformers.
Water keeps this part of the waveguide cool, therefore the waveguide stays in tune.
4.2.1.3
Description of the feedback section of the rectangular waveguide
This is a description of the feedback section of the rectangular waveguide.
On high energy linear accelerators (with feedback), the remaining RF energy is moved around and
added to the input power. This increases the speed of the waveguide.
4.2.2
Description of the mode transformers
This is description of the mode transformers which align the RF energy in the waveguide with the
electrons that are emitted from the electron gun.
The RF that is input to the accelerating waveguide moves at a velocity that is too high to align
with the electrons from the gun. The input mode transformer changes the Field Mode of the
wave from transverse electric (TE) to transverse magnetic (TM).
At the output end of the accelerating waveguide, the output mode transformer restores the TE
Field Mode.

4.2.3
Description of the RF probes
This is a description of the RF probes which are installed in the accelerating waveguide.
The input RF window has a RF probe that supplies one of two sample signals for the phase error
detector of the automatic frequency control (AFC) system. The center joint of the accelerating
waveguide has a second RF probe that gives the other sample signal to the phase error detector.
4.3
Description of the HT and RF system control
This is a description of the HT and RF system control.
The TCS software and monitor items control the HT and the RF systems.
The HTCA includes the PCBs that follow:
•
Programmable pulse generator (PPG) PCB - which controls the charge of the HT
system, the current for the electron gun filament and the magnetron tuner, RF phase
sample and the AFC system.
•
HT control (HTC) PCB - which controls the quantity of charge that the HT PSU gives to
the PFN. This PCB also has the protection circuit.
•
Thyratron pulser unit - which controls the pulse of the thyratron and therefore the
discharge of the PFN.
•
Magnetron tuner/gun filament (MT/GF) drive interface PCB - which gives the drive
signals from the PPG PCB to the UPD PCBs.
•
HT PSU driver PCBs or HT PSU trigger PCB - which controls the power to the switch
devices.
Note:
HT PSU driver PCBs are used with the Darlington pair transistors (on machine number range from
105361 to 151574) and the new HT PSU trigger PCB is used with IGBTs (on machine numbers
151575 forwards).
•
Universal power drive (UPD) PCBs - these are in two pairs. One pair gives the
magnetron tune solenoid current and the other pair supplies the electron gun filament
current.
•
Programmable PSU - which gives the magnetron filament current.
•
HTCA optical receiver - which gives the isolate signals interchanged between the PCBs
of the HT and RF systems.
•
HT crowbar detector PCB- this gives the protection against fault conditions.
•
Modulator isolation PCB - which conditions PCB signal, LED indication of HT faults, and
monitor test points.
•
HT isolation unit - which gives optical isolation for the protection circuit signals from
the HT crowbar detector PCB and the charging transformer.
To give the control of the HT and RF systems, the TCS sends a large number of control items to the
systems, and receives many monitor items. The TCS monitors and controls:
•
HT charge
•
Magnetron magnet current
•
Magnetron tuning and AFC
•
Magnetron filament current
•
Electron gun filament current

4.5
System description of the HT system
4.5.1
Overview of the HT system
This is a overview of the HT system of the digital accelerator.
The high tension (HT) system changes the three-phase primary electrical supply into high power
pulses that operate the magnetron and the electron gun in the radio frequency (RF) system.
The HT system has three primary parts, which are the:
•
HTCA
•
HT PSU
•
Modulator assembly.
The high tension control area (HTCA) contains the PCBs that the treatment control system (TCS)
uses to control the HT system. Signals from the HTCA to the TCS show the necessary adjustments.
The signals also show when it is necessary to shut down the system if there is a malfunction.
The HT PSU contains the:
•
Primary input filter and rectifier
•
Switch devices and their driver PCBs
•
Charging transformer
•
Crowbar detector PCB.
In linear accelerators that use the Darlington pairs, each of the two transistors has a driver PCB. In
linear accelerators that use the Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistors, one trigger PCB operates the
two Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistors.
The modulator assembly contains the:
•
Thyratron
•
Pulse transformer
•
PFN
•
Magnetron
•
Other parts of the HT and RF systems.

4.5.2
Operation of the HT system
This is a description of the operation of the HT system.
The high tension (HT) power supply unit (PSU) is the source of the high voltage that charges the
pulse forming network (PFN). The PSU charges the charging transformer with a controlled
quantity of energy, and then transfers the energy to the PFN (see Figure 4.3).

Figure 4.3
Schematic diagram of the HT system
A three-phase, full wave bridge rectifier and smoothing circuit gives approximately 600 VDC
directly from the primary supply. When the switch devices pair are switched on, this applies
600 VDC to the primary winding of the charging transformer. This causes the current to increase
linearly in the primary winding by di = V/L.dt. During this period, the voltage across the
secondary winding of the charging transformer is negative and the current flow is blocked by
diodes in the transformer.
The energy kept in the transformer is in proportion to the square of the current. The switch
devices are switched off at a set value of current to accurately control the quantity of energy kept
in the transformer.
When the switch devices are switched off, the energy causes the voltage across the secondary
winding of the charging transformer to become positive. The current that results is in a cosine
waveform, and goes through the diodes to the PFN. When all of the energy is transferred to the
PFN, the secondary voltage falls. This reverse biases the diodes again and the PFN stays charged.
For a charge of 20 joules, the primary current switches off at approximately 160 A.
When the thyratron is started, the energy kept in the pulse forming network (PFN) is discharged
through the primary winding of the pulse transformer. The waveform travels to the opposite end
of the PFN and is sent back. The time for this change gives the length of the pulse (approximately

4.5.2.1
Operation of the primary electrical supply
This is a description of the operation of the primary electrical supply.
The three-phase primary electrical supply to the HT system is connected through circuit breaker
CB1 and a number of contactors in series. Each of the contactors has a dedicated interlock chain
that controls the contactor operation.
When all the interlocks operate correctly and CB1 is ON, the primary electrical supply goes to the
high tension (HT) PSU assembly.
4.5.2.2
Operation of the HT charge cycle
This is a description of the operation of the HT system charge cycle.
The high tension (HT) PSU supplies the input power to the modulator. The pulse transformer and
the pulse forming network (PFN) in the modulator supply the HT pulses that operate the cathode
of the magnetron and the cathode of the electron gun.
The HT PSU and the modulator together give a short pulse of between 35 kV and 50 kV. This is
through a number of energy transfer steps (see Figure 4.4).

When the voltage across the PFN has become stable, the thyratron operates to
supply the high 3 µs pulses. These pulses first drive the primary coils of the
pulse transformer and then the anode of the magnetron.
During the discharge phase, the PFN operates as an applied transmission line
(rather than a simple capacitor). This is because the PFN is a network of
capacitors and inductors.
In high power mode, two charge cycles occur before the thyratron starts. This
gives a higher PFN voltage.
After the operation of the thyratron, the modulator operates as a transmission line that has a
primary impedance of 8 Ω and a secondary impedance of 225 Ω. The PFN supplies half of its open
circuit voltage into a load (that is a 20 kV PFN charge results in 10 kV on the primary of the
transformer, or 53 kV on the secondary because of the 5.3:1 step up ratio).
The magnetic field strength gives the magnetron voltage and the modulator adjusts the
magnetron current. If there is an important variation in the operation of the magnetron, away
from 225Ω, gives a mismatch of the modulator. If the variation is too high, the energy is
transferred to the PFN.
The modulator also supplies HT to the electron gun. The gun resistor, and the of the gun
transformer and HT cables, give a RC circuit. This gives an interval in the voltage increase time at
the gun to the magnetron pulse. The interval gives time for the RF to become stable in the
waveguide before the electrons are put in the waveguide.
4.5.2.3
Description of the HT protection circuits
This is a description of the HT protection circuits which give the HT system protection against a
number of fault conditions.
The HT protection circuits give the HT system protection against a number of fault conditions. The
fault conditions include:
•
Unwanted signals
•
Too much current
•
Too much voltage
•
Reverse diode overload
•
High temperature.
If one or more of these fault conditions occur, the HTC PCB does not send the HT drive pulse to
the HT circuit.

4.5.4.5
Operation of the HT crowbar detector PCB
This is a description of the operation of the HT crowbar detector PCB.
The HT crowbar detector PCB is installed on the HT PSU chassis assembly. The HT crowbar
detector PCB senses voltages on the secondary winding of the charging transformer. If it senses a
voltage that is too high, it sends a signal to stop the charge current.
A tap on the secondary winding of the charging transformer supplies a voltage to the HT crowbar
detector PCB. If the voltage is too high, this starts a pair of thyristor switches. The thyristors cause
the power held in the charging transformer to be put into load resistor R2 on the HT PSU chassis
assembly. When this occurs, a signal is sent to the crowbar timer on the HTC PCB to prevent more
charges for a period of 1.5 seconds.
See the Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Reference Manual for information about the
input and output signals to and from the HT crowbar detector PCB.

4.5.4.9
Operation of the charging transformer
This is a description of the operation of the charging transformer.
The charging transformer gives the HT CHARGE signal to the PFN in the modulator assembly.
The switch devices TR1 and TR2 are connected to the primary winding at terminals P2 and P1.
When the devices operate, they give approximately -300 V and +300 V in relation to the neutral
connection. This enables the current flow through the primary winding. This makes a high flux
density in the core of the transformer.
When the switch devices TR1 and TR2 are switched off, the current flow in the primary winding
stops which closes the magnetic field . This changes the direction of the voltage across the
secondary winding of the charging transformer to cause the high voltage charge.
The HT CHARGE signal is applied to the modulator assembly from terminal S3 through a coaxial
cable. The secondary return at terminal S1 and the pulse ground (earth) at terminal S2 are
applied to the HT crowbar detector PCB.
The charging transformer assembly is water-cooled.

4.5.5.1
Operation of the thyratron
This is a description of the operation of the thyratron.
The thyratron discharges the PFN through the pulse transformer. The device is a hydrogen filled
tetrode with a ceramic envelope and two grids (G1 and G2) between the cathode and the anode.
The thyratron is a very fast, high current switch, that uses the hydrogen gas as the switch
medium. The hydrogen gas is ionized to make a conductive plasma. The temperature of the
cathode is then increased to free the electrons. Grid G1 is positive to attract the electrons which
ionizes the hydrogen. The grid 1 voltage decreases when there is plasma and current flows
between the cathode and grid 1.

Item
Description
Cathode heater
A 6.3 V AC supply increases the temperature of the cathode and
releases the electrons.
Ionization voltage
Grid G1 receives a +140 V DC supply which operates the hydrogen
ionization. As the hydrogen ionization occurs, the voltage measured
on grid 1 decreases to a level of between 12 V and 22 V.
Hold off grid
When the PFN charges, there is a high voltage between the anode
and the cathode. Grid G2 is therefore held negative (-140 V) to
isolate the plasma from the high PFN voltage on the anode. This
prevents current flow between the cathode and the anode.
Grid G2 receives a large positive pulse of +900 V DC for 3 µs, which
causes the plasma to expand in the envelope. This causes the
thyratron to operate momentarily.
When the PFN is fully discharged, the voltage between the anode
and the cathode is negligible. The operation of the thyratron stops
and is switched off, to prepare for the next charge cycle.
Replenisher
The hydrogen gas is kept as titanium hydride in metal containers in
the valve, and is filled by heating the containers. The input to the
replenisher is the 5.5 V AC power supply, which is accurately set to
release the correct gas pressure for the operation of the device.
As the thyratron ages, the gas pressure decreases and causes the G1
voltage to increase. The gas pressure can be increased if the
replenisher heater voltage is increased.

Thyratron life
In usual operation, the hydrogen in the valve envelope gradually
diffuses to air, therefore the life of a thyratron usually ends because
of the depletion of hydrogen. However, if the replenisher voltage is

spontaneously conduct (known as fire through). If the replenisher

shortens the life of the valve. It is therefore essential that the
thyratron is set to operate under the correct conditions.

4.5.5.5
Operation of the pulse forming network
This is a description of the operation of the pulse forming network.
See the Linear Accelerator System Diagrams Manual.
The PFN circuit controls the shape and length of the voltage input to the pulse transformer. The
pulse forming network (PFN) has eight LC circuits contained in an assembly installed on the
modulator assembly.
The HT CHARGE signal from the charging transformer in the HT PSU is supplied to terminal T1 of
the PFN. The free end of the PFN at terminal T0 is connected to the primary winding of the pulse
transformer.
When enabled, the HT CHARGE signal charges the PFN to between 14 kV to 19 kV
(approximately). When the thyratron starts, the PFN discharges through the pulse transformer.
4.5.5.6
Operation of the pulse transformer
This is a description of the operation of the pulse transformer.
See the Linear Accelerator System Diagrams Manual.
The pulse transformer T1 supplies the high voltage pulses to the cathode of the magnetron and
the cathode of the electron gun. The transformer has a voltage step-up ratio of 1:5.3. This gives
an output of approximately 52 kV in the high power mode and 38 kV in the low power mode.
The pulse from the PFN is supplied to connector P2 and is input to the positive end of the primary
winding. The output from the secondary winding is a pulse at terminal S4 and is input to the
magnetron and the electron gun through coaxial cables.
When loaded with the magnetron impedance across the secondary winding, the primary winding
of the pulse transformer has an impedance that is approximately equal to the impedance (Zo) of
the PFN (Zo = 8 Ω). Voltage VN is therefore shared equally between Zo and the reflected
impedance (for example, VN = 21 kV gives 10.4 kV across the primary winding).
When the voltage is at 80% of the full pulse level, the magnetron gives current (see Figure 4.12).
To get the correct rate of the voltage increase and make sure that the magnetron starts in the
correct mode, an array of capacitors (C3 to C10) is connected across the secondary winding of the
pulse transformer. The capacitance of the array mixes with the capacitance and leakage
inductance of the pulse transformer to give the rate of magnetron voltage increase (110 kV/µs).

4.6.5
Operation of the diode overload detector
This is a description of the operation of the diode overload detector circuit.
This circuit gives the modulator and the magnetron protection from an electrical arc and short
circuits. If these conditions occur, they can send the energy to the PFN.
An electrical arc can occur in the magnetron, usually when first used after a long standby period.
The magnetron is not damaged by an electrical arc, but it is necessary to know the quantity of
energy that goes through the diode overload circuit. This is because the circuit cannot remove the
power continuously.
It is therefore necessary to know the number of times that the diode operates. The reverse diode
overload detector knows when a specified number of in sequence of opposite energy occurs. The
number of changes in direction are as follows:
•
12 in sequence full changes of direction in the high energy mode
•
24 in sequence full changes of direction in the low energy mode.
The voltage of signal HT CHARGEmonitors the diode current. This is developed across resistor R5
in series with the diode D1. This voltage is a negative pulse which decreases very quickly. The
pulses, signal REVERSE DIODE O/L, are then supplied to connector P6 on the modulator isolation
unit.
At the modulator isolation unit, the REVERSE DIODE O/L signal is applied to a diode circuit that
has D5, R18 and C7. Each pulse charges C7 which increase its voltage in steps in a negative
direction. The voltage across C7 is then applied to detector IC3 which senses the level. IC3
operates at -10 V set by resistors R20 and R21.
When the voltage across C7 is less than 10 V, the output of IC3 is low and fiber-optic connection
OPTO 4 is illuminated. When the voltage across C7 is more than 10 V, the output of IC3 goes high.
This switches off the output of OPTO 4 and at the same time discharges C7 through diode D6 and
resistor R23.
The fiber-optic from the diode overload detector is inverted to give the active high REVERSE
DIODE O/L input to the HTC PCB.
The reverse diode overload detector gives the PFN protection. The HT CHARGE signal develops a
voltage at resistor R1. The voltage is applied to the modulator isolation unit as signal PFN V MON.

4.6.6
Operation of the gun filament transformer
This is a description of the operation of the gun filament transformer.
The gun filament transformer isolates the 50 kV supply between the gun filament power supply
circuit and the electron gun. The gun filament transformer is installed in the modulator Area 30.
The magnetron tuner/gun filament filter supplies the primary winding of the transformer. The
secondary winding of the transformer supply the output to the cathode of the electron gun. A
resistor (R6) puts a short interval in the pulse. To decrease the primary current, the gun filament
transformer has a step down ratio of 3:1.
4.6.7
Operation of the magnetron tuner gun filament filter
This is a description of the operation of the magnetron tuner/gun filament filter.
The magnetron tuner and gun filament use an EMC filter to give the protection against noise. The
EMC filter is installed in the FTM rack.
The magnetron tuner drive signals from the two magnetron tuner UPD PCBs are applied to the
filter and then to the solenoid of the magnetron tuner.
The gun filament drive signals from the two gun filament UPD PCBs are applied to the high
electrical current filter and then to the gun transformer.
4.6.8
Operation of the magnetron
This is a description of the operation of the magnetron.
The magnetron is a high power oscillator that changes high voltage pulses at its cathode into a
pulse of RF power. The magnetic field intensity and the amplitude of the voltage at the cathode
give the level of the RF output. The RF output is then input to the waveguide system.
The magnetron has a peak output of 5 MW. It operates at a nominal frequency of 2856 MHz. A
servo control system tunes the magnetron to the frequency that is necessary.
The magnetron is water cooled and evacuated, and the magnetron magnet is water cooled. The
RF power goes through an output window to the waveguide. This part of the waveguide is kept
cool by the SF6 gas.
4.6.8.1
Operation of the magnetron cathode and filament
This is a description of the operation of the magnetron cathode and filament in the digital
accelerator.
The cathode has a hot spiral filament that operates at a temperature of approximately 840 °C.
The two terminals of the filament are attached to the cathode.
The magnetron cathode has negative pulses with voltages in the range 38 kV to 52 kV from the
pulse transformer in the modulator. This gives pulse currents to a maximum of 250 A. This makes
a voltage between the cathode and the ground (earth) anode . This gives the large electric field
that is necessary to make the electrons go to the anode.
A servo controlled power supply increases the temperature of the filament. This gives the small
adjustment of the current through the filament to keep the correct temperature. Control of the
filament temperature is necessary to remove the effects of back bombardment when the
magnetron is in operation.

4.6.8.2
Operation of the magnetron anode
This is a description of the operation of the magnetron anode.
The anode block is a cylinder that has a number of vanes that are configured to make 12 different
resonant cavities. Six of the 12 cavities have a prong that moves in and out of the cavity. The six
prongs move together, operated by a fast moving magnet in a fixed solenoid. The position of the
prongs changes the physical dimensions of the cavities, and therefore adjusts the frequency at
which the magnetron operates.
The case of the anode is connected to ground (earth) to supply a high voltage between the anode
and the cathode.
4.6.8.3
Operation of the magnetron tuning
This is a description of the operation of the magnetron tuning.
In Auto mode, the PPG PCB keeps the frequency at which the magnetron is tuned. This is in
response to the RF phase data from the phase error detector of the AFC system. The TCS applies
signals which control a pair of UPD PCBs that operate the magnet of the tuning solenoid. The
current through the solenoid gives the actual position of the solenoid magnet. The current is
monitored, and this data is sent back to the TCS as a monitor item. The TCS controls the
magnetron tuning when the control software is in Manual mode only, therefore the servo control
loop does not use the monitor signal.
When an energy is selected at the start of a treatment, the low power (LP) phase shifter of the
AFC system uses the phase error detector. This sets the RF phase error to zero.
4.6.8.4
Operation of the magnetron magnet
This is a description of the operation of the magnetron magnet.
The magnet is around the magnetron. The magnet gives the strong magnetic field that changes
the RF power output of the magnetron into the transverse electric field. This field is necessary to
move through the rectangular section of the waveguide system.

4.6.9.1
Operation of the electron emission of the electron gun
This is a description of the operation of the electron emissions of the electron gun.
The cathode of the electron gun is energized by the same pulses that are applied to the cathode
of the magnetron. R6 and the capacitance of the HT cable and the gun transformer give a delay to
the pulses. When the negative voltage is applied (at a maximum of -50 kV), a pulse of electrons is
output from the cathode to make a space charge. This increases the speed of the electrons, at a
velocity of approximately 0.4 C, in the direction of the first cell of the injector section of the
waveguide.
The shape of the gun, and that of the input mode transformer, changes the field gradient to move
the electrons along the axis of the waveguide. The electrons are then and put into the injector
section.

4.6.9.2
Operation of the electron gun initial acceleration
This is a description of the operation of how the electron gun gives the initial acceleration in the
speed of the electrons.
To increase the speed of the electrons through the waveguide the axial RF electric field is
maximized. The phase velocity of the RF wave is synchronized to the velocity of the electrons. The
high voltage pulse at the cathode initially increases the speed of the electrons to 0.4 C. The RF is
synchronized with the RF, which decreases to 0.4 C by the first cell of the injector section of the
waveguide.
4.6.9.3
Operation of the gun filament control
This is a description of the operation of the gun filament control.
The electron gun is part of a servo system that keeps a constant beam energy in the X-ray mode
and a constant output dose rate in the electron mode. This is controlled by the gun filament
current, and therefore the beam current.
The electron energy from the linear accelerator is in proportion to the beam current. In the X-ray
mode, this property controls the beam energy. Signals from the inner and outer hump beam
intensity detectors of the ionization chamber in the BLD sense the changes in energy. The signals
that result adjust the beam current by control of the gun filament current to keep a constant
beam energy.
In the electron mode the beam current is small. Therefore electron energy operates almost
independently of the level of the beam current. But, small changes in beam current change the
dose rate. The dose rate signal from the ion chamber is therefore controls the gun filament
current to keep a constant dose rate.
4.6.9.4
Operation of the gun filament power supply
This is a description of the operation of the gun filament power supply.
The PPG PCB and two UPD PCBs supply the controlled AC electrical power for the heater current

Item

Radiation absorber
A small proportion of high energy RF leaks through glass
envelope of the magnetron. The radiation absorber makes sure
that the energy leak is absorbed (by conversion to heat), near
the magnetron.
RF isolator
The RF isolator inhibits magnetron moding effects by preventing
the accumulation of standing waves in the transition section of
the waveguide. The isolator passes the forward RF but absorbs
the reflected waves. In the forward direction, RF is passed with
losses of only 0.6 dB (approximately): in the reverse direction
there is at least a 13 dB rejection of RF. The isolator is therefore
an almost constant impedance to the magnetron, so reflected
waves are rejected.
The isolator has a length of rectangular waveguide to which a
large, fixed external magnet. In the isolator there is a set of
internal ferrite plates that are magnetically connected to the
magnet. In the magnetic field, the magnetic elements of the
ferrite align to give a low loss to forward RF and a high loss to
reflected waves.
The RF isolator is water-cooled. The internal ferrite plates are
covered by ceramic Berylia plates. These conduct the heat in
the ferrite to the walls of the isolator. The heat is then
decreased by the cooling water system.
Directional sidewall coupler
The directional sidewall coupler is part of the residual RF
feedback path. Its purpose is to transfer an optimum amount of
the returning RF from the accelerating waveguide to the RF
output of the magnetron.
The directional sidewall coupler has two connected sections of
rectangular waveguide, with a number of holes in the adjacent
walls. The holes are set at a distance of ¼ wavelength apart.
When in phase, the RF goes into the section that moves the
source RF from the magnetron. This is approximately 4 dB,
therefore approximately half of the RF power is sent back. The
balance is sent to the RF load, where it is removed as heat (see 
Figure 4.17).
RF load
The RF load is a section of waveguide that tapers at one end.
The change in impedance caused by the different physical
dimensions of the taper in the waveguide changes the RF to
heat. This is subsequently removed by the cooling water
system.
The RF load has an above temperature switch that operates
with the interlock system.
RF input window and flexible
waveguide
The rectangular waveguide is pressurized to approximately
0.8 bar by a dielectric gas that prevents high tension breakdown
in the waveguide. The accelerating waveguide is evacuated to
better than 10-5 m bar. Two ceramic windows separate these
extremes of pressure, one at the input to the accelerating
waveguide and one at the output.

4.6.11.2
Operation of the accelerating waveguide (linear accelerator)
This is a description of the operation of the accelerating waveguide.
The accelerating waveguide has two cylinder shape waveguide sections that are connected at the
center. One section of the accelerating waveguide is known as the injector (or buncher) section
and the other is known as the relativistic section.
Each section has a cylinder shape copper waveguide. These have copper irises along their length
to make a number of dome-shaped resonant cavities. The two sections connect at the center
joint to make one accelerating waveguide. The center joint has a RF probe that the automatic
frequency control (AFC) system uses.
The injector section has different spaces between the irises. The first six cavities of this section
accelerate the RF field and, therefore, the electrons. In the relativistic section, there is a small
increase in the velocity of the wave, and gain in electron energy is because of the related increase
in mass.
A vacuum is kept in the accelerating waveguide by two, 35 liters/second ion pumps - one at each
end of the waveguide. The vacuum is sealed at the two mode transformers, and at the center
joint, by indium wire which helps electrical conduction.
Small changes in temperature can change the dimensions of the accelerating waveguide. This can
have an effect on the tuning and performance of the linear accelerator. The accelerating
waveguide assembly has a water-cooled casing, the temperature of which is very accurately
controlled.
4.6.11.3
Operation of the input and output mode transformers
This is a description of the operation of the input and output mode transformers of the
accelerating waveguide.
There is a mode transformer at each end of the accelerating waveguide assembly. The mode
transformers are installed in the first (input) and last (output) resonant cavities of the accelerating
waveguide.

The input mode transformer changes the RF from the TE mode in the rectangular waveguide into
the TM mode that is necessary to accelerate the electrons. The round section of the input mode
transformer is the first cavity of the accelerating waveguide. The RF is input to the transformer
from the side.
The input mode transformer turns the RF through 90°. The RF electric field, which is at a
maximum between the long walls of the rectangular waveguide, aligns with the RF electric field
which is axial in the accelerating waveguide. The slope of the cell in the waveguide gives the
phase velocity of the RF, which aligns that of the linear accelerator.
The size of the rectangular section of the input mode transformer is decreased in two steps. This
decrease in the impedance that results causes heat. The input mode transformer is therefore
water-cooled.
The output mode transformer removes the RF from the accelerating waveguide and changes the
electrical Field Mode from TM to TE to move through the feedback section of the rectangular
waveguide.

This is a description of the operation of the RF output window and the flexible waveguide.
The RF output window keeps the evacuated accelerating waveguide from the gas pressurized
feedback section of the rectangular waveguide.
The section of waveguide before the RF output window is flexible to give the connection of the
90° twisted section of waveguide.
4.6.11.5
Operation of the 90° twisted waveguide section
This is a description of the operation of the twisted section of the waveguide.
After the output flexible waveguide section, the RF goes through a waveguide section that is
twisted through 90°. The twisted section adjusts the phase of the RF to align with the sidewall
coupler.
4.6.11.6
Operation of the high power phase shifter
This is a description of the operation of the high power phase shifter.
The high power (HP) phase shifter adjusts the phase angle of the RF to align it with the phase
angle of the input RF. This correction increases the primary RF from the magnetron, which is
necessary to get the highest energies.
The HP phase shifter has two sections of rectangular waveguide connected together to make a
3 dB directional coupler. Each of the waveguide sections has a coplanar short circuit piston. The
motors operate the two pistons to move in and out of the related waveguide section together.

The resonant frequency of the magnetron must be controlled continuously. This is to make sure

phase error. The samples are from the RF probe at the gun end of the waveguide: and from the

4.6.14.1
Operation of the automatic positioning of the magnetron tuner in the capture
range
This is a description of the operation of the automatic positioning of the magnetron tuner in the
capture range.
The capture range of the AFC system makes it is necessary to set the magnetron tuner to the
correct position in the capture range when the HT is switched on. This must apply at during a cold
start or multiple treatments. The tuner rest item Item 97 from the TCS, controls the automatic
position of the magnetron tuner in the capture range.
The AFC servo controls the position of the magnetron tuner while the magnetron and the linear
accelerator warm up. First, the TCS sets the tuner rest position. When an energy is selected and
the HT is switched on, the LP phase shifter (which is already in position), moves the phase error
detector to set the RF phase error to a zero. This is the rest position. The LP phase shifter has no
more functions while the linear accelerator delivers the selected energy. This becomes active
again only when a new energy is selected and the HT is switched on again.
When the HT is switched on, the magnetron tuner starts at its current position (the rest position if
the HT has been off for some time). In Auto mode, after each pulse, the PPG PCB calculates the
phase error, which corrects the position of the tuner. When the HT is switched off, the TCS
continues control until the tuner goes back to the rest position.
When the HT is switched off, the TCS senses the temperature decrease of the linear accelerator
and records the last position of the magnetron tuner. The TCS then moves the magnetron tuner
gradually. Therefore if the HT is switched on again, the magnetron tuner position (frequency) is in
the capture range of the AFC system.
The magnetron can be tuned down only if power supplies are available. If power supplies are not
available, then the position is calculated and the magnetron tuner is moved to the correct
position when power is restored.
4.6.14.2
Operation of the phase adjustment
This is a description of the operation of the phase adjustment.
The two samples of the moving RF wave are applied to the phase error detector. At the rest
position, the phase error detector continues to monitor the RF phase difference at the two
sample points. This gives two different phase leg outputs to the PPG PCB. There is one output for
each phase signal, with a phase difference of 90° between them (imposed by the phase error
detector). On the PPG PCB, the phase leg signals are calculated and sent to the TCS. The phase leg
signals are also compared in the PPG PCB to give an error signal to the TCS.
The current through the solenoid shows the actual position of the solenoid magnet. The current
is monitored, and this data is sent back to the TCS as part of the position servo control loop.

4.7.2.3
Operation of the HT pulse generation
This is a description of the operation of the HT pulse generation.
With Item 433, Item 434 and Item 443 set, the FPGA on the PPG PCB sets internal signal HCE to
the PPG PCB. The circuit sets signal HT_CHARGE_EN to logic 0 for 25 µs at the PRF. This is then
input to the HTC PCB as signal CHARGE ENABLE.
The HTC PCB, changes the CHARGE ENABLE input to signal HT DRIVE PULSE. The HTC PCB stops
the HT DRIVE PULSE if the protection circuits sense one or more of the fault conditions:
•
Multiple charges by noise
•
HT overload
•
The voltage on the primary side of the charging transformer is too high
•
Reverse diode overload.
If no fault condition found, the HT DRIVE PULSE is sent through a coaxial cable to the HTCA optical
receiver. The FTCA Optical receiver isolates the signal. The signal is then routed through the HT
isolation unit to HT PSU PCBs.
The output of the HT PSU PCBs switch on the devices to set the 600 V DC supply to the charging
transformer.
The HT DRIVE PULSE controls the FET switches on the HT PSU PCBs, which quickly turn the
switches off at the end of the charge pulse period. This removes the 600 V supply from the
primary side of the charging transformer.

Operation of the thyratron pulse generation
This is a description of the operation of the thyratron pulse generation.
When Item 433, Item 434 and Item 443 are set, the FPGA on the PPG PCB the internal signal

This is then supplied to the modulator through the HTCA optical receiver and the modulator
isolation PCB.
In the modulator, the THY_TRIG signal is supplied to the thyratron trigger PCB in the thyratron
pulser. The thyratron trigger PCB conditions the trigger signal. Therefore when THY_TRIG is set, a
positive pulse of approximately 900 V of a time of three µs is supplied to grid G2 of the thyratron.
This causes the thyratron to discharge the PFN through the primary side of the pulse transformer.

device is cold. When the thyratron is warm, only the edge part of the pulse is used (see Figure
4.25).

4.7.3.3
Operation of the HT overload signals
This is a description of the operation of the HT overload signals of the protection circuits.
The protection circuits monitor an HT overload condition at the secondary side of the charging
transformer. This is supplied to the HT crowbar detector PCB. In a fault condition, the voltage of
the charging transformer increases to 25 kV and therefore applies 1500 V (6% of 25 kV) to the HT
crowbar detector PCB. A diode circuit on the HT crowbar detector PCB operates to give an output
HT OVERLOAD DETECTOR. This signal is supplied to the HTC PCB through the HT isolation PCB and
the HTCA optical receiver.
The input at the HTC PCB as signal HT O/L DET I/P, prevents the HT DRIVE PULSE output from the
HTC PCB if there is an HT overload.
The input to the HTC PCB is supplied to the DIE-HTB PCB as signal HT O/L DET O/P. The DIE-HTB
PCB then supplies the monitor item Item 83 for the TCS. If there is an HT overload, the FPGA on
the DIE-HTB PCB sets Item 83 to the value 0. Usually Item 83 is kept at the value 1.
4.7.3.4
Operation of the reverse diode overload signals
This is a description of the operation of the reverse diode overload signals of the protection
circuits.
The reverse diode overload detector in the modulator isolation unit senses unwanted reverse
current flow in the modulator. The modulator isolation PCB develops a monitor voltage from the
HT CHARGE signal. The modulator isolation unit measures the level of this voltage. This gives an
active high signal REV DIODE O/L. This signal goes through the HTCA optical receiver and is an
input to the HTC PCB as signal REV DIODE O/L I/P.
On the HTC PCB, the active REV DIODE O/L I/P signal prevents the HT DRIVE PULSE output from
the HTC PCB if there is a reverse diode overload.
The signal REV DIODE O/L O/P is input to the DIE-HTB PCB. The DIE-HTB PCB supplies monitor
item Item 84 for the TCS. If there is a reverse current flow in the modulator, the FPGA on the DIEHTB PCB sets Item 84 to the value 0. Usually Item 84 is held at the value 1.
4.7.3.5
Operation of the modulator temperature signals
This is a description of the operation of the modulator temperature signals of the protection
circuits.
A sensor in the pulse transformer monitors the temperature of the modulator. The output of the
temperature sensor is an input to the modulator isolation unit PCB as signal MODULATOR O/T.
This signal is an output from the modulator isolation unit and input to the DIE-HTB PCB through
the HTCA optical receiver.
The DIE-HTB PCB supplies monitor item Item 87 for the TCS. If the modulator temperature is too
high, the FPGA on the DIE-HTB PCB sets Item 87 to the value 0. Usually Item 87 is held at the
value 1.
4.7.3.6
Operation of the PFN voltage monitor signal
This is a description of the operation of the pulse forming network (PFN) signals of the protection
circuits.
The PFN voltage monitor circuit gives the voltage protection at the PFN. Level detectors in the
modulator isolation unit set different voltage thresholds for the high and low energy modes. This
gives signals PFN V MON H.E. and PFN V MON L.E.

4.7.3.7
Operation of the HT crowbar detection signals
This is a description of the operation of the HT crowbar detection signals.
The HT crowbar detector PCB senses if the PFN voltage is about to go above the rate of charge.
This condition is usually caused by unwanted operation of the switches by noise. The output of
the HT crowbar detector PCB is signal CROWBAR DETECTOR. This is then input to the HTC PCB
through the HT isolation PCB and the HTCA optical receiver. The input to the HTC PCB is
CROWBAR DET I/P.
On the HTC PCB, the CROWBAR DET I/P signal prevents the HT DRIVE PULSE output from the HTC
PCB if a crowbar operates.
The signal CROWBAR O/P is applied to the DIE-HTB PCB. The DIE-HTB PCB supplies monitor item
Item 89 to be read by the TCS. If the PFN charge voltage is too high, the FPGA on the DIE-HTB PCB
sets Item 89 to the value 0. Usually Item 89 is held at the value 1.
4.7.3.8
Operation of the HT PSU temperature signals
This is a description of the operation of the HT PSU temperature signals.
The DIE-HTB PCB monitors the HT OVERTEMP DETECTOR signal that shows the temperature
status of the HT PSU. The signal source is at the bellows switch (SW2) of the charging transformer
and the heat sink fan (SW1). The signal is applied to the DIE-HTB PCB through the HT isolation
PCB and HTCA optical receiver.
The DIE-HTB PCB supplies monitor item Item 251 for the TCS. If the measured temperature is to
high, the FPGA on the DIE-HTB PCB sets Item 251 to the value 0. The value of Item 251 is 1 during
usual conditions of operation.
4.7.3.9
Operation of the charging transformer current control signals
This is a description of the operation of the charging transformer current control signals.
The rate of charge is set by the control item Item 330 from the TCS. This is the maximum current
permitted at the primary side of the charging transformer. The control item is an input to the
AO12-HTA PCB as a 12-bit analog word. This then used by the AO12-HTA PCB to set the voltage of
the HT threshold. This value is then input to the HTC PCB as signal PRI I REF I/P.
A current transformer on the HT PSU heat sink assembly senses the current level at the primary
side of the charging transformer. Signal PRI I MON shows the monitored current. This is an input
to the HTC PCB as signal PRI I I/P.

4.7.4.4
Operation of the gun filament current demand signal processing
This is a description of the operation of the gun filament current demand signal.
The gun filament current value of Item 538 is an input to the AO12-HTA PCB, which changes the
12-bit digital input into an analog signal. This signal is an input to the PPG PCB.
The PPG PCB has a field programmable gate array (FPGA). This changes the gun filament current
to the GUN_FIL_DEMAND signal for the UPD PCBs. The GUN_CONTROL signal from the SIB
controls the amplitude of the GUN_FIL_DEMAND signal to set the applicable X-ray or Electron
mode. The GUN_FIL_DEMAND signal is also synchronized to the thyratron start signal. Therefore
when the radiation pulse is generated, the gun filament current is zero.
The GUN FIL DEMAND signal from the PPG PCB gives an input to the MT/GF interface PCB. The
MT/GF changes the current value of the demand to a voltage. This is sent to UPD A of the bridge
gun filament UPD PCBs through the backplane of the FTM rack.
The gun filament UPD PCBs use the voltage of the GUN FIL DEMAND signal to supply the correct
AC current pulses to the filament of the electron gun. UPD B supplies the positive pulse and UPD
A the negative pulse.
4.7.4.5
Operation of the gun filament current enable signal processing
This is a description of the operation of the gun filament signal processing.
The PPG PCB also supplies a gun enable signal GUN_FIL_EN. This signal is permanently enabled
(logic 0).
The GUN_FIL_EN output from the PPG PCB is input to the ROC-HTA PCB. The signal goes through
the contacts of a relay (RLB2). Relay RLB2 puts vacuum system interlock conditions into the gun
filament control circuit. The fault conditions are shown by monitor items that are output by the
vacuum system through the DIE-HTB PCB:
•
Item 227 - the vacuum pressure at the gun end of the waveguide.
•
Item 238 - the 10-4 vacuum trip signal for the gun end of the waveguide system.
•
Item 493 - shows a fault in the vacuum readout system.
If the vacuum pressure is incorrect or there is a fault in the vacuum monitor system, the contacts
of RLB2 open . This disconnects the GUN FILAMENT ENABLE signal from the MT/GF interface PCB.
The MT/GF interface PCB monitors some power supply rails and the cooling fans of the FTM rack.
If there is a fault, it removes the GUN FILAMENT ENABLE signal to remove the gun filament
current. The GUN FILAMENT ENABLE signal is set to logic 0 during usual conditions.
From the MT/GF interface PCB, the GUN FILAMENT ENABLE signal is applied to the gun filament
UPD PCBs. If there is a fault, the signal is set to a logic 1. This stops the outputs of the UPD PCBs
to switch off the gun filament current.

4.7.4.6
Operation of the gun filament current and voltage monitor signal processing
This is a description of the operation of the gun filament current and voltage monitor signal
processing.
The current and voltage levels of the output of the gun filament UPD PCBs are monitored by the
TCS. On each PCB, a sample of the current output and a voltage derived from the current output
are applied to the MT/GF interface PCB. This is as signals GUN FIL I and GUN FIL V.
The MT/GF interface PCB mixes the two current samples to give a one signal GUN FIL I. Signal
GUN FIL I is input to the SCC-HTA and AI12-HTA PCBs, the output of which is a 12-bit digital value.
This signal is read by the TCS as monitor item Item 217.
The two voltage samples are also mixed to give a single signal GUN FIL V. This is a voltage that is
the RMS current supplied by the gun filament UPD PCBs. Signal GUN FIL V is input to the SCC-HTA
and AI12-HTA PCBs, the output of which is a 12-bit digital value that is read by the TCS as monitor
item Item 216.

A sample of the analog version of the gun filament signal is read by the TCS. Item Item 416 selects
the gun filament signal as the output channel of the monitor multiplexer on the AO12-HTA PCB.
This signal is input to the SCC-HTA and AI12-HTA PCBs, the output of which is a 12-bit digital value

4.7.5
Operation of the magnetron filament control
This is a description of the operation of the control circuit of the magnetron filament.
The filament of the magnetron cathode makes the cathode hot to control the emission of
electrons. When the magnetron operates, electrons that are sent back increase the temperature
of the cathode increases by the electrons that are sent back. The effect is in proportion to the HT
current and therefore, to keep the cathode at the correct temperature, the filament current is
decreased.
A programmed PSU supplies the magnetron filament in the gun filament PSU (Area 33). The TCS
controls the PSU through the AO12-HTA PCB. The PPG PCB gives synchronization pulses to make
sure that the filament supply is blank before each occurrence of the magnetron trigger.

4.7.7
Operation of the magnetron tuner and AFC control circuits
This is a description of the operation of the magnetron tuner and the AFC control circuits.
When the HT is off, the magnetron tuner is always at the rest position shown by control item Item
97. This position is set during the test program and is correct for operation at the lowest PRF rate
of six pulses for each second.
The TCS quickly adjusts the tuner to keep the correct frequency during the initial warm up period.
After the warm up, a RF beam is made and RF phase angle information is supplied to the phase
error detector in the AFC system.
The phase angle signals make a mixed phase error signal that is sent from the AFC system to the
magnetron tuner servo. The error signal can be positive or negative, and causes the tuner
solenoid to move the tuning prongs in the direction necessary to keep the resonant frequency of
the magnetron.

4.7.7.4
Operation of the magnetron tuner demand signal processing
This is a description of the operation of the magnetron tuner demand signal processing.
To move the magnetron tuner to the correct start position:
•
Item Item 161 uses the position information from Item 231
•
Item Item 161 uses the cold start value from Item 97 or the warm start value from the
calibration block.
The warm start value changes with the time since the HT is switched off. The correct point on the
cool curve is continuously calculated and is used when the HTCA power supplies are on.
In the Auto mode, Item 182 is set to 1 and the phase error, shown by Item 236, tunes the
magnetron for the optimization output, if:
1 
The PPG PCB transmits the sample pulses when Item 444 is set to 1.
2 
The value of Item 232 and Item 233 is greater than 5.
The 12-bit digital value of Item 553 is input to the FPGA on the PPG PCB. The data word
calculated by the FPGA changes to an analog value. This is then applied to the MT/GF drive
interface PCB as signal MAG TUNE DEMAND.
The MT/GF drive interface PCB, changes the current value to a voltage. This is sent to UPD A of
the magnetron tuner UPD PCBs through the same mode noise suppression filter.
Together the magnetron tuner UPD PCBs use the voltage of the MAG TUNE DEMAND signal to
give the correct AC current pulses to the solenoid of the magnetron tuner. UPD B supplies the
positive pulse and UPD A the negative pulse. The solenoid is energized and the tuning is moved to
the position in the spaces of the magnetron anode.
4.7.7.5
Operation of the magnetron tuner enable signal processing
The magnetron tuner enable signal MAG_TUNE_EN is supplied by the PPG PCB. This signal is
permanently enabled (logic 0).
The MAG_TUNE_EN output from the PPG PCB is an input to the MT/GF drive interface PCB. This
PCBs monitors some power supply rails and the fans of the FTM rack . If it senses a fault, it sets
the MAG TUNER ENABLE to logic 1 to remove power from the magnetron tuner. If not, the MAG
TUNER ENABLE signal stays at (logic 0).
From the MT/GF drive interface PCB, the MAG TUNER ENABLE signal is supplied at the same time
to the two magnetron tuner UPD PCBs. If a fault sets the signal to (logic 1), the output drivers of
the UPD PCBs are prevented. This sets the magnetron tuner current off.

4.7.7.6
Operation of the LP phase shifter drive signal processing
This is a description of the operation of the LP phase shifter
To set the phase error detector to the correct position, the calibration block supplies Item 163
with information about the temperature and the motor position of the LP phase shifter. This sets
the value of Item 555.
The 8-bit digital value of Item 555 is an input to the AO8-HTA PCB. This supplies the signal SET
SPEED to UMD PCB 11-5. The amplitude and polarity of the SET SPEED signal (±5 V) show the
necessary speed and direction of rotation of the motor of the LP phase shifter.
UMD PCB 11-5 is permanently enabled by the logic 0 (CGPS) connection. The PCB has a SET
SPEED signal which causes a pulse wave modulated signal for the motor of the LP phase shifter.
The motor then rotates and operates the phase adjuster in the phase error detector to the
position, at which the RF phase error is at zero.
4.7.7.7
Operation of the LP phase shifter monitor signal processing
This is a description of the operation of the LP phase shifter monitor signal processing.
The potentiometer RV1 monitors the movement of the LP phase shifter motor against +10V
supply from the SCC-HTB PCB. The potentiometer supplies a POSITION signal to Channel 11 of the
AI12-HTB PCB. This changes the position voltage to a 12-bit digital value for the TCS as monitor
item Item 230.
A sample of the analog version of the LP phase shifter signal is read by the TCS. Item Item 409
selects the SET SPEED signal as the output channel of the monitor multiplexer on the AO8-HTA
PCB. This version of the SET SPEED signal is input to the SCC-HTB and AI12-HTB PCBs. This gives
an 8-bit digital value that is read by the TCS as monitor item Item 391.
4.7.7.8
Operation of the phase error signal processing
This is a description of the operation of the phase error signal processing.
The signal GUN RF3 from the RF probe at the input window of the rectangular waveguide is
supplied to input A of the hybrid coupler. This is through the phase adjuster. Signal CJ RF4 from
the RF probe at the center joint of the accelerating waveguide is applied to input B of the hybrid
coupler. This is through a 3 GHz filter. The filter removes RF signals at unwanted high frequencies
that can occur during some beam conditions.
The RF power through ports A and B of the hybrid coupler decreases by 3 dB at output ports X
and Y. The phase of the X output from the Y output is also 90° out of phase. Each output port
therefore supplies an in phase part and a 90° phase move part of the input signals.
If the signal amplitudes at inputs A and B are equal and in phase, the amplitudes at outputs X and
Y are equal. This is the null point, when the phase error is at zero. A difference between the input
signals occurs, gives a difference in amplitude at outputs X and Y.
Output X and Y from the hybrid coupler are supplied, through 10 dB attenuator pads, to two RF
diodes. These change the signals and apply them to the PPG PCB as signals RF_PHASE_1 and
RF_PHASE_2.
During the center part of the RF pulses, the PPG PCB reads a sample of the phase error signals.
The sample pulses are then compared and applied to the SCC-HTB and AI12-HTB PCBs. Item Item
444 enables the sample procedure.

4.7.8
Operation of the HP phase shifter
This is the operation and analysis of the HP phase shifter.
A servo controls the DC motor that moves the pistons of the HP phase shifter. The motor gets the
feedback from a potentiometer that monitors the positions of the pistons. The movement of the
pistons moves the directional coupler in the waveguide system. This adjusts the phase angle of
the re-cycled RF to align that of the primary RF.
An analog position signal from the potentiometer is applied to the TCS. The TCS selects the
position of the phase shifter as given by the input treatment data. This sends a digital servo
control signal to an AO8 PCB, where it is changed to an analog speed signal. This signal is applied
to a UMD PCB which moves the motor until the potentiometer shows the necessary position.

5.1
Doing the HT and RF system troubleshooting
This is the recommended procedure to use to do the necessary troubleshooting to correct the
faults that can occur in the HT and RF systems of the linear accelerator.
WARNING 5.1
Do not do work on the digital accelerator without a second person near. The HT and RF systems
have high energy levels which can give you an electric shock. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.2
Do not remove a cover from the digital accelerator unless you are qualified and authorized to
do so. If you ignore this warning you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.3
Do not remove the covers or cables from the equipment unless special instructions in this
document tell you to. The covers give access to high voltage electric parts. Always install the
covers and cables again before you use the equipment. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.4
Do not touch or go near any part of the equipment when the HT is switched on or the circuits
are electrically charged. The HT circuit has voltages of up to 50 kV. If you ignore this warning,
you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.5
Do not touch or go near the HT or RF systems until the reservoir capacitors are fully discharged.
It is approximately 12 minutes before the capacitors discharge to a safe level. If you ignore this
warning, you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.6
Do not touch any part of the HT circuit unless you switch off all electrical power. Use the HT
discharge rod to fully discharge high voltage capacitors. If you ignore this waning, you can cause
fatal injury.
WARNING 5.7
Do not work on the RF isolator unless you wear the applicable protective equipment (face
masks and gloves). The RF isolator contains Beryllia. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
serious injury.
1 
Put the free end of the safety discharge rod on the anode (positive terminal (+)) of diode D1
of the supply transformer.
2 
Let the capacitors fully discharge for a minimum of 12 minutes.
3 
When the PFN is discharged, remove the HT safety discharge rod from the anode of diode
D1.

5.2
Doing the troubleshooting of the pulse forming network
This is the recommended procedure to use to do the troubleshooting to correct the faults that can
occur in the PFN of the HT system of the digital accelerator.
WARNING 5.21
Do not do work on the digital accelerator without a second person near. The HT and RF systems
have high energy levels which can give you an electric shock. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.22
Do not remove a cover from the digital accelerator unless you are qualified and authorized to
do so. If you ignore this warning you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.23
Do not remove the covers or cables from the equipment unless special instructions in this
document tell you to. The covers give access to high voltage electric parts. Always install the
covers and cables again before you use the equipment. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.24
Do not touch or go near any part of the equipment when the HT is switched on or the circuits
are electrically charged. The HT circuit has voltages of up to 50 kV. If you ignore this warning,
you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.25
Do not touch or go near the HT or RF systems until the reservoir capacitors are fully discharged.
It is approximately 12 minutes before the capacitors discharge to a safe level. If you ignore this
warning, you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.26
Do not touch any part of the HT circuit unless you switch off all electrical power. Use the HT
discharge rod to fully discharge high voltage capacitors. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause fatal injury.
WARNING 5.27
Do not work in the modulator area with the modulator cover removed unless you wear a face
shield, a protective jacket, and protective gloves. If the diode D1 fails, shards of ceramic
material and dielectric oil may be ejected. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious
injury.
1 
If an HT PFN fault occurs, use the flowchart that follows to do the troubleshooting to
identify and correct the fault (see Figure 5.4).

5.2.1
Doing a test of the thyratron trigger pulse and cables
This is the procedure to do a test of the thyratron trigger pulse and cables.
Prerequisites
Oscilloscope
WARNING 5.28
Do not work in the modulator area with the modulator cover removed unless you wear a face
shield, a protective jacket, and protective gloves. If the diode D1 fails, shards of ceramic
material and dielectric oil may be ejected. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious
injury.
1 
At the service panel, connect an oscilloscope to the THY G2 test point
2 
Examine the waveform on the oscilloscope, make sure that the PFN charges and discharges
to 4 V or 8 V.
Note:
It is possible to do a check of the THY G2 signal if the equipment room door is open.
3 
If the PFN does not charge and discharge correctly, interchange the fiber-optic cable for a
replacement that you know is serviceable.
4 
Make sure that there are no warnings on the screen, for example, HT overtemperature.
5.2.2
Doing a test of the voltages of the pulse forming network
This is the procedure to do a test of the voltages of the pulse forming network (PFN) of the HT
system of the digital accelerator.
Prerequisites
Oscilloscope
WARNING 5.29
Do not work in the modulator area with the modulator cover removed unless you wear a face
shield, a protective jacket, and protective gloves. If the diode D1 fails, shards of ceramic
material and dielectric oil may be ejected. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious
injury.
1 
At the service panel connect an oscilloscope to the PFN V test point.
2 
Measure the signal.
3 
At the TCS, make sure that the status of Item 88 is 1 (charge enable).
4 
Do a check of the HE fiber-optic cable of the PFN.
5 
If it is necessary, interchange the HE fiber-optic cable for a replacement that you know is
serviceable.
6 
Do steps 1 to 3 for the low power mode.
7 
Do a check of the LE fiber-optic cable of the PFN.
8 
If it is necessary, interchange the LE fiber-optic cable for a replacement that you know is
serviceable.

Method D
1 
Use a multimeter in Ohmmeter mode to test a thyristor.
a
Connect the positive output lead of the multimeter to the anode and the negative
lead to the cathode.
b
Make sure that the multimeter shows no continuity.
2 
Short circuit the gate of the thyristor to the anode. Make sure that the multimeter shows
continuity through the thyristor.
Note:
When the gate short circuit is removed from the anode, conduction can stop or continue if the
multimeter supplies enough current to keep the device above its holding current level.
Note:
If the multimeter shows continuity through the thyristor before the gate is touched to the anode,
it shows that the thyristor is shorted.
Note:
If the multimeter will not show continuity through the thyristor after the gate was touched to the
anode, it shows that the thyristor is open circuit.

6.2
Removing the thyratron
This is the procedure to remove the thyratron from the modulator assembly in Area 30 of the
linear accelerator.
The thyratron is installed behind the rectifier unit of the magnetron filament.
WARNING 6.1
Do not do work on the linear accelerator without a second person near. The HT and RF systems
have high energy levels which can give you an electric shock. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause fatal injury.
WARNING 6.2
Do not do work on the high voltages areas of the system, until you switch off the HT circuit
breaker and discharge the charge circuit. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 6.3
Do not touch or go near the HT or RF systems until the reservoir capacitors are fully discharged.
It is approximately 12 minutes before the capacitors discharge to a safe level. If you ignore this
warning, you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 6.4
Do not work on the equipment if the gantry can move or is out of balance. Always attach the
gantry locking straps when you do work on the equipment. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
1 
Rotate the gantry to approximately 315° (-45°).
2 
Lock the gantry.

7.3.4
Operation of the gun warm up
With the NULL energy cal block loaded, after 30 minutes the gun current is increased to the value
set in Item 601 part 1 for 15 minutes. During the initial 15 minute warm up timers, the gun
current is also increased to this Item 601 part 1 level.
This function was included to help users with machines, that had cold start-up problems. It
greatly increases the gun filament wear out though. The value of part 1 of item 601 should be the

2.1
Overview
This chapter gives the information about the Treatment Control System (TCS) software items and 
parts.
2.1.1
Software items
To control and monitor the digital accelerator, the TCS software is divided into small packages 
known as items. All of the systems and subsystems of the machine, and many individual 
components, have related items.
There are three main types of item:
•
Receive items - which collect data from the digital accelerator and are connected to the 
RTUs in the RHCA, HTCA and ICCA
•
Transmit items - which send data to the digital accelerator and are connected to the RTUs 
in the RHCA, HTCA and ICCA
•
Control items - which take data from receive items and pass data to transmit items.
Each item has a unique identifying number: for example, i15, i200 and so on. At present, items i0 to 
i835 are assigned to the digital accelerator and the Precise Table, and items i2000 to i2271 are 
assigned to the MultiLeaf Collimator and Beam Modulator™. However, it should be noted that 
individual item numbers, the function of an item, and the range of item numbers are subject to 
change as equipment is developed. 
Detailed information on all software items is given in Section 2.1.5.
2.1.2
Parts
Each software item have many different parameters known as parts, which are arranged in a 
standard format. The parts change data values to actual MU (volts, amps, degrees, millimeters and 
so on). Conceptually, the parts can be considered as a database of several thousand parameters that 
are accessed by the software items at need. However, not all parts are used by every software item.
Detailed information on the parts is given in Section 2.5 for the digital accelerator and Precise 
Table, in Section 2.5 for the MultiLeaf Collimator, and in Section 2.6 for the Beam Modulator™.
2.1.3
Calibration blocks
The active, dynamic information about the digital accelerator is shown in a database. This database 
has the machine-specific settings (such as the electron gun current), and data that is specific to the 
selected energy.
The energy-specific information is shown in groups of data known as calibration blocks. The 
calibration block for the applicable energy is read by the software when the energy is selected, and is 
updated with new values when the Save Energy Cal. Blocks command is used.

2.3
Definitions of parts for the digital accelerator 
This section explains the purpose of significant parts used by the software items in the digital 
accelerator. It is applicable for Desktop Pro™ R7.0x and Integrity™ R1.x, some parts may not exist for 
earlier software releases but may be applicable to later software releases.
2.3.1
Parts 0 to 99
2.3.1.1
Part 1 - Setting value
This part contains the requested or required value.
2.3.1.2
Part 2 - Tolerance high
This part sets the high limit of the value in part 1.
2.3.1.3
Part 3 - Exception code
This part contains the exception code. For information on Exception codes see Chapter Appendix 
A.
2.3.1.4
Part 4 - Actual value
This part is the read back part in calibrated units. The value of part 4 is obtained by multiplying the 
valid value by the calibration gain divided by 2048. Thus:
part 4 = part 110 × (part 11/2048)
2.3.1.5
Part 5 - Change queue
This part defines default change queue.
2.3.1.6
Part 6 - Tolerance low
This part sets the low limit of the value in part 1.
2.3.1.7
Part 10 - Calibration offset
This part is the offset value that is applied to part 111 during calibration.
2.3.1.8
Part 11 - Calibration gain
This part is the gain value that is applied to part 110 during calibration.
2.3.1.9
Part 12 - Calibration inverse
This part is the inverse gain value that is applied to limits to obtain raw limits.
2.3.1.10
Part 13 - Access pointer
This part is the index to all fac 1 arrays and can be used together with the control pointer access to 
gain access to any variable in the system.

2.3.2
Parts 100 to 199
2.3.2.1
Part 101 - F1 item type
This part enables reduction of the Item type for use by Facility 1:
0 = Rx Integer 
1 = Tx Integer 
2 = Rx Boolean 
3 = Tx Boolean 
4 = Process types. 
2.3.2.2
Part 102 - F1 count 
Count of the number of times this channel has been transmitted (Tx), received (Rx) or processed.
2.3.2.3
Part 103 - Physical address
This part is the physical address of an item. It comprises of three elements that can be decoded from 
the value of the item:
RTU address from 0 to 5 (part 104)
Device address from 0 to 127
Read\write bit 0 or 1.
2.3.2.4
Part 104 - RTU address
This part is the address of the RTU to which the associated item points. It is part of the physical 
address. Only receive and transmit items have a direct connection to the hardware, but process items 
show an RTU address of 0 (ICCA-A) which is not true.
2.3.2.5
Part 105 - Device address
This part is the device address, indicating the PCB and channel with which the item is 
communicating
2.3.2.6
Part 106 - Read/Write address
This is the read/write address.
Read = 1
Write = 0.

2.3.2.7
Part 110 - Valid value
This part is the raw value that is added to the offset part. The value of part 110 is calculated by 
adding the calibration offset value part 10 to the raw data part 111.
2.3.2.8
Part 111 - Raw data
This part is the raw data read from an AI12 PCB or a DIE PCB. The raw data can be a 12-bit digital 
representation of an analog value from an AI12 PCB, or a binary value that is 1 bit of a 16-bit word 
from a DIE PCB. The value of part 111 is not the true value of the source data, due to 0 volt 
differences.
The value of part 14 distinguishes between incoming analog or digital data.
2.3.2.9
Part 112 - Required setting
This part is the required setting part, initially derived from part 1 × part 12 (inverse gain). For 
process items and stand-alone transmit items, part 112 is used as a set value. For servo process 
items, the value may be adjusted automatically by feedback when the servo is enabled.
2.3.2.10
Part 114 - Change raw value
This part is the accumulated error from the output of the servo process item. The part is used 
mainly in transmit items as the new set value, to correct any error in the corresponding transmit 
item.
2.3.2.11
Part 120 - Limit enable
When set enables Facility 1 log faults due to limit errors.
2.3.2.12
Part 121 - High limit binary
This part is uncalibrated units derived from part 19. Part 121 has the same function as part 19, but 
with different units. Thus:
part 121 = part 19 × (part 12/2048) + part 10
2.3.2.13
Part 122 - Low limit binary
This part is the uncalibrated units derived from part 20. Part 122 has the same function as part 20, 
but with different units. Thus:
part 122 = part 20 × (part 12/2048) + part 10
2.3.2.14
Part 123 - Absolute high limit
This part is the upper design limit. The part functions in the same way as part 121 but cannot be 
adjusted.
2.3.2.15
Part 124 - Absolute low limit
This part is the lower design limit. The part functions in the same way as part 122 but cannot be 
adjusted.
2.3.2.16
Part 125 - Max output
Clamps maximum value of Tx items.

Part 126 - Min output
Clamps minimum value of Tx items
2.3.2.18
Part 127 - Limit fault

2.3.2.19
Part 130 - Process/filter identification
This part is the process identification part: for example, the filter type for receive items.
For items that display the value -32767 when HT is Off, the real value can be displayed by setting the 
value of part 130 to 10.
2.3.2.20
Part 131 - Parameter 1 function
The function of part 131 varies, depending on the item in which it is contained. 
For example, in movement start items, part 131 is the gain value of the check potentiometer.
2.3.2.21
Part 132 - Parameter 2 function
The function of part 132 varies, depending on the item in which it is contained. 
For example, in movement start items, part 132 is the offset value of the check potentiometer.
2.3.2.22
Part 133 - Parameter 3 function
The function of part 133 varies, depending on the item in which it is contained. 
For check potentiometer items, part 133 is the amount by which the value of the check 
potentiometer can vary from that of the coarse potentiometer without an error.
For steering servo items 2R and 2T, part 133 is a pointer to the lookup table that the item is using. 
Thus:
2R low = 0
2T low =1
2R high = 2
2T high = 3
2R mid = 4
2T mid =5
2.3.2.23
Part 134 - Parameter 4 function
The function of part 134 varies, depending on the item in which it is contained.
For demand items, part 134 contains the quadratic gain.
For the light field item, part 134 is the time delay before the light is switched Off.
For movement control items, part 134 is the raw value of the maximum permitted unexpected 
movement.
For magnet systems, the change threshold should be 1.
2.3.2.24
Part 135 - Parameter 5 function
The function of part 135 varies, depending on the item in which it is contained.
For demand items, part 135 contains the linear gain.

This part is used to determine the separation between closed leaves (in units of 0.1 mm).

Gantry/collimator rotation gradient (of ramp up) feed-forward demand.

Part 194 - Dynamic gain
This is used to scale the speed contribution derived from the dose per loop during dynamic therapy.
2.5.1.7
Part 195 - Desired
This part returns the desired position of the diaphragm in same units as raw value (part 101).
2.5.1.8
Part 216 - Scaled speed
This part is the speed demand sent to the BLD.

This is used to calculate the positional tolerance to be used when checking the dynamic positioning

This is the distance that must be moved before the system has overcome any inertia, in units of 0.01

The Normal Dose Rate (NDR) Beam Start Up (BSU) transient tolerance offset is the offset added to

Minimum value = 0
Maximum value = 900

of the step or restart from pause, in units of 0.01 degrees and 0.1 mm (for leaves).
Default value = 50
Minimum value = 0
Maximum value = 450

the gantry/collimator/diaphragm/PSS tolerance accumulator.

Maximum value = 150

0.01 degrees (for gantry/collimator) and 0.1 mm (for leaves/diaphragm).

Minimum value = 1
Maximum value = 8
2.5.1.28
Part 237 - NDR transient tolerance time
This is the number of cycles before the tolerance accumulator is reduced.
Default value = 15
Minimum value = 0
Maximum value = 35

1.1
Important safety instructions
It is important to install, operate, maintain, and dispose of the equipment according to the
information in the product documentation, and in compliance with local regulations. For the
safety of the users and the patients, before a user operates or works on the equipment, they
must read, understand, and obey all:
•
Warnings, cautions, instructions, and notes in this document and the related
documents.
•
Safety instructions, emergency procedures, and information in this document and the
related documents.
•
Warnings, cautions, and safety markings on the equipment and the accessories of the
equipment.
If you have local work instructions for the equipment, then Elekta recommends that you include
the warnings, cautions, and notes from this document in your local work instructions.
1.1.1
Conventions for warnings, cautions, and notes
The conventions give information about the class and the level of the risk in the warnings and
cautions, and the content of notes.
WARNING 1.1
A warning is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of fatal or serious
injury, injury, or clinical mistreatment, if you do not obey the instructions.
CAUTION 1.1
A caution is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of damage to the
equipment, data, or the environment, if you do not obey the instructions.
Note:
A note gives more information about a related text.
1.1.2
Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can
keep the equipment safe to operate.
WARNING 1.2
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each
week of the year. If the equipment is used more frequently than this, the frequency of the
planned maintenance must increase accordingly and the extended life checks must also be
brought forward accordingly.

Safety precautions
1.2.1
Safety precautions for the compatibility of the equipment
WARNING 1.3
Do not use parts, accessories, or other equipment, without approval by Elekta of their
compatibility. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury and damage to the
equipment.
Only operate the equipment with Elekta supplied or approved, compatible equipment or parts.
Accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by or do not have the approval of
Elekta can cause an incorrect treatment delivery. They can also have an effect on the performance
of the electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), which can increase the emissions or decrease the
immunity of the equipment.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of other equipment or parts.
1.2.2
Safety precautions for the electromagnetic compatibility
The design and manufacture of Elekta products is in compliance with applicable EMC standards.
The intended result of the standards is to minimize the risk of electromagnetic interference by RF
devices. The type of device and the distance to the equipment has an effect on the intensity of
the electromagnetic interference. The equipment includes the linear accelerator and accessories,
the control cabinets, the computers in the control room, and equipment from other
manufacturer.
