4.11.7
VMAT - A description of the Inertia Compensation Distance (ICD)
The geometry parameters do not always move at the maximum velocity. The geometry
parameters have inertia, that is, time is necessary for them to increase and decrease in speed.
The control system makes the adjustments for the inertia of geometry parameters. It causes them
to move temporarily faster than their maximum velocity until they are in the correct position.
The software takes account of the inertia compensation distance, when it calculates the
movement time for each geometry parameter.
For distances above the ICD the movement time is correctly specified as Distance / Maximum
velocity.
For distances less than ICD the movement time is approximate as the delivery time is not easily
predicted.
In the worst condition the movement time must be less than the time to go to the ICD (that is,
Inertia Compensation Distance / Maximum velocity). In the best condition the geometry item has
an initial velocity equal to the maximum velocity, in this case the movement time is Distance /
Maximum velocity.
The linear accelerator server does approximate between these two values based on the initial
velocity to estimate the movement time.
When a change of direction is necessary the angular velocity at start for the step is assumed to be
zero, the gantry is decreased in speed by the control system.

Doing a check of the jockey wheels
7.3.1
Doing a functional check of the jockey wheels
The jockey wheels stop forward and rearward movement of the gantry drum during rotation.
1 
Make sure that the linear accelerator is in a balanced condition.
2 
Set the gantry arm to 180°.
3 
Rotate the gantry through 360° and look at the jockey wheels.
4 
Make sure that only two of the jockey wheels touch the rim of the gantry drum during
rotation.
5 
Do steps 1 to 4 two more times.
6 
If it is necessary, do steps 1 to 5 again.
7 
If it is necessary, adjust the jockey wheels.
Related Links:
Doing the set up of the jockey wheels on page 133
7.3.2
Doing the set up of the jockey wheels
1 
Make a clean, lint-free cloth moist with a cleaning agent, and clean the rim of the gantry
drum.
2 
Move the gantry to the position at which all three jockey wheels touch the gantry drum at
the same time.
3 
To adjust the jockey wheel on the gantry motor side of the gantry base, move the gantry
limit switch away from the jockey wheel.
4 
Loosen one of the front adjustable jockey wheels.
5 
Set a clearance of 0.2 mm between the jockey wheel and the rim of the gantry drum.
6 
Rotate the gantry and make sure that only two jockey wheels are in contact with the gantry
drum.
7 
If three jockey wheels touch the gantry drum, stop the rotation immediately.
8 
Do 4 to 7 again, until only two jockey wheels are in contact with the gantry drum during
rotation.
9 
If it is necessary, move the gantry limit switch to its initial position.

7.11
Calibrating the movement speeds
The TCS uses the maximum velocity and the ICD for each movement to calculate the dose rate for
each step of a VMAT delivery. The default value for maximum velocity is the maximum speed of
the movement. The ICD is the distance necessary for each movement to be at its maximum
velocity. The default value of the ICD is the recommended value for that movement.
Each of the geometry parameters have a maximum velocity at which they can move. Therefore,
the TCS uses the maximum velocity and the ICD for each movement to calculate the necessary
dose rate. The TCS does this for each step of the VMAT radiation delivery. When the movement
cannot keep up with the delivery, radiation delivery pauses. When this occurs the maximum
velocity or the ICD are too high, compared to the movement. You can decrease the values as a
temporary solution until you repair the movement speed.

1.1
Document scope
This Planned Maintenance manual (PMM) describes the regular maintenance tasks and the
extended life checks that must be done to linear accelerators. The intended audience is qualified
service engineers. These can be engineers employed directly by Elekta, qualified representatives
of Elekta, or qualified representatives of the customers of Elekta.
Use this document together with the applicable corrective maintenance manual for information
on the necessary safety precautions and how to do related maintenance tasks and procedures.
This document supersedes all the related planned maintenance manuals for the applicable
treatment table, XVI, and iViewGT subsystems.
If you find an error in this document, or identify a possible improvement, raise a case in the
Customer Lifecycle Management (CLM) system, or an Engineering Change Request (ECR) in the
Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) system.

1.2
Description of the planned maintenance
It is necessary to do regular planned maintenance tasks to keep the operation of the system safe
and satisfactory. The regular planned maintenance checks help to prevent a sudden malfunction
with subsequent repair and downtime of the equipment.
This document gives information on the procedures to do the necessary planned maintenance
checks. It also gives you the planned maintenance tasks for extended service life, after 10 years of
normal use.
If a planned maintenance is unsatisfactory, do the necessary troubleshooting and repair to correct
the fault.
1.3
Description of the different types of maintenance
This manual gives information on the necessary tasks to do the planned maintenance checks.
There are three types of planned maintenance checks:
•
Safety - The mandatory checks that you must do for the protection of the patient, the
User, and the equipment.
•
Performance - The mandatory checks that you must do because they have an effect on
the performance of the system.
•
Reliability - The recommended checks that help the continued reliability of the system.
1.4
Description of the check table information
Each of the planned maintenance checks has a table, which gives this information:
•
The interval in months between the checks.
•
The category of the check (Safety, Reliability or Performance).
•
The time in minutes to do the check.
•
It is necessary to do a quality assurance check.
The example in Figure 1.1 tells you:
•
To do this check at 12-monthly intervals.
•
It is a performance check.
•
40 minutes is necessary to do this check.
•
Tell the User to do a quality assurance check before the start of clinical operation.

2.1
Important safety instructions
It is important to install, operate, maintain, and dispose of the equipment according to the
information in the product documentation, and in compliance with local regulations. For the
safety of the users and the patients, before a user operates or works on the equipment, they
must read, understand, and obey all:
•
Warnings, cautions, instructions, and notes in this document and the related
documents.
•
Safety instructions, emergency procedures, and information in this document and the
related documents.
•
Warnings, cautions, and safety markings on the equipment and the accessories of the
equipment.
If you have local work instructions for the equipment, then Elekta recommends that you include
the warnings, cautions, and notes from this document in your local work instructions.
2.1.1
Conventions for warnings, cautions, and notes
The conventions give information about the class and the level of the risk in the warnings and
cautions, and the content of notes.
WARNING 2.1
A warning is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of fatal or serious
injury, injury, or clinical mistreatment, if you do not obey the instructions.
CAUTION 2.1
A caution is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of damage to the
equipment, data, or the environment, if you do not obey the instructions.
Note:
A note gives more information about a related text.
2.1.2
Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can
keep the equipment safe to operate.
WARNING 2.2
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each
week of the year. If the equipment is used more frequently than this, the frequency of the
planned maintenance must increase accordingly and the extended life checks must also be
brought forward accordingly.

Safety precautions
2.2.1
Safety precautions for the compatibility of the equipment
WARNING 2.3
Do not use parts, accessories, or other equipment, without approval by Elekta of their
compatibility. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury and damage to the
equipment.
Only operate the equipment with Elekta supplied or approved, compatible equipment or parts.
Accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by or do not have the approval of
Elekta can cause an incorrect treatment delivery. They can also have an effect on the performance
of the electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), which can increase the emissions or decrease the
immunity of the equipment.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of other equipment or parts.
2.2.2
Safety precautions for the electromagnetic compatibility
The design and manufacture of Elekta products is in compliance with applicable EMC standards.
The intended result of the standards is to minimize the risk of electromagnetic interference by RF
devices. The type of device and the distance to the equipment has an effect on the intensity of
the electromagnetic interference. The equipment includes the linear accelerator and accessories,

the control cabinets, the computers in the control room, and equipment from other
manufacturer.
It is necessary to have special precautions for EMC emissions. Elekta recommends that you obey
these precautions when you use RF devices near the equipment.
•
Do not use RF devices unless they are in compliance with international standards for
electromagnetic compatibility, for example, the CE or FCC mark.
•
Do not use a two-way emergency radio in the treatment room or the control room.
Only use an emergency radio if there is an emergency.
•
Do not use cellular telephones, or other devices with cellular modems near the
equipment. The Instructions for Use contains information on the minimum safe
distance of these devices from the equipment.
•
When you use a device that is enabled for wireless operation, it must be a minimum of
10 cm from the equipment.
•
Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID) readers, when activated to do a scan of a RFID
tag, must be a minimum of one meter from the equipment.
Note:
The RFID systems that Elekta supply use lower power levels. You can safely use these RFID systems
when you obey the procedures in the Instructions for Use for the product.
The system must be installed, put into service, and maintained in compliance with the EMC
information in the Instructions for Use.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of parts and equipment.
WARNING 2.4
Do not put portable or mobile radio frequency (RF) communication devices near to the
equipment. The emissions from such RF devices can be more than the EMC standards, and can
have unwanted effects on the equipment operation. If you ignore this warning, the RF
emissions can cause the equipment to have a malfunction. A malfunction can cause fatal injury,
clinical mistreatment, or damage to the equipment.
WARNING 2.5
Do not use accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by Elekta. They can have
an effect on the EMC performance, which can increase EMC emissions or decrease the
immunity to RF interference of the equipment. If you ignore this warning, incorrect radiation
delivery and other malfunctions can occur, which can cause fatal injury or clinical mistreatment.

2.2.14
Safety precaution for the removal of parts from the radiation head
WARNING 2.22
Do not touch the flight tube, bending magnet, or other parts near to them until a check for
induced radioactivity is completed. Excessive exposure to radioactivity is dangerous. If you
ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.
After the operation of the linear accelerator at high energy, the parts in the radiation head can
become radioactive and a radiation hazard. Before you do work on, or remove parts from the
radiation head, use a calibrated radiation detector to measure the level of induced radioactivity.
Use the applicable safety procedures when you remove radioactive parts and material. The
maximum dose rate for the safe removal of radioactive parts and material is 50 µSv/hr
(microsievert per hour). Do not remove the radioactive parts and material from the treatment
room before they are correctly prepared for safe removal.
2.2.15
Safety precautions for maintenance, modification, and
decommissioning
WARNING 2.23
Do not do work, or make modifications to the equipment without the correct training and
authority. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury, clinical mistreatment, and
damage to the equipment.
Only do work on, or make modifications to, the equipment if you are an Elekta approved person
with the applicable authority. Such work must use best practice and obey the laws and
regulations in the jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed.
Modifications or work that does not have approval by Elekta, and is not done by an Elekta
approved person with the correct authority, can cause:
•
Fatal injury
•
Incorrect radiation delivery
•
Malfunction of the equipment
•
Damage to the equipment
•
The warranty to be canceled.
2.2.16
Safety precautions for work in areas of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for work in areas of induced radioactivity are the precautions to prevent
an excessive exposure to, and serious injury from, induced radioactivity.
When you operate or do work on the equipment, Elekta recommends that you use the applicable
radiation protection functions, devices, systems, procedures, and accessories. Always obey the
applicable laws and regulations for induced radioactivity for the jurisdiction in which the
equipment is installed.
The safety precautions are applicable to:
•
Maintenance, modifications, and decommissioning
•
Measurement of the induced radioactivity
•
Removal and movement of parts with induced radioactivity.

2.2.16.1
Safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity are the necessary safety
precautions to know to prevent excessive exposure to radioactivity, which can cause serious
injury or damage to the environment.
Always use two radiation detectors to measure the level of induced radioactivity. Only use
radiation detectors that have an applicable calibration certificate. The period of time since the
last calibration date must be less than 12 months. Do not use the radiation detectors if the period
of time since the last calibration date is more than 12 months.
WARNING 2.24
Do not move radioactive material (by air, sea, or land) unless you obey the applicable laws and
regulations for induced radioactivity and disposal of radioactive material of the jurisdictions
through which the movement occurs. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury
and damage to the environment.
2.2.16.2
Safety precautions for handling parts with induced radioactivity
The handling of parts with induced radioactivity must comply with the laws and regulations of the
jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed. The safe levels of radiation applicable in the UK
do not apply in all jurisdictions. The permitted level of radioactivity must always be as low as
reasonably achievable (ALARA). This level may vary depending on local rules, therefore the safe
working levels from the applicable local rules must be considered as the acceptable working limit.
If there are no safe levels available for a jurisdiction, use the UK value as a guideline, which is a
maximum of 150 cps at the surface for a maximum duration of 72 minutes. The following table
shows the conversion from this value to other units.

2.3.2
Recommendations for emergency procedures
Before you use the equipment, Elekta recommends that you know all the local emergency
procedures and the locations of all the emergency switches.
The Elekta equipment includes:
•
The STOP MOTORS buttons on the handheld controllers and user interface panels in
the treatment room, and FKP in the control room.
When you press these buttons, it disconnects the electrical supply from the motors,
stops all movements of the equipment, and stops kV and MV radiation.
•
The EMERGENCY POWER OFF buttons in the treatment room, control area, and areas
near the equipment.
When you operate these buttons, it disconnects the electrical supply to the linear
accelerator. The buttons disconnect the electrical supply from many electrical circuits,
but not from all the circuits.

3.1.3
Disposal of the equipment
End of life (EOL) disposal is the procedure to disassemble, remove, and discard the equipment, in
full or in parts, to a condition where it is not possible to operate the equipment for its intended
use.
Only a Qualified Expert (QE) and an approved facility with an applicable license, may remove and
discard the equipment and recycle the material.
A full description of disposal requirements is detailed in a separate document Product Disposal
Information. This document is available on request from Elekta.
The customer owns the data on the storage media. If there are any data storage media such as
HDDs, remove them from the device and hand them to the customer for disposal. If the customer
entrusts the disposal team to dispose of the data, the data must be destroyed in accordance with
relevant cybersecurity regulations.

4.1
Description of the planned maintenance tasks
This document gives the procedures to do safety, reliability and performance related planned
maintenance checks for the system. The document also contains a set of checklists to record the
results of the planned maintenance checks.
If a planned maintenance check identifies a defect, you must do the necessary corrective action
to make the equipment serviceable again.
The planned maintenance checks of the system are usually completed at the specified intervals.
Before you start a planned maintenance check, you must make a copy of the checklist, and
complete it for each planned maintenance check.

This document does not contain the times to do the corrective maintenance or physics QA after a

If you find a damaged or defective part during a planned maintenance check, replace the part
with a new part with the applicable part number. You must then do the maintenance procedure
again to make sure that the new part is serviceable.
If the correct service part is not available, the Service User must contact the applicable business
unit.
Use this information with the applicable Corrective Maintenance information procedures.

5.1
Preparing for the planned maintenance
Before you start the planned maintenance, make sure that you:
•
Make a copy of the applicable checklist.
•
Have a copy of the applicable Results list.
Note:
You do not have to use the Results list if you put all the results from the planned maintenance
checks in the Planned Maintenance database.
For more information on how to use the checklist, see Recording the planned maintenance
results.

5.12.6.2
Description of the Agility™ MLC calibration
This workflow runs tests to calibrate the Agility™ MLC leaf bank. If it is necessary, you can save
the new calibration values. If you do not save the new calibration values, all previous calibration
values are restored.
The workflow does these tests:
1 
Mechanical Diaphragm Calibration
This test calculates the gain calibration and offsets for each diaphragm. It does not use
radiation.
2 
Optical System Calibration
This test calculates the gain calibration and offsets for each leaf. It does not use radiation.
3 
Position of MV Detector Panel
4 
Pixel Size
This test calculates the ratio of millimeters at isocenter to MV detector panel pixels. The
workflow uses the ratio to display test results in millimeters at isocenter.
5 
Radiation Center
This test finds the center of rotation of the radiation beam.
6 
Diaphragm Calibration
This test does the fine calibration of the diaphragms. It finds the correct position of each
diaphragm from the radiation center.
7 
Leaf Calibration
This test does the fine calibration of the leaves. It finds the correct position of each leaf
from the radiation center.

buttons diametrically opposite on the BLD. The two buttons drive the BLD in the corresponding
direction. The set up is such that the initial speed can be set much slower than the final speed for
the fine adjustment of the BLD angle.

–
Part 132 sets the initial, slow speed
–
Part 131 sets the time period for which this speed is maintained (in cycles)
–
Part 133 sets the next time period over which ramp-up to maximum speed occurs.
Note:
Part 133 must therefore always be greater than part 131.
2 
The default values for the head control items are as follows for Items 351 and 352:
–
Part 121: 3000
–
Part 122: 1000

8.1.1
Description of the task to replace the crosswire screen (Agility™)
The crosswire screen gives protection from the UV light which the BLD emits. Because of the wear
of the crosswire screen, it must be replaced after a maximum time period of 3 years.
The replacement task should be combined with the check Doing the optical system check (Agility)
to prevent duplicated work.

Examining the alignment of the crosswires (Agility™) on page 163
Doing the optical system check (Agility™) on page 162
8.1.2
Description of the task to replace the Mylar® mirror (Agility™)
Because of the wear of the Mylar® mirror, it must be replaced after a maximum time period of 3
years.
The replacement task should be combined with the check Doing the optical system check (Agility)
to prevent duplicated work.
Related Links:
Doing the optical system check (Agility™) on page 162

12.1
Introduction to the extended service life tasks
It is necessary to do regular planned maintenance and safety audit checks to keep the operation
of the system safe and satisfactory. The regular planned maintenance checks help to prevent a
sudden malfunction with subsequent repair and downtime of the equipment.
WARNING 12.1
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
This document gives the necessary procedures to do the planned maintenance checks for
extended service life, after 10 years of normal use.
The usual planned maintenance tasks continue after the 10 years of normal use. The additional
extended service life are then added to the planned maintenance schedule, in the frequency
specified for the extended service life checks.

WARNING 12.2
Do not work on the linear accelerator before you know the date and time of when the system

linear accelerator can be configured to stay in an Initialized state when not in working hours. If
you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury.

13.1
Recording the planned maintenance results
An approved Elekta service engineer must record that the planned maintenance tasks were done,
and the applicable corrective actions, measurements, and results. The tool used to make the
measurement shall be recorded, this includes its serial number. The status of the result is usually
recorded as one of:
•
Not Applicable, A
•
Completed as specified
•
Done by customer, C
•
Test Fail, F, with the details why the check failed
•
Not done at customer request, N, with the name of the contact person who made the
request
•
Test Pass, P
•
Test Pass, P, following repair with the details of the repair
•
Not Done, X, with an explanation why the test was not done.
The Elekta Customer Lifecycle Management (CLM) system is usually the system that you use to
record this information.
Note:
It is possible that a different system is used to record the results, for example the Planned
Maintenance database, or that the results must be recorded manually in a Results list at the
request of the User.
Note:
Follow the procedures for the applicable region. If it is necessary to attach an electronic copy of a
completed Results list to the servicing work order, you can use the applicable Results list in this
manual.
1 
Follow the specified procedures in this manual to do all the applicable planned
maintenance tasks for the planned maintenance inspection visit.
2 
When you complete a task, record that the planned maintenance check is satisfactory or
that a corrective action is necessary. Record the applicable measurements and results.
3 
Complete the applicable CLM records.
13.1.1
Using the Results list for the extended service life
Note:
You do not have to use the Results lists if you put all the results from the checks in the Planned
Maintenance database.
Before you start a inspection, read and understand the steps that follow:
1 
Make a copy of the applicable Results list for the extended service life, and the applicable
monthly or annual PM check.
2 
Use the procedures in this document to do checks that the system is operational after the
10 years or normal use. Make sure that a representative of the customer is available to
attend the checks.
The representative must sign and date the checklist when the tasks are completed.
3 
When you complete a task, write in the Results list to show that the check has Passed or
Failed. If necessary, add corrective actions to the Comments column.
4 
When all the checks and tasks are completed, you and the User, or their representative,
must sign and date the Results list.

1.1
Document scope
The corrective maintenance manual (CMM) helps service engineers troubleshoot, repair and
maintain the systems, subsystems and components of the linear accelerator. The target audience
is qualified service engineers. These may be engineers employed directly by Elekta, qualified
representatives of Elekta or qualified representatives of Elekta's customers.
The manual provides:
•
A description of the system or sub-system in question.
•
A troubleshooting section to identify the problem areas.
•
A set of detailed procedures used to replace FRUs (field replaceable units).
•
A section on how to return the device to work.
If you find any mistakes in this document, or identify areas for improvement, please raise a CLM
(customer lifecycle management) case and assign it to the relevant queue.

The role of Radiation Therapists, also referred to as Radiotherapists, Radiation

different regions and sites.
Note: Radiation Therapists are trained on all aspects of system operation, but
not trained on installation, calibration or service maintenance.
Note: Radiation Therapists who work at the site when the system is installed
will be trained by an Elekta trainer. After the system is introduced, Elekta
authorized trainers, or experienced Radiation Therapists who are already
trained on the equipment, can train Radiation Therapists who are new to the
equipment.

1.4
Glossary of terms
Table 1.3
Glossary of terms
Term
Definition
Autotrack function
The autotrack function automatically moves the diaphragms or
leaves to their prescribed position.
Cal block
The Cal block contains the item and part values that, when
loaded, configure the linear accelerator for a given energy.
Clinical Mode
In Clinical Mode, Clinical Users use the linear accelerator and its
accessories for the radiation therapy treatment that a licensed
medical practitioner prescribes.
Gating
Gating is the procedure by which an external system or manual
task pauses and starts the radiation delivery as a result of
information received relating to the treatment position of the
patient.
Interdigitation
Interdigitation is an overlap of the opposite adjacent leaves of a
multileaf collimator.
Service life
Service life is the length of time that the regular servicing and
repair procedures can keep the machine in operation.
Service Mode
In Service Mode, Service Users do the necessary maintenance
tasks and calibration of the equipment.

2.1
Important safety instructions
It is important to install, operate, maintain, and dispose of the equipment according to the
information in the product documentation, and in compliance with local regulations. For the
safety of the users and the patients, before a user operates or works on the equipment, they
must read, understand, and obey all:
•
Warnings, cautions, instructions, and notes in this document and the related
documents.
•
Safety instructions, emergency procedures, and information in this document and the
related documents.
•
Warnings, cautions, and safety markings on the equipment and the accessories of the
equipment.
If you have local work instructions for the equipment, then Elekta recommends that you include
the warnings, cautions, and notes from this document in your local work instructions.
2.1.1
Conventions for warnings, cautions, and notes
The conventions give information about the class and the level of the risk in the warnings and
cautions, and the content of notes.
WARNING 2.1
A warning is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of fatal or serious
injury, injury, or clinical mistreatment, if you do not obey the instructions.
CAUTION 2.1
A caution is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of damage to the
equipment, data, or the environment, if you do not obey the instructions.
Note:
A note gives more information about a related text.
2.1.2
Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can
keep the equipment safe to operate.
WARNING 2.2
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each
week of the year. If the equipment is used more frequently than this, the frequency of the
planned maintenance must increase accordingly and the extended life checks must also be
brought forward accordingly.

Safety precautions
2.2.1
Safety precautions for the compatibility of the equipment
WARNING 2.3
Do not use parts, accessories, or other equipment, without approval by Elekta of their
compatibility. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury and damage to the
equipment.
Only operate the equipment with Elekta supplied or approved, compatible equipment or parts.
Accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by or do not have the approval of
Elekta can cause an incorrect treatment delivery. They can also have an effect on the performance
of the electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), which can increase the emissions or decrease the
immunity of the equipment.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of other equipment or parts.
2.2.2
Safety precautions for the electromagnetic compatibility
The design and manufacture of Elekta products is in compliance with applicable EMC standards.
The intended result of the standards is to minimize the risk of electromagnetic interference by RF
devices. The type of device and the distance to the equipment has an effect on the intensity of
the electromagnetic interference. The equipment includes the linear accelerator and accessories,
the control cabinets, the computers in the control room, and equipment from other
manufacturer.

It is necessary to have special precautions for EMC emissions. Elekta recommends that you obey
these precautions when you use RF devices near the equipment.
•
Do not use RF devices unless they are in compliance with international standards for
electromagnetic compatibility, for example, the CE or FCC mark.
•
Do not use a two-way emergency radio in the treatment room or the control room.
Only use an emergency radio if there is an emergency.
•
Do not use cellular telephones, or other devices with cellular modems near the
equipment. The Instructions for Use contains information on the minimum safe
distance of these devices from the equipment.
•
When you use a device that is enabled for wireless operation, it must be a minimum of
10 cm from the equipment.
•
Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID) readers, when activated to do a scan of a RFID
tag, must be a minimum of one meter from the equipment.
Note:
The RFID systems that Elekta supply use lower power levels. You can safely use these RFID systems
when you obey the procedures in the Instructions for Use for the product.
The system must be installed, put into service, and maintained in compliance with the EMC
information in the Instructions for Use.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of parts and equipment.
WARNING 2.4
Do not put portable or mobile radio frequency (RF) communication devices near to the
equipment. The emissions from such RF devices can be more than the EMC standards, and can
have unwanted effects on the equipment operation. If you ignore this warning, the RF
emissions can cause the equipment to have a malfunction. A malfunction can cause fatal injury,
clinical mistreatment, or damage to the equipment.
WARNING 2.5
Do not use accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by Elekta. They can have
an effect on the EMC performance, which can increase EMC emissions or decrease the
immunity to RF interference of the equipment. If you ignore this warning, incorrect radiation
delivery and other malfunctions can occur, which can cause fatal injury or clinical mistreatment.

Safety precaution for the removal of parts from the radiation head
WARNING 2.21
Do not touch the flight tube, bending magnet, or other parts near to them until a check for

After the operation of the linear accelerator at high energy, the parts in the radiation head can
become radioactive and a radiation hazard. Before you do work on, or remove parts from the
radiation head, use a calibrated radiation detector to measure the level of induced radioactivity.
Use the applicable safety procedures when you remove radioactive parts and material. The
maximum dose rate for the safe removal of radioactive parts and material is 50 µSv/hr
(microsievert per hour). Do not remove the radioactive parts and material from the treatment
room before they are correctly prepared for safe removal.

with the applicable authority. Such work must use best practice and obey the laws and
regulations in the jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed.

Fatal injury

Incorrect radiation delivery

Malfunction of the equipment

equipment is installed.

•

•

2.2.16.1
Safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity are the necessary safety
precautions to know to prevent excessive exposure to radioactivity, which can cause serious
injury or damage to the environment.
Always use two radiation detectors to measure the level of induced radioactivity. Only use
radiation detectors that have an applicable calibration certificate. The period of time since the
last calibration date must be less than 12 months. Do not use the radiation detectors if the period
of time since the last calibration date is more than 12 months.
WARNING 2.23
Do not move radioactive material (by air, sea, or land) unless you obey the applicable laws and
regulations for induced radioactivity and disposal of radioactive material of the jurisdictions
through which the movement occurs. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury
and damage to the environment.
2.2.16.2
Safety precautions for handling parts with induced radioactivity
The handling of parts with induced radioactivity must comply with the laws and regulations of the
jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed. The safe levels of radiation applicable in the UK
do not apply in all jurisdictions. The permitted level of radioactivity must always be as low as
reasonably achievable (ALARA). This level may vary depending on local rules, therefore the safe
working levels from the applicable local rules must be considered as the acceptable working limit.
If there are no safe levels available for a jurisdiction, use the UK value as a guideline, which is a
maximum of 150 cps at the surface for a maximum duration of 72 minutes. The following table
shows the conversion from this value to other units.

Disposal of the equipment
End of life (EOL) disposal is the procedure to disassemble, remove, and discard the equipment, in
full or in parts, to a condition where it is not possible to operate the equipment for its intended
use.
Only a Qualified Expert (QE) and an approved facility with an applicable license, may remove and
discard the equipment and recycle the material.
A full description of disposal requirements is detailed in a separate document Product Disposal
Information. This document is available on request from Elekta.
The customer owns the data on the storage media. If there are any data storage media such as
HDDs, remove them from the device and hand them to the customer for disposal. If the customer
entrusts the disposal team to dispose of the data, the data must be destroyed in accordance with
relevant cybersecurity regulations.

4.1
Overview of the power supplies and interlocks
The digital accelerator uses high voltages, makes hazardous radiation, and has parts that move
automatically. For the protection of patients and other persons near to the machine, the control
system of the digital accelerator has a number of safety circuits. The safety circuits operate
different interlocks that prevent the operation of the digital accelerator if there are hazardous
conditions.
4.2
Description of the electrical power supplies of the linear
accelerator
The linear accelerator supplies electrical power for a number of user systems and subsystems.
The user systems are the:
•
Three-phase electrical power supply
•
Low voltage power supplies (high current)
•
Low tension (LT) power supplies (low power)
•
Interlock system.

4.3
Description of the electrical power supplies to the linear
accelerator
The linear accelerator connects to three-phase electrical supplies from the hospital electrical
power supply. The electrical supplies are:
•
220 VAC to 250 V AC, or
•
380 VAC to 440 VAC.
The linear accelerator gets its primary three-phase electrical supply through an isolator in the
control room. The isolator sets the electrical power on and off.
The isolator supplies the electrical power supply to the reeling interface cabinet (RIC). The RIC
contains the circuit breakers and contactors, through which the electrical supplies go to the
different user systems.

4.4
Description of the mains power supply connections in the
RIC
The three-phase mains power supply to the reeling interface cabinet (RIC) connects to the screw
connectors on terminal block TS73A in Area 73. The connectors are:
•
TS73A-34 for phase 1 (A)
•
TS73A-35 for phase 2 (B)
•
TS73A-36 for phase 3 (C)
•
TS73A-37 for neutral (N).
Each of the line fuses has a fuse rating of 40 A.
The primary ground (earth) connection of the mains power supply connects to ground (earth)
terminal 1 (ET1) in the bottom of the RIC.
4.5
Description of the client interface supplies
The client interface supplies are customer specified power supplies. The reeling interface cabinet
(RIC) sends the client interface supplies through a mains distribution unit (MDU) to the treatment
control cabinet (TCC). The TCC supplies the client interface supplies to the related user systems,
which are the:
•
Vacuum system
•
Room lights
•
Wall lasers
•
Ready alarm circuit
•
Radiation alarm circuit
•
External water cooler remote start.
A stand-alone uninterruptible power supply (UPS) or the MDU supply power to the peripheral
equipment in the TCC.
Note:
Some of the subsystems get their power supply through the client interface which is not part of
the three phase electrical supply. Some of the subsystems can have power applied when the three
phase isolator is set to OFF.
4.6
Description of the low voltage power supply unit
The LV PSU is in Area 13 on the gantry. A thyristor controls the operation of the LV PSU to supply a
constant current DC power supply. The LV PSU supplies current for the focus, bending magnet and
magnetron magnet systems. The LT contactor system controls the mains power supply to the
LV PSU.

When the contactors energize, the contacts of the contactors close. The closed contacts of the
contactors supply the applicable electrical supply to the correct system.
If the system operates correctly:
•
The hardware interlock chains send a +24 V signal to energize the related contactors.
•
Each hardware interlock chain has a number of directly connected switches and relay
contacts in the +24 V supply line to the related contactor.
•
Each switch or relay is set by an interlock condition (for example, EMERGENCY STOP).
•
When all the interlock conditions are set, the switch and relay contacts in the interlock
chain stay closed to supply +24 V to the contactor.
If an interlock fault condition occurs:
•
The monitor circuit senses the condition.
•
The monitor circuit sends a signal which opens the contacts of the related switch or
relay. This breaks the interlock chain and removes the +24 V power supply from the
related contactor.
•
The contacts of the contactor open to remove the mains power supply from the
related system.
4.8.2.1
Description of the main interlock circuit
The main interlock circuit controls the 24 V power supply to the main system contactor, CON-A.
This is the first device in a chain of contactors which are connected in series with the three-phase
mains power supply. When only CON-A is energized, the machine state is always System On.
The EMERGENCY OFF switches in the treatment room and the control room are part of the main
interlock circuit. Operation of an EMERGENCY OFF switch removes the three-phase mains power
supply from the digital accelerator.

4.8.2.2
Description of the LT interlocks
The LT interlocks circuit controls the low voltage, three-phase power supplies of the digital
accelerator. The LT interlock operates LT contactors CON-F and CON-H. The contacts of these are
connected in series with the mains power supply to the LV PSU. When the contactors CON-F,
CON-H and CON-A are energized, the machine state of the digital accelerator is Closed.
The LT interlock conditions for operation are:
•
The LT circuit breaker is on
•
The TCS enables the LT contactors.
See the Elekta Digital Accelerator Systems Diagrams Manual for more information.
Related Links:
Operation and analysis of the LT interlock circuit on page 56
4.8.2.3
Functional description of the movements interlock
The movements interlock controls the supply of the single-phase mains power supply to the
motors of the movement systems. The movements interlock has a primary interlock circuit and a
secondary interlock circuit.
The primary movements interlock operates the contactor CON-B. The STOP button on the
handheld controller (HHC) and the movement stop switches control the operation of the primary
movements interlock. The secondary movements interlock operates the contactor CON-C. The
touchguards control the operation of the secondary movements interlock.
Contactors CON-B and CON-C are connected in series, and control the 26 V power supplies to the
movement system motors. When the digital accelerator is in the Preparatory machine state, CONC energizes. The closed contacts of CON-C send a 26 V power supply to the secondary movements
interlock. When CON-B energizes, the movements system interlock sends 26 V power supplies to
the movement system motors.
If a dangerous condition occurs, or the emergency shut down relay in the TCC operates, the
contacts of the contactors open. The open contacts of the contactors break the movements
interlock chain. This removes the 26 V power supply from the movement system motors and
stops movements.

4.8.2.4
Description of the HT interlock
The HT interlocks control the distribution of the three-phase mains power supply to the HT PSU.
The HT interlock has a dual circuit which applies the mains power supply to the HT PSU:
•
The HT1 (primary) interlock circuit operates contactor CON-J.
•
The HT2 (secondary) interlock circuit operates contactor CON-K.
Each contactor is connected in series with the three-phase mains power supply. The contactors
must be energized or set before they can apply the mains power supply to the HT PSU. When the
HT contactors are all energized, the machine state of the digital accelerator changes to
Intersegment.
An HT soft-start circuit decreases the mains voltage for a while before it applies full power to the
HT PSU.
The HT interlocks set these conditions for operation:
•
The room doors are closed
•
The vacuum pressure is correct
•
The dosimetry system parameters for operation are correct
•
The collimators and filters in the BLD are in the correct position.
•
All the software conditions necessary to apply the HT supply are correct.
•
The START, TERMINATE and INTERRUPT keys on the hand held controllers (HHCs) are
correctly set.
•
The control area RTUs are in the correct condition.
Related Links:
Operation and analysis of the primary HT interlock (HT1) on page 64
Operation and analysis of the secondary HT interlock (HT2) on page 67
4.8.2.5
Description of the PRF interlock
The PRF interlock monitors the thyratron trigger pulses sent to the RF subsystem (see Figure 4.2).
The PRF interlock has two circuits:
•
PRF A monitors the RTUs on the A-side of the Serial communications link
•
PRF B monitors the RTUs on the B-side of the Serial communications link.
If a dangerous condition occurs, the PRF interlock stops the transmission of thyratron trigger
pulses to the RF subsystem. When the PRF interlock chain is completed, the machine state of the
digital accelerator changes to Radiation.

4.8.3
Description of the firmware interlocks
The PLDs on the DIE PCBs in each control area have firmware interlocks. The firmware interlocks
operate the relays in the hardware interlock chains. They also compare the condition of the digital
accelerator with each other, and against other values. This makes sure that the conditions are
compatible.
The DIE PCBs each have two PLDs. Each PLD receives a control code of the digital accelerator from
the TCS. Each PLD also receives a control code from the TCS. The TCS monitors the status of each
PLD to make sure that the control code is valid. If the control code is not valid, the digital
accelerator closes down.

and compatible. This is a duplicate activity to the hardware and firmware interlock operations.

•
Dosimetry

Performance verification

Digital accelerator protection.

System description of the power supplies and interlocks
4.9.1
Operation and analysis of the low voltage power supply unit
The LV PSU assembly has three transformers (T1, T2, and T3). T1 is the high power transformer.
The transformers supply decreased voltage inputs to five different power supply circuits on the
assembly, which are the:
•
Bending coarse current to the bending magnet in the beam physics system
•
Bending fine current to the bending magnet in the beam physics system
•
Focus 1 coil in the beam physics system
•
Focus 2 coil in the beam physics system
•
Magnetron magnet in the RF system.
Apart from the bending coarse current, each LV PSU circuit is electrically the same. Each LV PSU
circuit has:
•
A thyristor array
•
A control PCB
•
A feedback shunt resistor
•
A circuit to smooth the output.
A secondary winding of T1 supplies power to the LV PSU circuit. A secondary winding of T3
supplies 15 V AC (rms) power supply for the control PCB in the circuit.
The control PCB receives a command signal from the related TCS control area to supply trigger
pulses to control the thyristor gates.
Each LV PSU circuit also supplies:
•
The solenoid power supply
•
A sample of the positive output voltage
•
A current monitor signal, from the feedback voltage of the circuit shunt resistor.
The bending coarse current controls a three-phase supply, and therefore, uses three different
control PCBs. The TCS controls the PCB that has the positive output line (PCB 13C). T1 applies
three different 11.5 V power supplies to three related pairs of 80 A in parallel fuses (FS13A, FS13B
and FS13C). This gives a 160 A current on each supply line. T2 supplies 15 V AC (rms) to the
control PCBs of the bending coarse current.
The parts of the LV PSU assembly are on a heat sink assembly that has a cooling fan to control the
temperature. T1 also has protection against high temperatures. Each positive supply line from the
secondary windings of T2 and T3 includes a positive temperature coefficient (PTC) device. This
gives the transformers protection against high currents.
Refer to the Elekta Digital Accelerator Systems Diagrams 4513 330 7057.
Refer to the Elekta Oncology Products Service Parts Catalog for a diagram of the LV PSU assembly.

circuit.

Operation and analysis of the control PCBs of the low voltage power supply

The control PCB of the LV PSU controls the operation of a thyristor, which is a SCR. The SCR
controls the power supplies of the LV PSU assembly.

Receive a demand current from the TCS as a 0 mA to 10 mA control signal (Type A

•
Monitor the feedback voltages from a shunt resistor in the LV PSU output.
•
Compare the demand values and monitored values.
•
Use the compared values to modulate the trigger pulses to the SCR in the LV PSU
power supply.

On-board power
supplies and sawtooth
generator
The internal ±15 V DC supplies come from the two 15 V AC supplies.
These are controlled by standard 1 A devices (IC1 and IC2).
Resistors R44 and R45 are fused resistors which prevent damage to the
PCB if a fault occurs. One of the 15 V AC supplies gives a +20 V for the
outputs that is not adjusted.
The 15 V AC supplies also give synchronization pulses at two times the
supply frequency to set the sawtooth generator (IC3A). RV1 on the PCB
gives the amplitude adjustment of the sawtooth waveform at a nominal
5.5 V peak. On the three-phase LV PSU, RV1 gives the adjustment of the
LV PSU control PCBs to get a balanced output waveform.
Servo control
Type A PCBs receive a 0 mA to 10 mA control signal from the TCS
through an AO12 PCB. An amplifier (IC4) sums the control signal with
the feedback voltage from the external shunt resistor. The result is a
servo error signal output which is fixed ±10 V to prevent an overload at
the next step.
The servo error output at PL1 pins a7 and c7 is connected externally to
PL1 pins a20 and c20. Therefore the servo error signal is sent back to
the PCB, where it is compared with the sawtooth waveform (IC3B). This

Type B PCBs do not have a current monitor and control circuit. They

Trigger pulse
generation
The oscillator (IC6) has a mark space ratio of 1:1.6. The pulse width
signals modulate the oscillator to give a burst of trigger pulses at
approximately 27 kHz.
The output part supplies the thyristor trigger pulses. This makes sure
that only the thyristor in the correct phase receives the pulses.
Slow start capacitor
The capacitor C10 cuts off the output pulses at the supply power on.
Therefore the sawtooth waveform increases slowly to increase the
output from a short pulse width. When C10 is fully charged, it has no
more effects on the circuit.
Current monitoring
circuit
On the type A PCB, a voltage, which monitors the external current,
supplies the circuit (IC5). This circuit changes the voltage to a 0 mA to 10
mA current controlled supply. This is then supplied to two SCC/A112
PCB for the TCS.
Calibration circuit
Earlier versions of the type A LV PSU control PCB have a calibration
circuit controlled by a relay connected to pins PL1 a1 and a2.
Later versions of the type A LV PSU do not have the calibration circuit
and relay.

4.9.4
Operation and analysis of an emergency shutdown by the TCS
The TCS software controls the operation of the two emergency shutdown relays in the TCC. The
operation of only one of the emergency shutdown relays is necessary to cause an emergency
shutdown of the digital accelerator.
Operation of an emergency stop switch sends an emergency shutdown signal to the TCS. The TCS
sends a shutdown signal to the emergency shutdown relays in the TCC. The contacts of the
emergency shutdown relays de-energize to remove the +22 V power supply to the digital
accelerator. The hardware interlock and PRF interlock circuits de-energize, which:
•
Stop radiation
•
Disable the HT power supplies
•
Stop movements.

4.9.8
Operation and analysis of the secondary movements interlock
The circuits of the secondary movements interlock uses a 24 V power supply to control the CON-C
contactor and connect the single-phase power supply to the movement system motors if the
CON-B contactor is energized. The secondary movements interlock makes sure that:
•
The BLD touchguards are not operated
•
The gantry movement is not operated out of the set limits
•
The iViewGT™ touchguard interlock is not operated
•
The necessary software interlocks are in their correct conditions for the operation of
the secondary movements interlock.
•
The system communications RTUs that control the touchguard, gantry base limit and
software interlock signals are in the correct global state.
During the correct conditions for operation, the circuits that control the secondary movements
interlock keeps the CON-C contactor energized and the contacts closed. If the CON-B contactor is
also energized, there is a 26 V power supply to the movement system motors. If the circuits
operate an interlock, they remove the 24 V power supply and de-energize the CON-C contactor.
The CON-C contacts open and removes the 26 V power supply to the movement system motors.

for a list of the secondary movements interlock conditions for operation.

4.9.9
Operation and analysis of the primary HT interlock (HT1)
The primary HT interlock controls the CON-J contactor. This is one of four contactors in series with
circuit breaker CB1 and the three-phase power supply. All four contactors, and the CB1, must be
energized to make the three-phase power supply available to the HT PSU.
A soft-start circuit decreases the mains voltage for a time before the full three-phase power
supply is made available to the HT PSU.
The primary HT interlock makes sure that:
•
The doors in the treatment room and the control room are closed.
•
The pressure of the vacuum in the waveguide is correct.
•
The TCS do a check of the necessary software conditions to make sure that they have
the correct settings for the operation of HT.
•
The collimator, the target shifter, the primary (scatter) filter and the secondary filter
are in the correct position.
•
The system communications RTU that controls the HT1 software interlock signals is in
the correct global state.
The HT1 interlock connects the contacts of switches and relays that supply the 24 V AC singlephase power to the coil of the HT1 CON-J contactor.
When all the HT1 interlock conditions are correct, the CON-J contactor is energized, the contacts
closed, and there is a three-phase power supply to the HT PSU. The operation of an interlock
removes the 24 V AC power supply and de-energize the CON-J contactor. The contacts open and
remove the three-phase power supply to the HT PSU.

4.9.10
Operation and analysis of the secondary HT interlock (HT2)
The secondary HT interlock controls the CON-K contactor. This is one of four contactors in series
with circuit breaker CB1 and the three-phase power supply. All four contactors, and the CB1, must
be energized to make the three-phase power supply available to the HT PSU.
The conditions for operation are:
•
The doors in the treatment room and the control room are closed.
•
The pressure of the vacuum in the waveguide is correct.
•
The dosimetry system enables the HT.
•
The primary collimator and secondary filter in the BLD are in the correct position.
•
The system communications RTU that controls the HT2 software interlock signals is in
the correct global state.
•
The TCS did a check to make sure that the START, TERMINATE and INTERRUPT keys
have the correct settings for operation of HT.
When all the HT2 interlock conditions are correct, the 24 V power supply keeps the CON-K
contactor energized. The contacts are closed and there is a three-phase power supply to the HT
PSU. The operation of an interlock removes the 24 V power supply to the CON-K contactor. The
contacts open and remove the three-phase power supply to the HT PSU.

The soft start circuit has two resistors, R1 and R3 that are in parallel connection with the contacts
of the CON-D contactor. When the CON-J and the CON-K contactors are energized, resistors
decrease the electrical power supply to the HT PSU. After a short interval, the CON-D contactor
energizes and makes the three-phase mains power supply available to the HT PSU.
The HT soft start PCB, IRC-74A, has a circuit that, in steps, supply increased electrical power to the
HT PSU. The soft start circuit includes the START key on the FKP, the CON-J and the CON-K
contactors. The circuit operates as follows:
1 
When you operate the START key on the FKP, the CON-J and the CON-K contactors are
energized and start the HT soft start circuit.
2 
After 500 ms the HT soft start circuit times out and supplies +22 V to the coil of relay RL4 on
the PCB IRC-74A.
3 
The contacts of RL4 close and supply 24 V to the coil of the CON-D contactor.
4 
The contacts of the CON-D contactor close and make the three-phase mains power supply
available to the HT PSU.
A software item, i72, gives the status of the CON-D contactor to the TCS.
See the Digital Accelerator System Diagrams Manual for a diagram of the soft start circuit .

and then to a PPG PCB.

of the relays close and send a PRF ENABLE signal through RTU B in each control area and then to
a PPG PCB.
The conditions of operation for the PRF B interlock are that:
•
The RTU B in each control area is in the applicable global state.
•
The LT and HT soft-start contactors are in the correct condition.
•
The BLD has the correct collimator, target and filter settings.
•
The dosimetry channel B is in the correct state.
•
The BLD has the correct wedges, filters and electron applicator.
•
The pressure of the vacuum at the gun end of the waveguide is correct.
•
The temperature of the HT PSU is correct.
•
The pressure in the dielectric gas system is correct.
•
A diode overload has not occurred.
•
The HT2 interlock is enabled.
•
The PRF is enabled.
•
The TCC emergency shut down relay is closed.

4.9.14.3
Operation of the client system interlocks
The client system interlock circuit includes the EMERGENCY STOP switches and the ON/OFF
switch of the digital accelerator.
Operation of the client system interlock de-energizes the contactor CON-A, which removes the
electrical power supply from:
•
The LT system
•
The HT system
•
The movements system
•
The cooling water system.
The ICCA, the vacuum system and the TCS stay energized. These functions operate through the
main interlock.
4.9.14.4
Operation of the room doors interlock
The client interlocks of the customer interface monitor the status of the different room door
switches installed by the hospital. These include:
•
Treatment room door switches
•
Equipment room door switches
•
Neutron door switch
•
More customer door switches.
The room door interlocks have two different circuits (1 and 2). The client makes the decision on
the number and positions of the door switches.
The room doors 1 interlock controls the HT1 interlock chain. When the door switches are closed
(safe), the 24 V supply goes through the client interlocks. If a door switch opens (the door open),
the 24 V supply stops and de-energize CON-J.
Item i258 gives the status of the room doors 1 interlock to the TCS through ROC-HTA.
4.9.14.5
Operation of the client beam termination interlock
The beam termination interlock in the client interlock circuit causes a beam termination that is in
compliance with the IEC 60601-2-1 standard. The operation of an external TERMINATE key opens
the HT1 interlock circuit.
One set of contacts on the TERMINATE key connects to pins 9 and 10 on PL73E to show that the
function operated. The input connects directly through IRC-74B, DIE-ICB and ROC-ICB to become
item i30 (external termination). The circuit is usually closed (100Ω), and the contacts open (100
kΩ) and cause a beam termination.

The client neutron door input is part of the room doors interlock. This input (together with the
neutron warning output), overrides the neutron door interlock. Therefore, the door can be left
open when:

The system is a constant generator of electrical current and increases the voltage to keep the

magnet voltage.

5.3
Correcting an HT overload inhibit
A software inhibit i83 can occur because the thyratron does not switch off in time for the next
charge cycle. Usually the life of the thyratron increases, as the replenisher voltage supplied to it
increases. Therefore if you decrease the thyratron replenisher voltage this decreases the time
that is necessary for the thyratron to switch off. To prevent a HT overload, the replenisher voltage
must be set as high as possible.

area at the interface cabinet. You can get a high voltage electric shock. If you ignore this
warning, you can cause fatal injury.

5.8
Correcting for a no HT supply fault
There is no HT supply because contactor K (CON-K) does not operate. The linear accelerator gives
an i79 or i72 inhibit.
Note:
The contactors CON-J, CON-K and CON-D must be energized to supply a three-phase HT power
supply to the HT PSU.
When the START button is pressed, CON J and CON K energize. This applies a soft start signal to
the HT PSU through the soft start resistors across HT CON D.
The circuit does a check that CON-J and CON-K are closed before a timer on interlock relay card
(IRC-74A) PCB starts. When the hardware timer times out, CON-D is energized. See the Digital
Accelerator System Diagrams Manual.

5.9
Correcting for PRF terminations i607
The PRF termination inhibit (software item i607) occurs at the end of the beam. If the time of the
default start cycle of the segment timer is too short, it can cause a PRF termination error.
The check fail PRF interlock makes sure that the segment timer stops approximately one second
after the dose counter stops. Operation of the check fail PRF interlock adds one second to the
start cycle time of the segment timer. The longer start cycle makes sure that the segment timer
does not operate during field delivery.
Adjust item i43 of part 131 to increase the default time of the start cycle of the segment timer.
The default time of the start cycle is five seconds for FTM linear accelerators and 13 seconds for
Non-FTM linear accelerators.

7.1
Testing the operation of the LV PSU
7.1.1
Configuring the bending coarse supply current
Prerequisites
Test equipment
•
Digital voltmeter
•
Oscilloscope.
WARNING 7.1
Be careful when you do work on the LV PSU. The LV PSU contains high voltages. If you ignore
this warning, a high voltage electric shock can cause fatal injury.
1 
Make sure that the bending coarse current can deliver currents of 25 ±0.25 A and 170 ±1.7
A.
2 
Measure across the side terminals of shunt resistor R1. Make sure that the current is stable
at 25 A and 170 A.
3 
Make sure that the ripple frequency at the input of choke L1 is 300 Hz at 25 A and 170 A.
4

1.1
Important safety instructions
It is important to install, operate, and do the maintenance correctly on all medical electrical
equipment. This is most important for safety related items. For your safety and the safety of the
patients, Elekta recommends that you read, understand, and obey all:
•
Warnings, cautions, and notes in this document and related documents
•
Warnings, cautions, and safety markings on the equipment and the accessories of the
equipment
•
Safety instructions and information in this document and related documents.
Before you operate, or do work on the equipment, it is important that you read and understand
the emergency procedures.
1.1.1
Conventions for warnings, cautions, and notes
WARNING 1.1
A warning is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions, where the result can be fatal
or serious injury, injury, or clinical mistreatment, if you do not obey the instructions.
CAUTION 1.1
A caution is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions, where the result can be
damage to the equipment, data, or the environment, if you do not obey the instructions.
Note:
A note gives more information about a related text.

electrostatic discharge
CAUTION 1.2
Do not touch the PCBs and other electronic parts unless you wear a grounded antistatic wrist
strap. The result can be an electrostatic discharge and a malfunction. If you ignore this caution,
you can cause damage to the equipment.
CAUTION 1.3

precautions when you do work on these parts. If you ignore this caution, you can cause
damage to the equipment.

These devices are known as electrostatic discharge sensitive devices. ESD can cause damage to
these devices and cause them to have a malfunction immediately or some time after the
electrostatic discharge. To prevent the ESD damage to these devices, always wear a grounded
antistatic wrist strap, and obey all the ESD precautions and procedures.

1.6.11.1
Recommended general cleaning procedure
Clean surfaces with a mild detergent solution. Then, dry the surface with a clean, lint-free cloth.
Do not use a solution, solvent, abrasive detergent, or polish that is corrosive. If you do not know
the properties of the solution, do not use it.
1.6.11.2
Recommended cleaning procedure for patient surfaces
Elekta recommends that you use one of these procedures to clean the surfaces that can touch
the patient during treatment:
•
Use a clean, lint-free cloth and apply, by hand, a detergent solution made from water
and a non-corrosive biocide. (Do not use a biocide made from chlorine bleach).
•
Use a clean, lint-free cloth to apply, by hand, denatured alcohol (ethanol) to the
surfaces.

2.1
Document scope
The Precise Treatment Table™ operates with the Elekta Medical Linear Accelerator range of
products and systems:
•
Precise Digital Linear Accelerator (Precise Treatment System™)
•
Electa Synergy® Platform
•
Elekta Synergy®
•
Elekta Infinity™
•
Versa HD™
•
Axesse™ (for China only)
The corrective maintenance manual (CMM) helps service engineers troubleshoot, repair and
maintain the device's systems, subsystems and components. The target audience is qualified
service engineers. These may be engineers employed directly by Elekta, qualified representatives
of Elekta or qualified representatives of Elekta's customers.
The manual provides:
•
A description of the system or sub-system in question
•
A troubleshooting section to identify the problem areas
•
A set of detailed procedures used to replace FRUs (field replaceable units)
•
A section on how to return the device to work.
If you find any mistakes in this document, or identify areas for improvement, please raise a CLM
(Customer Lifecycle Management) case and assign it to the relevant queue.
2.2
Expected service life of the equipment
WARNING 2.1
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each
week of the year.
The level of operation of the equipment can be different to ‘normal use’. This has an effect on
the length of the service life.
Because of wear of parts, the risk of a malfunction to occur can increase after 10 years operation.
Elekta recommends that before you continue operation after 10 years, you complete the regular
extended life checks.
Elekta can help the user with the correct safety checks, planned maintenance schedules, and the
regular extended life checks for continued safe operation of the equipment.
For information on the above checks and schedules, contact your local Elekta representative.

Longitudinal movement is along the horizontal axis in the G (gun) and T (target) directions. A
maximum of 1000 mm of movement is possible. Movement to the gantry of the host machine is
a positive longitudinal movement. Movement away from the gantry is a negative longitudinal
movement.
Lateral movement is along the horizontal axis in the A and B direction. A maximum of ±250 mm
of movement from the isocenter, in each direction, is possible. Movement in the B direction is a
positive lateral movement. Movement in the A direction is a negative lateral movement.
Height movement is along the vertical (Z) axis. A maximum of 1100 mm of movement is possible
from the lowest position to the highest position. Movement up is a negative height movement.
Movement down is a positive height movement. The distance from the isocenter will be different
for different types of treatment table tops.
Note:
When there is electrical power supply to the treatment table, the UPS can give an audible sound
when you move the treatment table up. It does not occur when you move the treatment table
down. The audible sound is not an indication of a system fault.

The iso-rotation assembly connects to the column rotation assembly, and the iso-rotation drive
mechanism is installed in a shallow pit in the floor of the treatment room. The iso-rotation
assembly therefore holds all the weight of the treatment table assembly. The isocentric rotation
assembly rotates the treatment table assembly, and the treatment table top, about the axis of
the host machine isocenter. The column rotation assembly connects between the isocentric
rotation assembly and the height mechanism. The column rotation assembly rotates the height
mechanism, the longitudinal/lateral carriage assembly and the treatment table top about the
column axis.
The height mechanism connects between the column rotation assembly and the longitudinal/
lateral carriage assembly. The height mechanism lifts and lowers the longitudinal/lateral carriage
assembly and the treatment table top. The longitudinal/lateral carriage assemblies connect
between the height mechanism and the treatment table top. The longitudinal carriage assembly
moves the treatment table top in the G and T directions along the horizontal axis. The lateral
carriage assembly moves the treatment table top in the A and B directions along the horizontal
axis.

3.4
Configuration and function of the user interface modules
The treatment table has two user interface modules, one on the A-side and one on the B-side.
Each user interface module has these controls:
•
Brake buttons
•
TOUCHGUARD OVERRIDE button
•
Thumbwheels
•
STOP MOTORS button
•
ENABLE bars.
The brake buttons are toggle action devices, which contain lamps to show the position of the
brake. The brake of each movement system is usually in the engaged position, and the lamp is
on. When the brake releases, the lamp goes off.
The TOUCHGUAD OVERRIDE buttons are momentary action devices, which contain lamps to
show the condition of the touchguard inhibit. The touchguard override function is usually off (the
button is in the off position), and the lamp is on. The user must hold the button in the on position
to override the touchguard inhibits. In this position, the lamp goes off.
There are four thumbwheels on the user interface modules which control the speed and
direction of the movement. Move the thumbwheel up or down to select the direction of travel.
Move the thumbwheel away from the center position to increase the speed of movement in the
selected direction. Release the thumbwheel to stop the selected movement.
Use the ENABLE bar at the same time as one of the four thumbwheels to enable movement. The
treatment table moves in the direction that you operate the thumbwheel. Release the ENABLE
bar after you release the selected thumbwheel and the selected movement stops.
The cover of the user interface module is in two parts (front and rear) that you can disassemble
to get access to the internal parts. Most of the internal parts are installed in the front part of the
cover. There are two PCBs in the user interface module. One PCB one holds the potentiometer
thumbwheels and the other PCB holds the switches and indicators of the buttons. The wires for
the user interface modules come from PCB 830B on the side of the height mechanism.
The treatment table can have one of these two types of user interface module:
•
Standard configuration, where one button releases the lateral and longitudinal brakes
(see Figure 3.11)
•
Configuration for an independently operated longitudinal and lateral brake system,
where there is one button for the lateral brake and one button for the longitudinal
brake (see Figure 3.12)
A modification kit (CN50-0162) is available to change the standard configuration to the
configuration for an independently operated longitudinal and lateral brake system.

Prevent damage to some parts of the treatment table during operation.

3.7
Description of the treatment table tops
3.7.1
Standard therapy table top
The standard therapy treatment table lets you deliver radiation from most directions without
barriers. It has a Mylar® cover and small and large panels that you can remove. The panels have
labels to help you to attach them in the correct position after removal. The rails on the sides let
you attach accessories.
3.7.2
C-Arm table top
The C-Arm therapy table top has a panel and accessory rails that you can remove. The panel can
be solid or it can have a tennis racket design with a carbon fiber or metal frame. Panels with a
carbon fiber frame give better X-ray translucence. The tennis racket design gives good patient
support with minimum absorbed radiation.
There are two C-shaped arms below the panel. Each arm can move through 180°, and there are
six stop positions 30° apart. Extension panels attach to the ends of the treatment table top to
give support to the head or feet of the patient.

3.10.1
Technical description of the longitudinal and lateral carriage
assemblies
The X/Y carriage assembly supplies longitudinal and lateral movement of the treatment table top.
The rails of the X/Y carriage assembly are installed in the roller bearing cages of the chassis. The
longitudinal rails of the X/Y carriage assembly are installed in the longitudinal roller bearing
cages. The lateral rails of the X/Y carriage assembly are installed in the lateral roller bearing
cages. The height interface plate is attached to the top of the height mechanism.
A DC motor moves the X/Y carriage assemblies along the related roller bearing cages. The
LATERAL and LONGITUDINAL thumbwheels on the user interface module control the operation of
the DC motor. The thumbwheels control the speed and direction of movement of the related
carriage assembly.

A toothed drive roller installs on the end of the drive shaft of the DC motor in each drive
subassembly. A drive belt is in contact with the drive roller and a set of potentiometer drive
gears. When the DC motor energizes, the clutch engages to rotate the drive roller and disengages
when the movement is completed. The drive roller turns the potentiometer drive gears and the
drive belt. The polarity of the drive signal to the DC motor sets the direction of movement. The
amplitude of the drive signal sets the speed of movement.
The two drive subassemblies share one interconnection printed circuit board (PCB830A) that is
installed on the height mechanism. The PCB supplies cable connections for the DC motor, brake
and clutch and position readout potentiometers (coarse, fine and check potentiometers).
The positional readout circuit has a coarse potentiometer, a fine potentiometer and a check
potentiometer. See Movement servo loops for more information.

Technical description of the longitudinal and lateral brake

The longitudinal and lateral brake assemblies stop the movement of the related carriage

two screws between the mounting blocks at each end, adjust the brake-band tension (see Figure

3.11.2
Technical description of the height mechanism drive motor
The height mechanism drive motor operates the gearbox assembly to increase or decrease the
height of the treatment table. The drive motor is installed on the gearbox in the three-angle box.
The drive motor operates the worm drive of the gearbox assembly, which extends or retracts the
upper and lower ball screws. The amplitude of the drive signal to the motor sets the speed of
movement, and the polarity of the signal gives the direction of movement. Spring pressure
applies the brake of the drive motor when no height movement is selected. A height movement
selection automatically releases the brake.
The HEIGHT thumbwheel on the user interface module controls the operation of the drive motor.
Operation of the thumbwheel controls the speed and direction of movement of the height
mechanism.

The gearbox assembly has a worm drive connected through a coupling housing to two rotating
nuts. The height mechanism motor drive operates the worm drive. The worm drive turns the two
rotating nuts at the same time and at the same speed. This synchronizes the movement of the
ball screws, which do not rotate, through the gearbox assembly. One rotating nut moves the
upper ball screw and the other rotating nut moves the lower ball screw. The rotating nuts change
the rotation of the worm drive into vertical movement of the ball screws.
Ball screw cups are attached to the end of the ball screws and to the upper and lower arms. A
high-tensile screw attaches the ball screw cup to the end of the ball screw. A pivot pin installs
through needle bearings to attach a ball screw cup to each arm. A screw locks the pivot pin in
position. The ball screw and ball screw cup rotate together on the needle bearings around the
pivot pin axis (see Figure 3.27).
