3.12.2
Technical description of the iso-rotation drive subassembly
The iso-rotation drive subassembly (see Figure 3.29) rotates the treatment table around the
isocentric axis through a 100° range of movement. The iso-rotation drive subassembly installs on
the triangular base of the iso-rotation assembly at the gun side of the drive platter.
The primary parts of the iso-rotation drive subassembly are the:
•
DC motor and clutch
•
Upper and lower drive gears
•
Timing belt.
The iso-rotation drive subassembly has a pillar and drive shaft installed between a top and a
lower plate. The DC motor and clutch unit installs vertically between the top and lower plates.
The drive shaft of the DC motor extends through the lower plate. The drive shaft engages in a
pair of lower drive gears installed on the external surface of the lower plate.
A toothed timing belt installed around the lower drive gears rotates the drive gears. The drive
shaft installed between the lower drive gears and upper drive gears rotates the upper drive
gears. A toothed drive belt, installed around the edge of the drive platter, engages on the upper
drive gears and moves the drive platter to the selected position. The polarity of the drive signal to
the DC motor sets the direction of movement. The amplitude of the drive signal sets the speed of
movement.
The ISO-ROTATION thumbwheel on the user interface module controls the operation of the DC
motor. Operation of the thumbwheel controls the speed and direction of movement of the isorotation assembly, and releases the ISO-ROTATION brake.
The ISO-ROTATION BRAKE button on the user interface module manually controls the operation
of the iso-rotation brake. A usually de-energized electromagnet holds the electrically operated
brake in contact with the floor pan (ON). Operation of the ISO-ROTATION BRAKE button applies a
26 V supply to energize the solenoid of the electromagnet, which releases the brake. Operation
of the ISO-ROTATION BRAKE button again removes the 26 V supply to the coil of the
electromagnet, which de-energizes to apply the brake.

3.12.3
Technical description of the floor parts of the iso-rotation assembly
The floor parts of the iso-rotation assembly give protection to the drive mechanism. The floor
parts are installed on mountings on the floor of the treatment table pit.
The primary parts of the floor are the:

The floor pan is a disk that has a location pin in the center. The location pin engages in the hole in
the center of the drive platter. A location pin on the column rotation assembly engages in a slot
in the floor pan. The floor pan rotates through an approximate 200° range of movement, 100° at
each side of the longitudinal axis.

3.14.2
Function of the mains input circuit of the power supply unit
The mains electrical power supply of 230 V (±15%) to the PSU comes from the UPS. There is an
amber neon lamp (N1) connected across the live and neutral lines that shows the condition of
the mains input.
The live line goes across a contact of circuit breaker CB1 to the primary winding of transformer
T1. Circuit breaker CB1 is a double-pole, 5 A device that isolates the primary side of transformer
T1 from the mains electrical power supply. The neutral line goes to the primary winding of T1
through the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistors on the LED PCB, which gives
protection from power surges. The mains transformer (T1) is a 1.2 kVA toroid, with an internal
thermal switch that operates if the transformer becomes too hot because of unusual,
continuous, high load conditions or an internal fault.
The transformer has two secondary windings. At a nominal input of 230 V AC:
•
Secondary winding Sy1 gives an output of 80 V rms to the 90 V line.
•
Secondary winding Sy2 gives outputs of 20 V, 0 V, and 20 V rms to the +26 V and -26 V
lines.
The 80 V rms output from secondary winding Sy1 of transformer T1 is full-wave rectified by REC1
and smoothed by capacitor C1. The 0 V output from secondary winding Sy2 is grounded. The 20 V
outputs from Sy2 are full-wave rectified by REC2 and smoothed by C2 and C3 to give +26 V DC
and -26 V DC.
3.14.3
Function of the discharge PCB in the power supply unit
The discharge PCB is installed above capacitor C1 in the PSU. The PCB is in the 90 V supply line,
where its function is to make sure that C1 discharges to a safe level in 15 seconds or less. If there
is a voltage, an LED (D1) comes on.
Note:
The safe level gives protection only from the risk from an electric shock. More than 15 seconds is
necessary to discharge all the energy.
The discharge PCB also contains a potential divider that gives a lower voltage to the LED PCB. This
voltage causes an LED to come on to show the condition of the switched 90 V output.
3.14.4
Function of the heatsink PCB in the power supply unit
The heatsink PCB has a current dump circuit to keep the ±26 V outputs to less than 1.7 V of the
supply level. To do this, switching devices (TR1 and TR2) come on when the output voltage
increases, and resistor packages (TO220 type) on the heatsink dump the current. The output of
the current dump circuit goes to the LED PCB through the contacts of CON A and CON B.
The heatsink PCB also has three voltage regulators. The rectified ±26 V signals go to the
regulators to give +5 V and ±15 V at 1.5 A (peak). A dropper resistor reduces the heat dissipation
of the +5 V regulator.
3.14.5
Configuration and function of the LED PCB in the power supply unit
The LED PCB has a number of LEDs that show on the front panel of the PSU. Each LED shows the
condition of a supply output. The LED will come on if there is a supply output, but will go off if
there is no supply output.
On the LED PCB, the +26 V and -26 V inputs from the heatsink PCB divide into three lines (lines 1,
2, and 3) which give six output lines. The PCB has a set of PTC fuses that automatically reset to

3.14.6
Function of the interlock circuits in the LED PCB
The interlock circuits have a set of relays, which control signal inputs energize to show the
interlock status of the host machine and treatment table. When all interlock conditions are
satisfactory, the contacts of the relays close and the circuit applies +26 V to the coils of
contactors CON A and CON B.

5 seconds. This makes sure that the brakes are applied and that all treatment table movements
stop when the interruption occurs.

3.15.1
Configuration of the uninterruptible power supply
There are two types of UPS. The UPS 45133318015 is in the EIM cabinet and the UPS 1515524 is
in the position adjacent to the EIM cabinet. Both of them are connected to the PSU. The
operation of the UPS differs if the treatment table includes an Emergency Down Drive (EDD)
timer extension module.
The UPS supplies power if a mains power supply failure occurs. This gives sufficient operating
time for the user to lower the table safely.
There are two different configurations of the UPS:
•
UPS with EDD timer extension module. (This is standard installation on digital
accelerators with Serial No. 152530 or earlier).
•
UPS without EDD timer extension module. (This is standard installation on digital
accelerators with Serial No. 152531 or later).
The EDD module is available as a ModKit (Part No. 8213 215 8674)
Note:
When there is mains power supply to the treatment table, the UPS can give an audible alarm. The
audible alarm can occur when you move the treatment table up. The audible alarm is not an
indication of a system fault if the mains power supply is available.

Shut down of the UPS takes approximately 90 seconds.
If the UPS TEST switch on the front panel of the PSU is set to the TEST position, a red test warning
LED illuminates and the UPS maintains power after the external mains supply isolator has been
tripped.
The integrity of the mains power supply is monitored by a 24 V AC input that energizes relay RL1.
The contacts of RL1 close to connect +26 V, via a resistor and zener diode, to the UPS shut–down
input, when the UPS TEST switch is in the NORMAL position.
If the 24 V AC host power supply is lost, or when the UPS TEST switch is set to the TEST position, a
switched outputs contactor is enabled by the assertion of stop motors signals STMPSS (24 V DC)
and STMLCU (4 V DC) only.
Note:
The UPS maintains its output whilst the mains input is present, even though a shut–down request
is in force. To ensure UPS shutdown the shut–down request must be in force for at least
0.5 seconds after the cessation of the mains supply.

Level translation of the reference voltage signals on the LTU PCB
Signal VREFALCU is the A-side input reference voltage from the LCU PCB. Signal VREFALCU goes

level of reference voltage +10VREFA at the source pin of the MOSFET.
The +10VREFA line is the output from the LTU PCB (PL1 A8/B8/C8) that goes to amplifiers (IC29
12/13/14 and 2/3/1) to get local A-side reference voltages -1VR, +1VR, -5VR, and +5VR. These
voltages are used for digital and analog level translation.
Signal VREFBLCU is the B-side input reference voltage from the LCU PCB. Signal VREFBLCU goes
through a buffer amplifier (IC48 8/9/14) to operate an integrating controller (IC43/IC41 and IC22/

Level translation of the brake control signals
In the iso-rotation system, the active low signal BRKILCU from the LCU PCB controls the manual
brake release. The signal goes to a CMOS inverter (IC51 3/4) that directly operates a smart
MOSFET power switch (TR17). The output from the MOSFET is the power enable signal BRKILTU,
which applies +26 V and 0 V across the coil of the brake to release it.
In the height movement system, the active low signal BRKZLCU from the LCU PCB controls the
manual brake release. The signal goes to a CMOS inverter (IC51 1/2) that directly operates a
smart MOSFET power switch (TR16). The output from the MOSFET is the power enable signal
BRKZLTU, which applies +26 V and 0 V across the coil of the brake to release it.
In the column movement system, the active low signal BRKCLCU from the LCU PCB controls the
manual brake release. The signal goes to a CMOS inverter (IC51 5/6) that directly operates a
smart MOSFET power switch (TR18). The output from the MOSFET is the power enable signal
BRKCLTU, which applies +26 V and 0 V across the coil of the brake to release it.
In the longitudinal movement system, signal BRKXLCU from the LCU PCB controls the manual
brake release. The signal goes to a CMOS inverter (IC51 11/10) which sends the signal to a
monostable (IC46). A comparator (IC49 10/11/13) uses the output of the inverter to operate the
gate of a p-channel MOSFET (TR7). The +26 V supply at the source pin of the MOSFET switches to
the drain pin, which applies the +26 V to one pin of the coil. The the other pin is permanently
connected to –26 V. Therefore, the power enable signal BRKXLTU applies +52 V across the coil of
the brake to release it.
After the trigger pulse, the MOSFET switches off, and the high signal from the monostable clocks
a flip flop (IC47 1 to 5). The high output signal of the flip flop operates the gate of the MOSFET
(TR8) through an amplifier (IC50 5/5/2). This switches on TR8, which applies 0 V and -26 V across
the coil of the brake. The length of the initial high pulse is adjustable, through R277 and C165.
In the lateral movement system, signal BRKYLCU from the LCU PCB controls the manual brake
release. The signal goes to a CMOS inverter (IC51 13/12) which sends the signal to a monostable

The LTU PCB receives safety interlock signals from the treatment table, the user interface

from +5 V to +15 V or +26 V, and electromechanical relays for hard-wired interlock signals.

3.18.2
Configuration of the interlock control circuits on the LTU PCB
The interlock control circuit on the LTU PCB has a two switches (SW1 and SW2) on the backplane.
With these switches, service engineers can disconnect the treatment table from the host
machine (or other equipment) to put it in stand-alone mode. When the contacts of the switches
are open, they disconnect some of the signals to and from the host machine and the other
equipment.
Note:
Stand-alone operation is not possible if PL801M is connected at the backplane.

Resistive voltage dividers (R169/R170) divide the signal, and two operational amplifiers (IC21
2/3/1 and IC21 6/5/7) rectify it, before the signal goes through a NAND gate with the flag signal
FLGHOST1LTU (IC20 12/13/11).
Signal TGFHOST2 from other equipment, is an active low touchguard fault indication. Resistive
voltage dividers (R163/R164) divide the signal before it goes through a NAND gate (IC20/1) with
flag signal FLGHOST1LTU. The gated signal TGFHOST2 goes through a second NAND gate with the
TGFHOST1 signal (IC20 9/10/8 and 4/5/6).
The result of this logic circuit is a NOR function, in which TGFHOST1 or TGFHOST2 can give the
touchguard flag signal TGFLTU. The touchguard flag signal TGFLTU goes through an inverting
buffer (IC27/2) that sends the active low output signal TGFLTU to the LCU PCB.

Signal ENBZHOST is the height motor enable signal from the digital accelerator. Resistive voltage

accelerator. The third input to the gate is signal ENBZHOSTLTU.

and lateral motor enable inputs. The inverted (IC24 5/6) output signal goes through a second

enable signals.

voltage dividers (R227/R228) divide the signal, and operational amplifiers (IC24 1/2) invert it. The
signal goes through a NOR gate (IC25/4), which gates the signal with the longitudinal and lateral
motor enable signals.

3.19.1
Configuration and function of the logic control unit PCB
The LCU PCB is the primary control PCB of the treatment table. It has a field programmable logic
array (FPLA) and five LED displays on its front edge for the troubleshooting.
The LCU PCB receives digital and analog signals from the treatment table, the user interfaces

From these inputs, and with the control of the FPLA, the LCU PCB gives:
•
Outputs that control switched functions such as brakes, clutches, and lamps
•
Analog outputs that control motor speeds
•
Logic outputs that send data to other parts of the control system.
The PCB has a number of circuits for these functions:
•
On-board power supply and reference voltage generation
•
Central processing
•
Digital input signal processing
•
Digital output signal processing
•
Analog input signal processing
•
Analog output signal processing
•
LED display control.

3.19.4
Description of the input signal processing
Digital input signal processing
There are 32 discrete digital inputs, and all of these signals are subjected to similar conditioning.
Each input is connected to a 10 kΩ pull-up resistor, and passes through an RC noise reduction
filter to a Schmidt-triggered inverter, which presents a clean, fast, digital signal to an input pin of
the FPLA.
For example, the active-low ENBXHOST input at PL1, pin A1 is the longitudinal movement enable
signal from the host machine. The 5 V logic input is filtered by R80, R74 and C88 and applied to
Schmitt-triggered inverter IC25 9/8 to become signal ENBXHOST. This signal is applied to the
INX_CONN pin of the FPLA.
Analog input signal processing
There are 40 analog inputs to the LCU PCB. The inputs comprise five sets of eight signals, of which
one input in each set is spare. Each set of inputs is assigned to a separate movement subsystem
and consists of the potentiometer, velocity readout and speed demand signals for the related

movement subsystem. All the analog signal inputs are in the range 0 V to +10 V. All the analog
signal inputs are conditioned in the same way.
Each signal is filtered against interference and noise by an RC filter of 100 kΩ resistors and 100 nF
capacitors. The line is protected against overvoltage and transient spikes by high-speed diodes
connected in reverse to the analog power supply rails (+15 V and 0 V). The filtered signal is then
buffered by a unity gain operational amplifier, which presents the incoming analog voltage to a
data acquisition system (DAS) without risk of transients. For example, longitudinal movement
velocity readout signal VFBXLTULCU from the LTU PCB is filtered by R126 and C141 while diode
D40 provides overvoltage and transient protection. The filtered signal is buffered by IC47 9/10/8
and applied as the AIN7 input to pin 2 of DAS IC46.

3.19.5
Description of the LED bar graph display
The LCU PCB has five different 10-bar LED displays attached to the front edge of the PCB. The
four top displays are assigned to the longitudinal, lateral, height and iso-rotation movement
subsystems and the lowest display is the same for all.
The LED displays are controlled by the FPLA, which outputs the display data on 10-bit bus
LED0:LED9. The bus signals are applied to five different 10-line, D-type, tri-state latches, which
are positive-edge triggered. The 10 outputs of each latch drives a separate LED display device.
The FPLA provides five separate clock outputs, one for each latch, and common output enable
signal OE. The assignments of the circuit are:
•
The longitudinal movement display uses latch IC28 and LED display device D11 and is
clocked by signal CLKOPT4.
•
The lateral movement display uses latch IC20 and LED display device D10 and is clocked
by signal CLKOPT3.
•
The height movement display uses latch IC18 and LED display device D9 and is clocked
by signal CLKOPT2.
•
The iso-rotation movement display uses latch IC17 and LED display device D7 and is
clocked by signal CLKOPT1.
•
The common display uses latch IC14 and LED display device D5 and is clocked by signal
CLKOPT0. The LED display driver signals are listed in the PCB input and output section.
The LCU PCB has a parallel port which communicates with the FPLA for test and future
development of the PCB. This parallel port gives versatile input and output to the logical core of
the LCU. The description of this parallel port is not available in this manual.

The FPLA also outputs an 8-bit data bus (OPDB 7:0) and a 3-bit address bus (A2:0).
Analog output signal processing
The analog outputs from the LCU PCB are the velocity demand signals to the UMD PCBs of the
movement subsystems. The outputs comprise five output signals, one for each movement
subsystem.
All the analog signal outputs are produced in the same way. Digital data word OPDB7:OPDB0
from the FPLA is applied to a separate DAC for each movement subsystem. The DAC converts its
digital input into an analog voltage representing the required speed demand to the UMD PCB of
the respective movement subsystem.
The output of the DAC is scaled and signed by the value of VREF10N (-10 V), which produces a
DAC output of 0 V to 10 V. This voltage is buffered and reduced by 5 V by a unity gain operational
amplifier, to provide a -5 V to +5 V output. The devices assigned to each movement subsystem
are:
•
The data word for the speed of longitudinal movement is handled by IC11 and
IC8 6/5/7.
•
The data word for the speed of lateral movement is handled by IC6 and IC8 2/3/1.
•
The data word for the speed of height movement is handled by IC3 and IC8 13/12/14.
•
The data word for the speed of iso-rotation movement is handled by IC5 and
IC8 9/10/8.
•
The data word for the speed of column rotation is handled by IC2 and IC7 9/10/8.

3.19.7
Description of the central processor and analog to digital signal
conversion
The central processor of the LCU PCB is the FPLA (IC15). You can think of the FPLA as a number of
functional blocks:
•
Manual brake release control
•
Motor enable
•
Brake control
•
Clutch control
•
Interlocks.
The configuration data of the FPLA is programmed through the EPROM (IC49) which has
reprogrammable FLASH memory. Each time the system is powered-up, the configuration data is
loaded to the FPLA via the serial DATA0 line. The output of the EPROM is enabled by the STATUS
signal from the FPLA, the chip is selected by the CONFIG_DONE signal, and device timing is
controlled by the DCLK signal.

The system clock is obtained from a 3.686400 MHz crystal (X1) and Schmitt-triggered inverters
(IC12 and IC13). The FPLA is reset on timeout by a watchdog timer (IC16), which monitors the
WDI signal from the FPLA.
Analog to digital signal conversion
Each DAS is a single-chip device that consists of an 8-bit multiplexer, an 8-bit A DC, an 8 × 8-bit
dual-port RAM, and address latching and control logic. The reference voltage is signal VREF10N.
Analog to digital conversion is a continuous channel-sequencing process in which the 8 analog
inputs are converted into separate 8-bit data words. The result of each conversion is assigned to
a separate RAM address and read under the control of address latch enable signal ALE and 3-bit
address bus A2 to A0 from the FPLA. The data word read from the RAM is output via on-chip tristate buffers as data word IPDB7 to IPDN0, which is applied to the FPLA.
Each DAS also outputs an active-low STAT signal that is used to indicate the start of an internal
data conversion cycle. The STAT signals are applied to the FPLA.

3.20.1
Configuration and function of the universal motor drive PCBs
There are five UMD PCBs in the EIM:
•
I-UMD in the iso-rotation system
•
X-UMD in the longitudinal movement system
•
Y-UMD in the lateral movement system
•
G1-UMD Ganty drive 1 (installed on digital accelerator Serial No. 152531 or later)
•
G2-UMD Ganty drive 2 (installed on digital accelerator Serial No. 152531 or later).
The UMD PCBs send the necessary signals to operate the motors of the longitudinal movement,
lateral movement, iso-rotation, and gantry movement. All movements can use the same type of
UMD PCB, with no setup or adjustment necessary.
Each PCB receives a ±26 V power supply from the PSU, and each PCB has two input signals: a
demand signal and an enable signal. The UMD PCB gives an output signal as a result of the
demand signal only when the enable input signal is low (logic 0). A positive demand signal gives a
negative output signal.
There are two different modes of operation for the UMD PCBs:
•
In the first mode, one UMD PCB drives the load from the ±26 V supply, and the return
from the load connects to 0 V. This is applicable to longitudinal, lateral and iso-rotation
movement.
•
In the other mode, two UMD PCBs operate in a bridge to apply the drive to the two
sides of the load. In this mode, the demand input to one UMD PCB is inverted to give
the demand input to the other UMD PCB. This is applicable to gantry movement.

speed. The servo senses the motor voltage and current, and subtracts the resistive or IR part.

Circuits on the universal motor drive PCBs
In the voltage regulator circuit, the internal ±15 V power supplies for the UMD PCB come from
the ±26 V power supplies, through standard 1 A regulators (IC4 and IC5). Fusible resistors (R1 and
R2) prevent damage to the PCB if a fault occurs, and decrease dissipation in the regulators.
In the current sensor circuit, the shunt resistors (R50 to R53) sense the output current. Resistor
R53 is always in the circuit with the load. Resistors R50 to R52 can be in or out of the cicuit. The
maximum necessary output current controls the links (in or out of the circuit) for resistors R50 to
R52 (the links are part of the rack wiring, and are therefore external to the UMD PCB). A
differential amplifier (IC1B) with high common mode rejection ratio (CMRR), and IC1C, increases
the shunt resistor voltage by a factor of 6.8. This gives a voltage at PL1, pin a14 in proportion to
the sensed current.
In the current limit circuit, Zener diodes (D5 and D6) control the output from the current sensor
circuit when the output becomes ±7.5 V (6.8 V + 0.7 V). This decreases the demand signal to IC1D

and applies a limit to the output current. When this occurs, the sense voltage across resistors R50
to R53 is 1.1 V.
In the IR compensation circuit, the current sensor output for the motor drives goes to one of the
IR compensation inputs (IR COMP 1 to IR COMP 5), which subtracts the current sensor output
from a sample of the output voltage in amplifier IC1A. The output of the amplifier is a voltage
that is in proportion to the speed of the motor. The circuit also uses this voltage to adjust for wire
and armature resistance.
In the error amplifier circuit, the DEMAND input (PL1, pin a9), with a range of ±5.0 V, adds to the
FEEDBACK at pin c9 or c10 to supply the gain necessary. The error amplifier (IC1D) increases the
result of the added signals and sends an output to a pulse-width modulator.
In the pulse-width modulator circuit, a 110 kHz triangular wave generator (IC2D and IC3B) sends
its output of approximately ±6.0 V (peak) to comparators IC2A and IC2B. Diodes D7 and D8 apply
a 3 V level shift, which gives a 1 µs deadband to the back and front edges of the bipolar
modulator output. Diodes D3 and D4 limit the output voltage of IC1D to give approximately 11 V.
The R21 and C16 phase-shift network make the circuit more stable.
In the output stages circuit, the positive output from the modulator switches on TR4. This
switches on the parallel p-channel MOSFETs (TR1 and TR2) through diode D10. To switch on TR1
and TR2 fully, the potential divider (R35 and R36, and R37 to R39) makes the gate (in the
MOSFET) go 10 V below the source. An emitter follower (TR3) discharges the gate-source
capacitance of the MOSFETs to switch them off. The typical time to switch on or off is 100 ns. A
configuration of the p-channel (D11 and R42 to R46) switches on and switches off the n-channel
MOSFETs (TR7 and TR8). Flyback diodes D12 and D13 limit the output to L1 during the deadband
period. An LC filter circuit (L1 and C20 to C22) with a threshold frequency of approximately 10
kHz controls the output to decrease unwanted, remaining, small changes in the output signal.
In the enable circuit, the ENABLE input signal at PL1 (pin c12) is active low. The input signal goes
to a comparator (IC2C) through a potential divider circuit (R31 to R33). In the disabled state, the
comparator gives a high output (pulled up by R34). The JFETs (TR9 and TR11) switch on to stop
the signal to the error amplifier and the output stage. When the ENABLE input is less than +5 V,
the output of the comparator (IC2C) changes to -15 V. This switches off the JFETs (TR9 and TR11)
to let the circuit operate.
In the power failure protection circuit, a comparator (IC2C) gives a high output that switches on
the JFETs (TR9 and TR11) to disable the UMD PCB if the -15 V supply fails. If the +15 V supply fails,
the gate to JFET TR10 goes to -15 V and TR10 switches on (fully). This stops the signal to the
output stage.
In the inverter circuit, when two UMD PCBs operate in a bridge, the input signals go to a unity
gain inverter (IC3C). The demand signal INVERTER INPUT goes to PL1 (pin a13) and the output
signal INVERTER OUTPUT comes from PL1 (pin c13). During bridge mode operation, the INVERTER
OUTPUT from one UMD PCB goes to the DEMAND input of the other UMD PCB of the pair.
3.20.3
Signal and power supply to the emergency down drive module
The EDD module lets you lower the treatment table to a safe position if a mains power supply
failure occurs while the UPS supplies power. The EDD module is not installed on digital
accelerators Serial No. 152531 and later. For systems 152531 and later, the UPS will shutdown
after approximately 90 seconds after a controlled shutdown. If there is a mains power supply
failure, the UPS will continue to supply power until the battery is discharged.
The 24 V AC interlock supply signal 24VACHOST goes from the host machine, through the
backplane, to the EDD module. When the mains electrical supply is present, the 24VACHOST
signal goes, through the (Normally Closed) contacts 21/22 of relay RL1, to relay RL1 on the LED
PCB within the PSU. Relay RL1 on the LED PCB determines which interlocks to use (that is, host or
local).
A nominal +26 V DC supply signal STMPSS from pin 3 of SK801U connects to coil connection A1 of
relay RL1. During mains power failure, internal batteries keep the output of the UPS stable, and

there is no power to timer relay RL2 and there will be no signal to the UPS to shut down. The UPS

During this time, the EDD will be available.

emergency off switch, on the wall of the treatment room, removes the mains supply to the UPS
and stops the 24VACHOST signal. This puts the system into EDD mode during the Closed machine
state and FACILITY 1 inhibits. If you operate the ENABLE bar when the EDD is active, the height
motor brake releases, and the treatment table slowly lowers. No other motorized movements
are permitted while the EDD is active.

3.21
Description and operation of the movement servo loops
3.21.1
Movement servo loops
In Integrity™ program, movement servo loops control the movement of each movement
subsystem.
The servo has a primary and secondary encoder that supply primary and secondary position
readouts to the digital accelerator.
•
The primary encoder has two potentiometers (coarse and fine) which supply the
position information at different resolutions.
•
The secondary encoder has a check potentiometer that monitors the operation of the
other two potentiometers.
Each potentiometer is directly connected to the movement assembly. The voltages read from the
potentiometers are in proportion to the actual position of the movement assembly. The voltages
are digitized and sent to the digital accelerator as servo feedback signals.

3.21.3
Movement encoders - coarse potentiometer
The coarse potentiometer has one wiper. The coarse potentiometer drive gear rotates the wiper
approximately 10 turns during the full range of movement in one direction.
The digital accelerator uses the coarse potentiometer outputs to identify the number of turns
that the fine potentiometer completes. The coarse potentiometer output lets the control system
select wiper A or wiper B of the fine potentiometer as the data source it will use.
The voltage curves of the check and coarse potentiometers are straight lines in the approximate
range 0 V to 10 V. The position of the potentiometer on the related drive shaft has an effect on
the actual value of the output. Usually there is a small offset between the output values of the
fine and coarse potentiometers. This offset must be kept to a minimum during setup.

of movement. This gives a sawtooth voltage waveform. The fine potentiometer has no end stops,

3.21.5
Movement encoders - check potentiometer
The check potentiometer has one wiper. The check potentiometer drive gear rotates the wiper
approximately 10 turns during the full range of the movement in one direction.
The check potentiometer is part of the secondary encoder, and its drive gear is not part of the
primary encoder. Therefore, if a malfunction causes a drive gear fault, a difference will occur
between the primary and secondary encoders.
The check potentiometer also has a dedicated signal path and reference voltage that is not part
of the signal paths for the fine and coarse potentiometers. If an electronic fault occurs, the
difference between the primary and secondary encoder signals will cause an error.
3.21.6
Movement encoders - positional resolution
The coarse potentiometer gives a low resolution indication of the movement position. For
example, in the isocentric rotation readout, the coarse potentiometer gives the actual value of
the isocentric angle at a resolution of approximately 36°/V. The coarse potentiometer also points
to one of the curves of the fine potentiometer, which gives the angle at a resolution of 1.8°/V.
Therefore, the readout circuit can show the isocentric rotation angle to two decimal places.
3.21.7
Movement encoders - potentiometer gearing
In the height movement subsystem, there is a ratio between the gearing of the fine and coarse
potentiometers. As the height carriage assembly moves through its full vertical range of
movement in one direction, the fine potentiometer will rotates approximately 20 times. The
output range of the fine potentiometer is 200 V, (20 × 10 V). This multiplies the total track length
by approximately 20, therefore, the readout and signal-to-noise ratio indications have an
accuracy of ±0.05%.
In the other movement subsystems, longitudinal, lateral, iso-rotation, and column rotation, there
is also a ratio between the gearing of the fine and coarse potentiometers. In each of these
movement subsystems:
•
The fine potentiometer rotates 10 times during the full range of movement in one
direction.
•
The readout and signal-to-noise ratio indications have an accuracy of ±0.1%.
3.21.8
Correlating the readout potentiometers
The control software of the digital accelerator must know the relation between the three
potentiometer curves to calculate the position of a movement. During the correlation procedure,
the table movements are made in Learn mode. Learn mode calculates the slope and intersection
point of each potentiometer curve.
The potentiometer tracks are not fully linear tracks. Therefore, before calibration, use Learn
mode to calculate the correlation coefficients of the potentiometers. The system saves the
correlation coefficients while the movement subsystem moves between its end points. The
correlation coefficients are only applicable to one set of potentiometers. If a new potentiometer
is installed, you must do the potentiometer correlation again.

circuit
When calibration of the three potentiometer circuit is necessary, the same calibration procedure

3.22.1
Longitudinal movement control
The buttons and thumbwheels on user interface modules control the movement of the
treatment table along the longitudinal axis. A user interface module is installed at each side of
the treatment table. There are two types of user interface module for treatment tables with, and
without, independent longitudinal and lateral brakes.
The treatment tables without independent longitudinal and lateral brakes have a LAT/LONG
BRAKE button. The treatment tables with independent longitudinal and lateral brakes have a
LONGITUDINAL brake button.
To move the treatment table, press and hold the ENABLE bar, and operate the LONGITUDINAL
thumbwheel, to move the treatment table. The treatment table moves in the direction that you
operate the thumbwheel. The thumbwheel also controls the speed at which the treatment table
moves.
When it is necessary, you can move the treatment table manually. But, make sure that you
release the brake first. Apply the brake after you complete the treatment table movements.

3.22.2
Longitudinal motor drive circuit
When the LONGITUDINAL thumbwheel of a user interface module is moved, the speed and
direction of movement are represented by the VELXPSS demand signal, which is an analog
voltage of 4.3 V to 5.7 V, centered on +5.0 V. The signal is applied to the LTU PCB, where it is
translated to a level of 0 V to +10 V. The voltage is then applied to the LCU PCB as signal
VELXPSSLTU. Another version of the VELXPSS signal, in the range 3.6 V to 6.4 V DC, is applied to
the digital accelerator as signal VELXPSSBUF.
The LTU PCB also receives signal VELXHOS, a longitudinal movement velocity demand signal in
the range -5 V to +5 V from the digital accelerator. The signal VELXHOST2 in the range -12 V to
+12 V is an alternative input from other equipment. On the LTU PCB, the velocity demand signals
are level translated and one of the demands is applied to the LCU PCB as signal VELXLTU in the
range 0 V to +10 V, centered on +5.0 V.
On the LCU PCB, the VELXPSSLTU or VELXLTU signal is converted into an 8-bit data word that
represents the demanded speed and direction of movement. The data bus is applied to the FPLA,
which is programmed to respond by issuing a motor speed and direction command in the form of
an 8-bit output data word. The output data word is then converted into analog drive signal
VELXLCU in the range -5 V to +5 V. The drive signal is applied to the X-UMD PCB.
When enabled by signal ENBXLTUXMD from the LTU PCB, the X-UMD PCB outputs signal MOTX to
the motor of the longitudinal movement subsystem. MOTX is a 0 V to ±26 V DC signal that drives
the motor at the commanded speed and direction.

3.22.3
Longitudinal movement enable circuit
The movement ENABLE bar of the user interface module is represented by active-low signal
ENBPSS, which is applied to the LTU PCB. The signal is logic 0 while the ENABLE bar is held
pressed. On the LTU PCB, the ENBPSS signal is subjected to logic gating with other interlock
signals. The movement enable output of the LTU PCB is signal ENBXLTU to the LCU PCB. If all
interlock conditions are satisfied, the ENBXLTU signal is logic 0.
On the LCU PCB, the ENBXLTU signal is applied as a single input to the FPLA. Longitudinal
movement enable signal ENBXHOST from the digital accelerator is also input to the same pin of

On the LTU PCB, the +26 V level of signal ENBXLCU is translated into 0 V to +15 V logic signal
EMBXLTUXMD, which gives the motor drive enable signal to the X-UMD PCB.

3.22.4
Longitudinal movement brake control circuit
When the longitudinal movement brake is released, the FPLA on the LCU PCB sends an active-low
brake release command BRKXLCU to the LTU PCB. On the LTU PCB, the signal is translated into
the power signal BRKXLTU, which applies +52 V, then +26 V, across the coil of the longitudinal
movement brake. The action of the coil overcomes the force of the mechanical spring that holds
the brake on.
When the longitudinal movement brake is applied, the FPLA removes the brake release
command BRKXLCU to logic 1, and therefore the power supply to the coil of the brake is
removed.

3.22.7
Longitudinal movement positional readout circuits
The three potentiometers of the longitudinal movement subsystem are each supplied with +10 V
and 0 V reference signals. The levels of the signals from the wipers of the potentiometers
represent the actual longitudinal position of the treatment table. These signals give positional
readback data in the range 0 V to +10 V, centered on +5 V.
The signals are:
•
CRSXPSS is the voltage from the wiper of the longitudinal movement coarse
potentiometer.
•
FNAXPSS is the voltage from wiper A of the longitudinal movement fine potentiometer.
•
FNBXPSS is the voltage from wiper B of the longitudinal movement fine potentiometer.
•
CHKXPSS is the voltage from the wiper of the longitudinal movement check
potentiometer.
Signal CRSXPSS is sent to the LTU PCB, where the signal is level-translated to become output
CRSXLTU to the digital accelerator and used to display the longitudinal position of the treatment
table.
The LTU PCB also converts the CRSXPSS signal to a voltage that is proportional to the speed of the
longitudinal movement. This gives a unipolar velocity feedback signal VFBXLTULCU to the
LCU PCB.
On the LCU PCB, the four readback signals and velocity signal VFBXLTULCU are converted into 8bit data words that give the position of the treatment table on the longitudinal axis and the
speed of movement. The data is applied to the FPLA on the LCU PCB, which uses the information
to modify drive signal VELXLCU to the X-UMD PCB.

3.29.2
Treatment table software parts
Each software item has many different parameters known as parts. These parts do different
functions, for example, change data values to actual units, voltage units, amps, degrees, and
millimeters.
In the control items assigned to the treatment table, there is a servo item for each movement
subsystem:
•
i156 iso-rotational movement servo item
•
i157 longitudinal movement servo item
•
i158 lateral movement servo item
•
i159 height movement servo item.
In each servo item, there are two parts that have an effect on the performance of the position
servo:
Product description
Description and operation of the software control for the treatment table system
Precise Treatment Table™
Document ID: 45133701862 10
Corrective Maintenance Manual
©2019 Elekta Limited.
Page 113

•
Part 132 - slow down point, at which speed is limited and deceleration occurs.
•
Part 141 - position gain, which determines the accuracy of the positioning.
There are also three parts that have an effect on the performance when small movements are
made:
•
Part 135 - threshold, at which ASU correction starts.
•
Part 142 - ASU increment gain, the increment value of each ASU correction.
•
Part 140 - deadband, the positional error value at which ASU correction starts.
Slow down point
Part 132 sets a distance value to the last position of the movement. At the set distance, the
maximum speed is decreased to make sure that the system decelerates. If the value of Part 132 is
increased, deceleration occurs earlier. Because of IEC requirements, the value of Part 132 must
not be decreased below the default value.
Position gain
Part 141 sets the gain of the servo and therefore determines the accuracy of the positioning. If
the value of Part 141 is too high, the movement tends to oscillate about the required positional
setting, so the value of Part 141 should be such that it does not oscillate or overshoot by an
unacceptable amount.
If the movement undershoots, the value of Part 141 should be increased. If the movement
overshoots or oscillates, the value of Part 141 should be reduced. The performance may be
different in the two directions, so it may be necessary to compromise between undershoot in
one direction and overshoot in the other.
Part 132 and Part 141 can both be used to prevent oscillation, but their effects are subtly
different. Part 141 has most effect close to the final position because, for larger errors, the speed
is limited by the speed limits or by the slow down position. In general, the value of Part 141
should be reduced only if it is not possible to prevent overshoot/oscillation by reasonable
adjustment of Part 132.
It may be advisable to disable the nudging facility while determining the optimum values for Part
132 and Part 141.
Threshold
Part 135 applies a starting correction so that the ASU correction does not start from zero, thus
reducing the time taken to reach the correction that causes movement. Part 135 has a range of 0
to 50.
ASU increment gain
For small movements, the positional correction may not provide sufficient drive to allow the
motor to overcome stiction. If no movement is detected, an ASU correction (process_param_7 of
the servo item) is applied. The ASU correction is incremented by Part 142 at each occurrence of
the host machine control system loop (every 120 ms), until movement occurs when the ASU
correction is reset to zero.
The ASU correction applies a series of nudges which move the treatment table to the desired
position. Since the amount of correction reduces as the movement nears the desired position,
the amplitude of the ASU correction to cause movement increases. The ASU correction thus
forms a sawtooth waveform of increasing amplitude.
Part 142 has a range of 0 to 5.
Deadband
ASU correction is not applied unless the positional error is greater than the value of Part 140.
This can be used to prevent small oscillations about the desired position, but will reduce the
accuracy of positioning. Part 140 has a range of 0 to 10. If the ASU_correction is plotted (using
the graphing facility) against time while holding down the PSS ASU buttons for about 10 to

3.29.3
Description of the XVI table factors
If the treatment table is installed on a digital accelerator with X-Ray Volume Imaging (XVI) system
R3.5 or later, and the treatment table has been re-calibrated, then the XVI table factors must be
put into the XVI computer. See the applicable XVI Corrective Maintenance Manual.
When you do work on the digital accelerator, it can be necessary to calibrate the movement of
the gantry or the treatment table. The software for the digital accelerator does not automatically
send this changed calibration data to the XVI software. This causes errors to occur when XVI
calculates the table correction values, because the calibration data does not agree.
Therefore, it is important that you use the XVI DCB utility in the XVI software to copy the
applicable changed calibration data to the XVI software.

Do not change the calibration of the gantry or treatment table movement, unless you copy the
applicable changed calibration data to the XVI software. Use the XVI DCB utility in the XVI
software to copy the changed calibration data. If you ignore this warning, you can cause clinical
mistreatment.

4.1.4
Lowering the bellows cover of the treatment table
To get access to the movement assemblies of the treatment table to do the troubleshooting or
maintenance, it is necessary to lower the bellows cover.
There are two possible positions for the treatment table at the start of this procedure. The
treatment table can be as near as is possible to its lowest position, or it can be at a higher
position if motorized movement is not possible. At the lowest position, it is possible for one
person to lower the bellows cover. At a higher position, two persons must lower the bellows
cover.
1 
Rotate the gantry to 0°.
2 
If necessary, retract the MV and kV imaging arms.
3 
If motorized movement is possible, move the treatment table as near as is possible to its
lowest position (see Figure 4.5). If motorized movement is not possible, go to step 4 .

4.1.8
Using the manual crank handle
If there are no motorized movements, operate the manual crank handle to lift or lower the
treatment table.
1 
Lower the bellows cover.
2 
Attach the manual crank handle to the output shaft of the height motor.
001898
©2013 Elekta Limited
Figure 4.17
Manual crank handle on the height motor shaft.
3 
Release the height motor brake. Follow one of these two procedures.
a
Use the brake release tool.
b
Attach a length of string or wire to the brake release handle.
4 
Pull the string or wire away from the brake release handle and along the axis of the height
motor.
5 
Turn the manual crank handle clockwise to lift the treatment table, or counterclockwise to
lower the treatment table.
Note:
800 turns of the crank handle is approximately equal to 1000 mm of movement.
6 
When the treatment table is in position, disengage the manual crank handle from the shaft
of the height motor.
Note:
800 turns of the crank handle is approximately equal to 1000 mm of movement.
WARNING 4.4
Do not use motorized movement of the treatment table until after you remove the manual
crank handle. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.
7 
If you used a string or wire to release the brake, remove these from the brake release
handle.

5.1
Repair and replacement of the floor pan
5.1.1
Removing the floor pan with motorized movement of the treatment
table
Prerequisites
Hoist
Lifting jig
Lifting straps.
If motorized movement of the treatment table is available, you can use the treatment table to
help you to remove the floor pan. If motorized movement of the treatment table is not available,
do the procedure to remove the floor pan without motorized movement.
Before you try this procedure, make sure that you can use this procedure with third-party table
tops.
1 
Rotate the column assembly to 0°.
2 
Move the lateral carriage assembly to 0 mm.
3 
Move treatment table in the longitudinal direction until the table top is above the rotating
floor pan.
4 
Attach the straps to the table top and hang the lifting jig on the straps. Make sure that the
position of the bolt on the lifting jig is more in the direction of the treatment table.
5 
On the user interface module, operate the HEIGHT thumbwheel until the lifting jig is above
the center of the floor pan.
6 
Attach the lifting jig to the floor pan with the bolt. If necessary, operate the LATERAL and
LONGITUDINAL thumbwheels to carefully align the lifting jig to the floor pan.
7 
On the user interface module, operate the ISO-ROTATION BRAKE button to release the isorotation brake.
8 
If the ISO-ROTATION BRAKE button does not release the iso-rotation brake:
a
Remove the floorboard to get access to the brake.
b
Tighten the nut (see Figure 5.1) on the iso-rotation brake to release the brake.

the front face of the gearbox.

5.31
Adjusting the height movement limit switches
5.31.1
Adjusting the upper limit switches of the height movement
mechanism
There are four limit switches and four adjustable actuators (two of each for the lower limit, and
the upper limit) installed on the height mechanism. The table top must be installed when you set
up the upper and lower limit switches.
1 
Set the column rotation to 0°.
2 
Lower the bellows cover.
3 
Attach a length of string or wire to the brake release handle of the height motor, this will let
you manually release the brake.
4 
On the user interface module, operate the HEIGHT thumbwheel to move the treatment
table up, until you can get access to the upper limit microswitches.
Note:
The upper limit microswitches are on the gun side of the upper arm assembly.
5 
Short circuit one of the two microswitches to disable its operation.
6 
Use the HEIGHT thumbwheel to lower the treatment table to the upper firmware limit
(minimum table height).
7 
Accurately measure the vertical distance between the upper surface of the table top and the
finished floor level. Record this distance as measurement H1.
Note:
The reference voltage for the minimum height H1 is defined in the Firmware of the LCU PCB in the
EIM cabinet. If the coarse and check potentiometers of the height mechanism are set incorrectly,
the treatment table can move to a very low position. If this occurs, the treatment table will
operate the limit switches.
8 
Pull the string or wire out along the axis of the height motor to manually release the brake.
9 
Turn the manual crank handle counterclockwise until the upper microswitch limit (minimum
table height) activates.
On the user interface module, the LEDs go off for three to five seconds.

10 Accurately measure the vertical distance between the upper surface of the table top and the
finished floor level. Record this distance as measurement H2.
11 Compare the measurements H1 and H2. If the coarse and check potentiometers are set
correctly, H1 will be 6 mm greater than H2.
12 Manually release the brake.
13 Turn the manual crank handle counterclockwise until the treatment table is at the upper
limit of mechanical travel.
14 At this point, you will feel an increased resistance as you turn the manual crank handle.
15 Accurately measure the vertical distance between the upper surface of the table top and the

16 If the limit switches are set correctly, measurement H2 will be 2 mm to 3 mm greater than

5.33.1
Disconnecting the electrical interface module from the electrical
supply
There is no electrical power supply to the EIM cabinet when the digital accelerator is off. But if it
is on, there is an electrical power supply to the EIM cabinet.
WARNING 5.14
Do not do work on the EIM if it is connected to the electrical power supply. Always disconnect
the electrical supply before you start the work. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal
injury.
WARNING 5.15
Do not do work on the EIM cabinet with the covers removed, until you disconnect the electrical
supply. There are high voltages at the UPS, although the electrical supply to the EIM cabinet is
disconnected. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury.
All the steps of this procedure must be completed to remove the electrical supply to the EIM
cabinet.
1 
On the front panel of the EIM PSU, switch CB1 to OFF to disconnect the electrical supply to
the PSU.
The UPS continues to supply power to the PSU, and the amber lamp below CB1 stays on.
2 
On the front panel of the UPS, press the OFF button to disconnect the electrical supply to
the PSU.
On the front panel of the EIM PSU, the amber lamp below CB1 goes off.
3 
On the interface cabinet, switch CB13 to OFF to disconnect the electrical supply to the UPS.

5.38.3
Examining the operation of the emergency down drive
1 
Start the digital accelerator to supply the 24VACHOST signal to the EIM cabinet.
2 
Set the digital accelerator to the Preparatory machine state.
3 
Move the treatment table to its highest position.
4 
Operate the EMERGENCY STOP button in the treatment room wall to simulate a failure to
the electrical power supply.
This removes the electrical power supply and the 24VACHOST signal from the EIM cabinet.
5 
Make sure that the operation of the ENABLE bar on each user interface module causes the
treatment table to move down.
6 
After six minutes:
a
Make sure that the LEDs in the buttons of each user interface module stay on.
This shows that the UPS has not shut down and the UPS battery is in a good condition.
b
Make sure that the ENABLE bar of each user interface module causes the treatment
table to move down.
7 
Reset the EMERGENCY STOP button in the treatment room.
This switches on the electrical power supply and supplies the 24VACHOST signal to the EIM
cabient.
8 
Set the digital accelerator to the Preparatory machine state.
9 
At the TCS, do a system shutdown.
This removes the electrical power supply to the EIM cabinet, but continues to supply the
24VACHOST signal.
10 Make sure that the LEDs in the buttons of each user interface module go off.
–
If the EDD Timer Module is installed (machines before Serial No. 152531), the UPS shuts
down after approximately 5 minutes (±1 minute). If necessary, you can adjust this time
at the EDD timer module.
–
If the EDD Timer Module is not installed (machines from Serial No. 152531), the UPS
shuts down after approximately 1 minute (±30 seconds).

For small movements, it is possible that the position correction

If the software senses no movement, it applies a Table ASU

cycle (120 ms intervals) of the control system software. These
increases continue until movement occurs. When movement
occurs, the software sets the Table ASU correction to 0 again.
The Table ASU correction applies a series of small movements
(nudges) that move the treatment table to the set position. The
size of the Table ASU correction decreases as the treatment
table moves nearer to that position. Therefore, the amplitude of
the Table ASU correction that is necessary to move the
treatment table will increase. The Table ASU correction will
make a sawtooth plot in which the amplitude increases. Part
142 has a range of 0 to 5.

Deadband

treatment table position error is more than the value of Part

decreases the accuracy of the treatment table position. If you
make a plot of the Table ASU correction against time, and at the
same time press the Table ASU buttons for approximately 10 to
15 seconds:
•
The sawtooth plot will have one to five peaks
•
The amplitude of each peak increases.
Part 140 has a range of 0 to 10, where each unit is 0.2 mm (or
0.2°).

Fine-tuning the ASU increment
This is the procedure to examine the service graph and fine-tune the ASU increment on a
movement servo on the treatment table. This is the applicable procedure for Integrity™ TCS with
triple potentiometers.
1 
Examine the service graph. (This is for Part 137 only).
Note:
Part 142 (which is usually set to 1) has an effect on the slope of the saw-tooth plot. If the value of
Part 142 increases, the slope of the sawtooth line increases, and the time between nudges
decreases. A value of 0 disables the nudge function.
2 
Set Part 142 to the lowest value (usually 2). This will let the treatment table move to the
necessary position in 6 to 8 seconds.
3 
If the treatment table is not in the necessary position in 6 to 8 seconds, you must make an
adjustment:
a
To decrease the time for the treatment table to move to the necessary position,
increase the value of Part 142. It has a maximum value of 5.
b
If the value of Part 142 is too high, it is possible that the treatment table will oscillate or
go through the set position (the correction intermittently changes from positive to
negative). If this occurs, decrease the value of Part 142 by 1 or 2 from its current
setting.
4 
Continue to adjust the ASU increment and deadband until the ASU is stable, with no
oscillation and in a time between 6 and 8 seconds.

Fine-tuning the deadband
This is the procedure to examine the service graph and fine-tune the deadband on a movement
servo on the treatment table. This is the applicable procedure for Integrity™ TCS with triple
potentiometers.
1 
Examine the service graph. Make sure that the graph shows that the treatment table
movement moves into tolerance of the set position in 10 to 15 seconds with minimum
oscillation.
Note:
If the value of Part 140 is more than 5, you will not get an accuracy of 1 mm. (For iso-rotation,
this value is 1°). A large value for Part 140 will disable the nudge function. A typical value is 2.
2 
If the treatment table is not in the set position in 6 to 8 seconds with minimum oscillation,
increase the value of Part 140.
3 
Continue to adjust the ASU increment and deadband until the ASU is stable, with no
oscillation and in a time between 6 and 8 seconds.

6.3.3
Elements of a signal name
Signal names have three elements:
•
The first three letters of the signal name identify the item being driven by the signal.
•
The next letter identifies the movement axis.
•
The next three letters identify the source of the signal.
A line (bar) immediately above the name of a digital signal is an indication that the signal is
active-low (logic 0). For example:
MBKXYLTU
The names of digital signals that do not have a line (bar) immediately above the name are activehigh (logic 1).

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 13

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 13

1.4.4
Safety precautions for the electromagnetic compatibility
These are safety precautions to prevent an unwanted effect on the operation of the equipment by 
the radio frequency emissions.
The design and manufacture of Elekta products is in compliance with applicable EMC standards. 
The intended result of the standards is to minimize the risk of electromagnetic interference by RF 
devices. The type of device and the distance to the equipment has an effect on the intensity of the 
electromagnetic interference. The equipment includes the linear accelerator and accessories, the 
control cabinets, the computers in the control room, and equipment from other manufacturer.
It is necessary to have special precautions for EMC emissions. Elekta recommends that you obey 
these precautions when you use RF devices near the equipment.
•
Do not use RF devices unless they are in compliance with international standards for 
electromagnetic compatibility, for example, the CE or FCC mark.
•
Do not use a two-way emergency radio in the treatment room or the control room. Only 
use an emergency radio if there is an emergency.
•
Do not use cellular telephones, or other devices with cellular modems near the 
equipment. The Instructions for Use contains information on the minimum safe distance 
of these devices from the equipment.
•
When you use a device that is enabled for wireless operation, it must be a minimum of 
10 cm from the equipment.
•
Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID) readers, when activated to do a scan of a RFID tag, 
must be a minimum of one meter from the equipment.
Note:
The RFID systems that Elekta supply use lower power levels. You can safely use these RFID systems 
when you obey the procedures in the Instructions for Use for the product.
The system must be installed, put into service, and maintained in compliance with the EMC 
information in the Instructions for Use.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of parts and equipment.
WARNING 1.4
Do not put portable or mobile radio frequency (RF) communication devices near to 
the equipment. The emissions from such RF devices can be more than the EMC 
standards, and can have unwanted effects on the equipment operation. If you 
ignore this warning, the RF emissions can cause the equipment to have a 
malfunction. A malfunction can cause fatal injury, clinical mistreatment, or damage 
to the equipment.
WARNING 1.5
Do not use accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by Elekta. 
They can have an effect on the EMC performance, which can increase EMC 
emissions or decrease the immunity to RF interference of the equipment. If you 
ignore this warning, incorrect radiation delivery and other malfunctions can occur, 
which can cause fatal injury or clinical mistreatment.

1.4.34
Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can keep 
the equipment safe to operate.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and 
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each 
week of the year.
The level of operation of the equipment can be different to ‘normal use’. This has an effect on the 
length of the service life. Because of wear of parts, the risk of a malfunction can increase after 10 
years operation. Elekta recommends that before you continue operation after 10 years, you 
complete the regular extended life checks.
Elekta can help the User with the correct safety checks, planned maintenance schedules, and the 
regular extended life checks for continued safe operation of the equipment.
The system must be maintained throughout its expected service life in compliance with the EMC 
information detailed in the appendix in this document.
For information on the above checks and schedules, contact your local Elekta representative.
1.4.35
Disposal of the equipment
This is the procedure for the disposal of the equipment at End of Life to prevent damage to health 
and the environment by radioactive and hazardous material.
End of life (EOL) disposal is the procedure to disassemble, remove, and discard the equipment, in 
full or in parts, to a condition where it is not possible to operate the equipment for its intended 
use.
Always use procedures that give the best possible protection to the environment when you 
remove and discard the equipment. The procedures must obey the laws and regulations of the 
jurisdictions in which you discard the equipment. Do not discard Elekta equipment through the 
domestic waste systems.
Only a Qualified Expert (QE) and an approved facility with an applicable license, must remove and 
discard the equipment and recycle the material. Do not discard material that is hazardous to 
health and the environment together with other material.
Before you remove and discard equipment, contact Elekta for information.

warning, you can cause fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
WARNING 1.38

systems or in the environment. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury 
and damage to the environment.

Navigating the linear accelerator corrective maintenance

This Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual has been designed in a modular format 
that will eventually comprise a fully integrated, electronically published suite of information. The 
main characteristics of modular documentation are that:
•
Where possible, a piece of information resides in one place only - it is not duplicated and 
is therefore easy to update.
•
Categories of information (for example, repair instructions) always appear at the same 
place in each module - so the information is easy to find.
•
Cross-references are used to direct users to associated and/or more detailed 
information.
The Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual set therefore comprises a number of 
modules, each of which is dedicated to a primary system of the linear accelerator. The modules are 
compiled into three volumes as listed in Table 3.1.
3.2.1
Architecture of the corrective maintenance manual modules
With the exception of this reference module, each module of the Linear Accelerator Corrective 
Maintenance Manual set conforms to a similar architecture that allows users to drill down through 
the document set at need. A high-level system overview leads to a suite of detailed technical 
descriptions followed by troubleshooting, repair and post-repair instructions. In general, each 
module:
•
Chapter 1 always contains important regulatory and safety information which are 
mandatory requirements of technical medical documentation. The chapter also includes 
a comprehensive glossary of acronyms and abbreviations, and a list of the 
cross-references to all other modules in the document set.

Chapter 2 provides an overview of the subject system(s) and summarizes the system 
functions within the linear accelerator. The narrative is usually supported by a schematic 
diagram of the system(s).

3.3
Safety information for service personnel
This section presents the complex safety issues that apply when an Elekta linear accelerator is 
serviced. Warnings of specific hazards also appear at the appropriate point of application 
throughout the entire Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual set.
3.3.1
General safety
The linear accelerator is Class 1, Type B equipment according to IEC 60601-2-1, Part 2C, Computer 
Controlled Radiotherapy Equipment.
To make sure that all service personnel work in a safe way, all warnings and cautions throughout 
the Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual must be strictly obeyed.
The use of this equipment should be controlled by qualified members of the hospital staff, whose 
responsibilities include:
The assignment of passwords to suitable persons for each of the various levels of 
authorization.
Making sure that all persons who work on the linear accelerator are competent to perform 
the procedures for which they are authorized.
The equipment should be used only by service personnel who are trained in the use of locally 
applicable regulations, standards and laws that govern the safe use of ionizing radiation, and in the 
specific use of this equipment.
Service personnel must be familiar with the contents of this document before attempting any 
procedure and/or instruction given in the Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual set.
Service personnel must use the equipment only as described in this manual, and be aware of all 
warnings given in this manual.
Elekta provides training courses for service personnel, which cover the safe use of this equipment. 
The members of the hospital staff who control the use of the linear accelerator must arrange for 
the regular maintenance of the equipment as stated in the operation and service manuals.
3.3.2
Powering up and powering down the linear accelerator
3.3.2.1
Emergency switches
Service personnel must be thoroughly familiar with the location and function of all emergency 
switches associated with the linear accelerator. These include:
•
The STOP button on the handheld controller(s) in the treatment room.
•
The emergency stop motors button on each user interface of the treatment table in the 
treatment room.
•
All locally installed emergency power OFF switches in the treatment room, the control 
room and the equipment room.
3.3.2.2
Powering up and powering down the linear accelerator
Usually, each hospital has a local procedure for powering up and powering down an Elekta linear 
accelerator and, if so, the local procedure should always be used. In the absence of local 
procedures, follow the instructions given in the applicable manual of Instructions for User - Service 
Mode for the TCS.

There continues to be a risk of high voltage electric shock after the power supply

include ionizing radiation and heavy moving masses.
Additional hazards to service personnel when the covers of the equipment are

3.3.6.3
High voltage
Using the HT discharge rod
The HT discharge rod (Brinckley Hook) is stowed on the side of the modulator (Area 30). The 
purpose of the device is to safely eliminate high voltage charges which may be present in the 
vicinity of the modulator and elsewhere on the linear accelerator.
To use the HT discharge rod:
1
Remove the HT discharge rod from its stowage position.
2
Touch the HT discharge rod to the point labelled D1 +ve on the modulator.
If a high voltage charge is present, a flash and audible bang will occur when the HT is 
discharged through the rod.
3
Replace the HT discharge rod in its stowage position.
WARNING 3.8
Do not remove the covers or cables from the equipment unless special instructions 
in this document tell you to. The covers give access to high voltage electric parts. 
Always install the covers and cables again before you use the equipment. If you 
ignore this warning, a high voltage electric shock can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 3.9
Voltages of up to 50 kV are present within the linear accelerator. Never touch or 
approach any part of the equipment when the HT is switched on, or when circuits 
may still be electrically charged.
Obey the instructions given in this manual to make the equipment safe before work 
is started.
If you ignore this warning, a high voltage electrical shock can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 3.10
Before handling any component in the high voltage circuits, switch off all electrical 
power: then use the HT discharge rod to fully discharge the associated high voltage 
capacitors.
The HT PSU has 600 V capacitors that may remain charged. Check the capacitors 
with a voltmeter or allow 12 minutes for them to discharge.
If you ignore this warning, a high voltage electrical shock can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 3.11
If work must be performed on the linear accelerator while the HT is on, obey all 
local operating procedures and the instructions given in this manual.
If you ignore this warning, a high voltage electrical shock can cause fatal injury.

Collision risks
The linear accelerator is fitted with a touchguard to protect against collision between the BLD and

If the treatment table is moved into a collision position, the system cannot alert the operator to 
the fact.
The positional limits of the treatment table may be customized. When the treatment table is 
positioned within the customized limits, the gantry is permitted to move as required when the ASU 
option has been selected.
ASU from the control room is done with the FKP. You can do ASU from the control room with room 
doors 1 open or closed. It is not possible to do ASU from the control room, if the service 
room/room doors 2 is open. Simultaneous ASU of gantry and table isocentric rotation is not 
possible.
ASU from the treatment room is done with the HHC. You can only do ASU from the treatment 
room with the HHC when room doors 1 is open. On the HHC, function control buttons < or > are 
used to set the functions controlled by the HHC. 
Refer to the manual Instructions for Use - Clinical Mode for more information.

trapped or damaged by the equipment.

Do not allow water or any other liquid to enter the linear accelerator otherwise short circuits

Solvent
Corrosive liquid

All parts of the linear accelerator, including the accessories and connection cables, can be

3.4
Elekta linear accelerators
Elekta linear accelerators are machines for use in clinical radiation therapy. They produce a beam 
of high energy particles that is accurately delivered to the target tumor in a patient reclining on a 
treatment table. A high tension (HT) and radio frequency (RF) source provides the energy that 
accelerates the particles. Travelling wave technology is used to transport the radiation beam, and a 
beam limiting device (BLD) with collimation is used to shape the beam and deliver it precisely to 
the target.
The linear accelerator is a drum and gantry structure that rotates through 360° around an 
isocentric axis. The components that produce the radiation beam are mounted on the drum and 
the gantry. The machine is the main component in a complete system for the delivery of 
therapeutic radiation to patients. The other parts of the system are:
•
Treatment table
•
Beam limiting device (BLD)
•
Control system
•
Imaging systems.
The linear accelerator is usually installed in a suite of three rooms which contain the following 
main parts:
•
Treatment room - gantry, BLD, treatment table, monitors, handheld controllers, imaging 
system components, covers, wall-mounted lasers. 
•
Control room - linear accelerator control system, function keypad, imaging system 
workstations.
•
Equipment room - gantry drum and all other equipment such as the interface cabinet, 
reeling post, gas cylinder, table electrical interface module (EIM), client’s interface 
terminal board (CITB) and so on.

3.4.1
Treatment table
The treatment table is located in the treatment room. The treatment table allows the patient to be 
very accurately positioned to receive the prescribed radiotherapy, and supports the patient during 
treatment.
An Elekta treatment table is usually installed with Elekta digital accelerators. The treatment table 
is not a topic in this Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual but is fully described in a 
dedicated document set. 
3.4.2
Beam limiting device (BLD)
The BLD is fitted at the delivery end of the gantry arm in the treatment room. The BLD provides 
final collimation of the X-ray or electron beam. Elekta digital accelerators are equipped with one 
BLD:
•
MultiLeaf collimator (MLCi/MLCi2)
•
Beam Modulator™
•
Agility™.
3.4.3
Control system
The control of Elekta digital accelerators is exercised by the treatment control system (TCS) 
running the digital accelerator. The system resides in a special treatment control cabinet (TCC).
The treatment control software has two main modes of operation:
Clinical Mode
Service Mode.
The control system is not a main topic in this Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual 
but is fully described in a dedicated document set. However, the Service Mode is used extensively 
during setup, troubleshooting, calibration and testing of the digital accelerator and is therefore 
discussed where applicable.
For detailed instructions on using Service Mode, see Instructions for Use - Service Mode for the 
TCS.
3.4.4
Imaging systems
Elekta Digital Accelerators are usually equipped with at least one imaging system. The imaging 
systems are not topics in this Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual but are fully 
described in dedicated document sets.
3.4.5
Clinical beams
The digital accelerator generates two types of clinical beam:
•
Electron - used to treat superficial tumors (less than 5 cm deep). The therapeutic energy 
range for electrons is 4 MeV to 22 MeV.
•
X-ray (photon) - used to treat deep-seated tumors. The therapeutic energy range of 
X-rays is 4 MV to 25 MV. Typically, X-ray beams are used in combinations (for example, 
opposed pairs), which deliver very high doses to the target, but with relatively low skin 
doses. X-ray beams provide up to three energy levels.

Brief description of the digital accelerator assembly
The digital accelerator itself comprises the following main assemblies:

•
Gantry arm
•
Interface cabinet
•

Gantry drum
The gantry drum is housed in the equipment room. Subunits of the digital accelerator are mounted 
in dedicated areas within the gantry drum and at the rear of the gantry drum.
Gantry arm
The gantry arm projects from the gantry drum into the treatment room. The arm contains the 
linear accelerating waveguide that transports the radiation beam from its source in the gantry 
drum to the BLD mounted at the treatment end of the gantry arm.
Interface cabinet
The interface cabinet is located in the equipment room. It provides the electrical interconnection 
between all the systems and subsystems of the digital accelerator.
Cable reeling post
The cable reeling post is located in the equipment room. It feeds and retracts the main cable loom 
to and from the gantry drum as the drum rotates. The reeling post also provides connections to 
external services such as cooling water and dielectric gas.

3.5.1
Principle of operation
An Elekta digital accelerator comprises a number of primary systems:
•
HT and RF
•
Beam physics
•
Power supplies and Interlocks
•
Dosimetry
•
Movements
•
Cooling, gas and vacuum
•
System communications
•
Covers
•

3.5.1.1
HT and RF systems
The HT and RF systems operating together produce a radiation beam of high-energy electrons or 
X-rays (photons).
Stable, high-voltage pulses are produced by the HT system. In the RF system, the HT pulses cause 
the generation of a travelling RF wave that is used to transport electrons through an accelerating 
waveguide and into the BLD.
The travelling RF wave is produced by a modulator that is powered by the high-voltage pulses from 
the HT system. A magnetron in the modulator generates an oscillating RF power input to the 
waveguide and thus forms the travelling RF wave. An electron gun, powered by the same HT 
pulses as the magnetron, injects electrons into the waveguide where they are transported by the 
RF wave.
The compact design of the digital accelerator is made possible by the use of the high-power 
magnetron as the RF power source.
See Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - High Tension and Radio Frequency 
Systems for a full description of the HT and RF systems.
3.5.1.2
Beam physics system
The RF energy is propagated along the accelerating waveguide as travelling waves. Energy is 
transferred from the travelling waves to the electrons, which are thus accelerated to emerge at the 
output of the waveguide with considerable gain in energy. The travelling waves of RF and electron 
energy are transported along their path by a set of magnets that surround the accelerating 
waveguide.
The high-energy electron beam passes through an achromatic bending magnet system that 
deflects the beam through different angles until it finally emerges at the target/window. Here the 
beam strikes a target that generates X-rays, or passes through a thin metal window to produce 
electron radiation. Beyond the target/window area, the radiation beam passes to the BLD.
See Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - Beam Physics System for a full 
description of the beam physics system.
