1.2.16.1
Safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity are the necessary safety
precautions to know to prevent excessive exposure to radioactivity, which can cause serious
injury or damage to the environment.
Always use two radiation detectors to measure the level of induced radioactivity. Only use
radiation detectors that have an applicable calibration certificate. The period of time since the
last calibration date must be less than 12 months. Do not use the radiation detectors if the period
of time since the last calibration date is more than 12 months.
WARNING 1.23
Do not move radioactive material (by air, sea, or land) unless you obey the applicable laws and
regulations for induced radioactivity and disposal of radioactive material of the jurisdictions
through which the movement occurs. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury
and damage to the environment.
1.2.16.2
Safety precautions for handling parts with induced radioactivity
The handling of parts with induced radioactivity must comply with the laws and regulations of the
jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed. The safe levels of radiation applicable in the UK
do not apply in all jurisdictions. The permitted level of radioactivity must always be as low as
reasonably achievable (ALARA). This level may vary depending on local rules, therefore the safe
working levels from the applicable local rules must be considered as the acceptable working limit.
If there are no safe levels available for a jurisdiction, use the UK value as a guideline, which is a
maximum of 150 cps at the surface for a maximum duration of 72 minutes. The following table
shows the conversion from this value to other units.

1.3.2
Recommendations for emergency procedures
Before you use the equipment, Elekta recommends that you know all the local emergency
procedures and the locations of all the emergency switches.
The Elekta equipment includes:
•
The STOP MOTORS buttons on the handheld controllers and user interface panels in
the treatment room, and FKP in the control room.
When you press these buttons, it disconnects the electrical supply from the motors,
stops all movements of the equipment, and stops kV and MV radiation.
•
The EMERGENCY POWER OFF buttons in the treatment room, control area, and areas
near the equipment.
When you operate these buttons, it disconnects the electrical supply to the linear
accelerator. The buttons disconnect the electrical supply from many electrical circuits,
but not from all the circuits.

2.1.2
Recommendations for training
The regulations for training give a description of the necessary training, regulations, and
compliance that apply to the operation of the equipment.
Different countries have different regulations for training. Make sure that you have the necessary
training before you operate or do work on the equipment. Make sure that your training is in
compliance with the laws and regulations of the jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed.
Training is available from Elekta. Contact Elekta for more information about the applicable
training courses.
2.1.3
Disposal of the equipment
End of life (EOL) disposal is the procedure to disassemble, remove, and discard the equipment, in
full or in parts, to a condition where it is not possible to operate the equipment for its intended
use.
Only a Qualified Expert (QE) and an approved facility with an applicable license, may remove and
discard the equipment and recycle the material.
A full description of disposal requirements is detailed in a separate document Product Disposal
Information. This document is available on request from Elekta.
The customer owns the data on the storage media. If there are any data storage media such as
HDDs, remove them from the device and hand them to the customer for disposal. If the customer
entrusts the disposal team to dispose of the data, the data must be destroyed in accordance with
relevant cybersecurity regulations.

CAUTION 2.2
Do not touch the parts identified with the ESD caution label. Always obey the ESD precautions
during work on these parts. If you ignore this caution, you can cause damage to the equipment.
Semiconductor devices, integrated circuits, and the parts that contain them, are ESD sensitive
devices. These devices are electrostatic discharge sensitive (ESDS) devices. ESD can cause damage
to these devices and cause them to have a malfunction immediately or some time after the
electrostatic discharge. To prevent the ESD damage to these devices, always wear a grounded
antistatic wrist strap, and obey the applicable ESD precautions and procedures.
Elekta recommends that all users receive the training about ESD. The training must include the
ESD caution label and these ESD precautions.

3.1
CMM Document scope
The corrective maintenance manual (CMM) helps service engineers troubleshoot, repair and
maintain the systems, subsystems and components of the linear accelerator. The target audience
is qualified service engineers. These may be engineers employed directly by Elekta, qualified
representatives of Elekta or qualified representatives of Elekta's customers.
The manual provides:
•
A description of the system or sub-system in question.
•
A troubleshooting section to identify the problem areas.
•
A set of detailed procedures used to replace FRUs (field replaceable units).
•
A section on how to return the device to work.
If you find any mistakes in this document, or identify areas for improvement, please raise a CLM
(customer lifecycle management) case or an ECR (Engineering change Request) and assign it to
the relevant queue.

room. For Harmony in the treatment room, there is an integrated HHC which can control the XVI
system. Use the HHC to control the position of the kV detector panel.
When the XVI system is not in operation, you can retract the kV source arm and move the kV
detector panel.

4.3
Principle of operation
When the XVI system is not in use, the digital accelerator operates in its normal clinical mode to
deliver radiotherapy to patients.
4.3.1
Software control
The XVI system is controlled by a software program running on the XVI control cabinet, where
parameters such as the timing and power characteristics of the X-ray pulses are configured. The
software is also used to examine and manipulate the acquired images.
4.3.2
Safety interlocks on the XVI system
The XVI system is connected to the interlock system of the host digital accelerator. The interlocks
prevent the emission of radiation by the kV generator if the system is in an unsafe condition, and

4.5
Detector Readback Safety Kit (DRSK)
Note:
The installation of the Detector Readback Safety Kit (DRSK) was mandatory and it is therefore
already installed on all systems.
Elekta released the Detector Readback Safety Kit (DRSK) modification kit because of a failure in
the position detection system. A defective potentiometer or slider switch on the kV Arm Control
Board (ACB), which can cause the incorrect position of the detector in the longitudinal or lateral
direction, would have caused such a failure.
An incorrect lateral position can have an effect on image registration, which can cause wasted
images and, as a result, wasted patient dose. More important, an incorrect longitudinal
potentiometer indication can cause incorrect interpretation of the patient position, and an error
in the subsequent table movement can cause mistreatment.
The DRSK modification kit included the installation of a new potentiometer assembly that
contains a second potentiometer wire. The first wire connects to the coarse and fine B
potentiometer, and the second wire connects to the fine A potentiometer. This configuration lets
the system detect changes in the phase relationship between the fine A and fine B
potentiometers to find a possible problem with one of the potentiometer wires.
The installation of the DRSK modification kit also included the installation of a breakout box that
separates the signal from the lateral and longitudinal potentiometer wires. This lets the extended
imaging module (XIM) change the analogue potentiometer indications into digital controller-area
network (CAN), to send to the XVI control system (PC) through the iViewGT™ CAN bus.
As part of the modification kit installation, an XVI software upgrade was also necessary. The XVI
software upgrade installed a new calibration tool that tells the software what the longitudinal and
lateral potentiometer positions are at each field of view (FOV). The software has inhibits that

4.6
kV generator - Sedecal SHF 435 DSI Series (non-applicable
for Harmony)
The Sedecal SHF 435 DSI Series generator is a 40 kW unit that can produce single and continuous
radiographic exposures of varying energy and dose.
When the foot switch or the kV Start button on the function key pad is pressed, the kV enable
signal to the kV generator is asserted, which sets the kV generator to the X-ray status (if all
interlocks are satisfied). On receipt of a TRIGGER pulse from the DCB, the kV Generator fires the
X-Ray tube to radiate the detector panel through the exposed object. This acquires an image. This
cycle continues while the foot switch is pressed continuously or the kV Start button on the
function key pad is pressed - so for each occurrence of the DCB TRIGGER, one X-ray pulse is
generated and one kV image is acquired.
The tube housing has a thermal cut-out for X-ray tube over temperature. The generator also
provides a 240 V AC power supply for the cooling fan on the X-ray tube, which is energized
continually when the generator is energized.
In the cabinet of the kV generator there are 2 Elekta-specific parts:
•
Elekta Interface PCB
•
Generator Adaptor assembly.
For a full description of the kV generator, refer to the documentation supplied by the
manufacturer.

4.8.1
Description of the kV source arm
The kV source arm is installed on a pair of parallel arms that extend through the front of the
gantry drum. The kV source arms are not telescopic. They are held in position by a latch roller
assembly on the gantry drum. When the kV source arm is retracted, the kV source arms are fully
contained in the gantry drum.
The kV source arm can be manually extended or retracted as necessary. A push button on the
cover unlocks the kV source arm. When the kV source arm is unlocked, it can be manually
extended to its full length of travel to the imaging position. When locked in the imaging position,
the kV source arm enables part of the kV interlock chain.
When the kV source arm is unlocked, it can be manually pushed in the direction of the gantry
drum to its full length of travel, where it automatically locks.
A retractile cable guide is installed between the kV source arm and the linear accelerator. The
cable guide prevents damage to the cables of the kV source arm during the full range of
movement between the extended and retracted positions.

The housing contains a primary collimator with an aperture that lets sufficient X-rays to pass
through the housing to encompass the different field of views, plus a margin. There is also a leadlined box structure with a secondary shielding plate to reduce leakage from the collimator
housing. The lead-lined box is 3.2 mm in thickness and has an X-ray absorption quality of 99.99%
TO (BS334 Type A).
The mounting assembly contains a thick plate that has an angled face to counteract the tilt angle
of the tube. The mounting plate also accommodates four stainless steel pillars that support the
collimator. The pillars effectively restrict any deflection of the collimator under its own weight.
An adjustable bracket assembly is fitted to the interface plate and bolted to the cable chain stand
off bracket. The adjustable brackets make sure that any load applied to the collimator when a
cassette is inserted is not transferred to the kV tube, causing the tube to twist. Instead, the load is
transferred to the tube mount casting.
The collimator also interfaces with the cover of the kV source arm. An aperture in the cover aligns
with the rails in the collimator housing allowing the collimator and filter cassettes to be inserted
and withdrawn.

4.8.6
Electrical grounding of the collimator housing
The collimator housing has two aluminum rails in which the collimation and filtration cassettes
run. The two rails are grounded near their leading edges (edges where each cassette is inserted
from.) This ensures compliance to the IEC 60601-1 and UL 60601-1 standards.
4.8.7
Suspended mass of the collimator housing
The collimator housing is considered to be a suspended mass. The assembly is compliant to the
Suspended Mass clause of IEC 60601-1/UL 60601-1.
4.8.8
Secondary collimation and filtration of the X-rays
Secondary collimation is provided by cassettes placed in the collimator housing of the kV source.
There are three types of cassette:
•
Collimator cassettes - which limit the X-ray beam differently by constraining it to a field
size when the kV detector panel is positioned at a certain FOV.
•
Filter cassettes - which shape the collimated beam by applying pre-defined filtration,
for example an aluminum bow-tie filter.
•
Calibration cassettes - which apply pre-defined beam attenuation and fiducial marks
for use during installation, service and maintenance of the XVI system.
Before a kV imaging session, a collimator cassette and a filter cassette are manually inserted into
the collimator housing by the user. These are the only beam shaping and filtration devices
encountered by the user during clinical use.

4.9.3
Close movement (non-applicable for Harmony)
The Close movement moves the kV detector panel from any deployed position to the closed
position in a combination of lateral, longitudinal and pivot movements. The kV detector arm is
first moved to the lateral centered position, then retracted fully, and finally pivoted up into the
closed position.
When the <CLOSE> button on the XVI HHC is pressed while the <ENABLE> button is held pressed,
the lateral movement drives into the slow speed region of the movement and searches for the
Panel_Centered microswitch. When the microswitch is operated, the middle arm drives towards
the gantry until the Middle_Arm_Retracted microswitch is operated. The kV detector panel then
drives towards the gantry.
When the detector locking position microswitch is reached, the detector locking solenoid is
released and the movement continues to drive towards the gantry. As the detector locking slot
passes over the solenoid, the solenoid locking pin locates and actuates the Detector_Locked
microswitch.
If the detector was moved back to its maximum retracted position, so the detector locking slot is
nearer to the gantry than the locking solenoid, the detector is moved away from the gantry.
When the detector locking position microswitch is deactivated, the drive is reversed and the
detector is driven back towards the gantry. The solenoid is then released and locates into the
detector locking slot as the movement retracts, as described above.
The pivot system logic is examined for the following conditions:
•
Lateral movement is centered (panel centered microswitch operated).
•
The detector is locked by solenoid locking pin (Detector_Locked microswitch
operated).

4.9.4
Center movement of the detector panel (Harmony only)
The center movement moves the detector panel from any position to the isocenter position.

4.9.5
Movement operation
The longitudinal movement comprises two separate actions:
•
The kV detector panel moves with respect to the middle arm.
•
The middle arm moves with respect to the shoulder casting.
These are referred to as the detector drive and middle arm drive respectively.
The two movements are controlled using a clutch and a brake to transfer the drive from one
motor.
When the kV detector panel is driven from the retracted position at the gantry end of the
longitudinal movement, initially the detector is moved with respect to the middle arm. The
detector cradle is moved to the detector imaging position (to minimize the backscatter into the
detector). The detector imaging position microswitch is actuated and movement is switched to
the middle arm drive. Longitudinal positioning is then achieved using the middle arm drive.
When the system is retracted, the middle arm is driven until the middle arm retracted
microswitch detects that the middle arm is fully retracted. Movement switches to the detector
cradle drive. The detector cradle can then be driven back until the detector retracted microswitch
is operated.
4.9.6
Illegal logic status
If the control logic of the longitudinal movement reaches a status where the control system does
not know the longitudinal position, the manual brake release buttons flash and the longitudinal
movement is disabled. This continues until the logic is corrected.
This condition occurs when:
•
The detector cradle is NOT at the imaging position (so backscatter may be introduced
into the image), AND
•
The middle arm is NOT fully retracted (so, for non-Harmony, the longitudinal scale is
incorrect; for Harmony, the covers are not aligned).
If the manual brake release is operated, the detector cradle can be manually moved to a correct
logic status, that is, a known position. By de-selecting the manual brake release, the arm can be
driven normally.
4.9.7
Isocenter pause
When approaching the imaging position, longitudinal movement is slowed down at
approximately 2 cm (depending on calibration) before the imaging position is reached. This is
independent of direction (not as visible as in the lateral movement), and permits a more accurate

Longitudinal extended limit
When the longitudinal movement reaches the furthest position from the gantry, the longitudinal

been reached, only movement away from the limit is possible, that is, towards the gantry.
4.9.9
Manual brake release
The longitudinal movement has a manual brake release which is operated by either of the two
buttons located on each side of the arm. When the manual brake release is operated, the
indicator lamps in the switches are switched off and the user can move the kV detector arm by
hand (in the longitudinal direction only).
When the manual brake release is selected, the movements of the middle arm and detector
assembly follow the same logic as when motorized movements are used.
If the detector is moved from the small, medium or large FOV towards the gantry, the middle arm
is initially allowed to move into the shoulder assembly. When the middle arm retracted
microswitch is operated, the brake on the middle arm drive is applied and the brake on the
detector drive is released, allowing the detector to be moved along the middle arm toward the
gantry.
The opposite logic applies if the detector is moved away from the gantry.
The manual brake release button is also used to indicate if the logic control is in an incorrect
status. The brake buttons will flash while the system is in an incorrect status and will return to
normal indication when the logic status is correct.
4.9.10
Lateral movement
The lateral movement is driven using a leadscrew system and does not have a manual brake
release.
4.9.11
Medium FOV pause
As with the longitudinal movement, the lateral movement decelerates when approaching the
medium FOV position. The speed is reduced approximately 1 cm before the medium FOV is
reached from either direction (depending on calibration). When the medium FOV is reached, the
movement is paused for approximately 1 second to allow the user to stop.
The lateral coarse potentiometer is used to determine the position at which the movement speed
is reduced. The potentiometer voltage is compared with a known voltage that is set during
calibration.
Using a similar voltage comparator system, the fine potentiometer is used to detect when the
detector is at the medium FOV position. Movement is paused for approximately 1 second.

Small and large FOV positions
The small and large FOV positions are the limits of the lateral drive. The lateral coarse
potentiometer is used to determine the limits of movement using a voltage comparator. When a
valid position is reached, the only possible movement is away from that position.
In the small FOV, to align the center of the panel with the center of the kV beam, the panel must
be driven towards the center axis of the kV source (115 mm), that is, the endpoint of the lateral
drive using the lateral movement button.
For large FOV, the panel must be driven away from the center axis of the kV source (75 mm), that
is, the endpoint of the lateral drive using the lateral movement button. If the user tries to leave
the kV panel in a position that is not one of the defined lateral imaging positions, an audible
warning is emitted.
Note:
This is a different audible warning to that produced when the kV panel touchguard is activated.
Refer to the XVI Instructions for Use manual for more information.

4.9.14
kV detector panel
The kV detector panel consists of a detector and a fluorescent screen. The X-rays emitted by the
kV source excite the fluorescent screen and therefore produce light. The detector converts the
light into an electrical signal that is read by electronics that surround the panel. The electrical
signal is converted into image data and sent to the XVI control cabinet.
CAUTION 4.1
When the XVI imaging system is emitting kV radiation, make sure that only the central area of
the kV detector panel is irradiated. Do not irradiate the panel electronics. Long term or direct
exposure to radiation could degrade the kV detector panel.
4.9.15
Trigger signal
A synchronization connection is used to trigger the panel and to send a frame synchronization
signal from the panel to the detector control board (DCB) when a complete frame has been read.
For the AL detector panel, a frame grabber in the XVI control cabinet receives image data through
a data link.
Note:
The AL detetor panel is non-applicable for Harmony.
For the AP detector panel, the XVI control cabinet receives image data with the Gigabit Ethernet
connection. The frame grabber is not a default for XVI control cabinet Mk6 or Mk6i.
4.9.16
LEDs on the kV detector panel
Two LEDs are visible on the kV detector panel. The LED furthest from the connector is on (green)
when the electrical power supply is present. The LED nearest to the connector flashes orange
when the panel is in external trigger mode, and flashes green when the panel is in free running
mode.
4.9.17
Amorphous silicon (a-Si) kV detector panel
The kV detector panel is a Perkin Elmer Amorphous Silicon (a-Si) detector. It has a resolution of
1024 x 1024 16-bit pixel images, with a panel size of 41 x 41 cm (approximately 26 x 26 cm at
isocenter).
Figure 4.20 shows how the detector is assembled.
A synchronization connection is used to trigger the kV detector panel and to send a frame sync
from the kV detector panel to the DCB when a complete frame was read.
Image data is read from the kV detector panel, through a data link into a framegrabber (except
the XVI control cabinet Mk6 and Mk6i) in the XVI control system.
The kV detector panel has two LEDs. The panel is energized when the green LED is on. It is the
LED, that is farthest from the connector. The LED nearest the connectors flashes orange when it is
triggered by the external trigger from the DCB, and flashes green when the kV detector panel is in
free running mode.

4.9.20
Modes of image acquisition
The table gives a list and description of the different modes of kV image acquisition for the XVI
system.
Acquisition
Description
PlanarView™
In this mode, the linear accelerator gantry is static and XVI acquires one
static planar image. A number of frames are acquired and averaged to
display one image.
MotionView™
In this mode, XVI acquires a sequence of planar images for a period of time,
while the gantry of the linear accelerator moves or is static. The image
sequence can therefore show the movement of anatomical structures that
are in the field of view.
VolumeView™
This mode includes Symmetry™, and XVI acquires images while the gantry of
the linear accelerator rotates. Elekta recommends that the minimum gantry
rotation you use for a small field of view (FOV) is 200°. The maximum gantry
rotation is 360°.
An acquisition with a 360° rotation of the gantry acquires approximately 650
images. XVI saves each projection image and the gantry angle at acquisition.
XVI uses this data to reconstruct a 3D image of the anatomical volume. You
can then register this 3D volume, in XVI, against an imported CT reference
image.
Symmetry
VolumeView™
Symmetry VolumeView™ is the acquisition of a 4D VolumeView™ image.
During 4D VolumeView™, XVI acquires images and reconstructs them in
relation to a period of time. This lets you see the different phases of the
breathing cycle for a patient.
To do a Symmetry VolumeView™ acquisition you must decrease the gantry
speed. XVI can then acquire sufficient projection data to collect multiple
phase data at each gantry angle. When XVI collects a sufficient number of
projection images, it then puts these images into a specified number of
phases (specified in the Symmetry preset) for XVI to reconstruct into 3D
images. XVI puts the projection images in sequence in relation to the largest
object that has the same movement as respiratory cycle movement in the
image. This sequence of 3D images makes up the Symmetry VolumeView™
image.
It is necessary to have a minimum gantry rotation of 200° for a Symmetry
VolumeView™ acquisition. A Symmetry VolumeView™ acquisition is
approximately 1400 images. The number of phases is specified in the
Symmetry preset as 10 (see the XVI Instructions for Use manual).
The more phases you have for your Symmetry VolumeView™ image, the
more information you have during the breathing cycle. But, a large number
of phases increases the time of the acquisition, and can decrease the image
quality.

imaging

images during an MV treatment field delivery. This can allow the user to:

4.10
Detector control board (DCB)
For non-Harmony, the DCB is located behind the B-side cover of the base assembly of the kV
detector arm. For Harmony, the DCB is located in the B-side of chassis casting under base cover.
The functions of the DCB are to:
•
Generate the frame-trigger pulses required for reading out images from the kV
detector
•
Generate a trigger signal to enable the pulsing of the kV radiation (when required)
•
Synchronize the kV image readout and the generation of kV radiation
•
Time stamp the gantry readout
•
Time stamp the kV expose trigger.
4.10.1
Row-trigger signal generation
The DCB receives XVI control CAN messages from the XVI control cabinet. A control message
contains an ENABLE FRAME READOUT bit that specifies whether the kV detector should be read.
If the ENABLE FRAME READOUT bit is asserted (logic 1), the DCB generates the frame trigger
signals necessary to read image frames from the kV detector. At the end of each complete frame,
a frame counter (8-bit) is incremented and then delayed for 40 ms before commencing to read
the next frame.
If the ENABLE FRAME READOUT bit in a received control message is not asserted (logic 0), the
DCB completes the readout of the current frame and then inhibits the triggering of any further
images until receipt of the next control message in which the ENABLE FRAME READOUT bit is
asserted. The frame counter is reset when frame readout is enabled.

4.10.2
Trigger signal generation
The XVI control messages also contain a MAXIMUM PULSE COUNT parameter that is used to
enable or disable the triggering of the kV generator during the periods between frame reads.
When the DCB receives the message, it records the embedded MAXIMUM PULSE COUNT in an
internal pulse counter. If the pulse count is greater than zero, the DCB generates a kV trigger pulse
at the start of the 40 ms period between each kV detector frame readout, and then decrements
the count. When the count reaches zero, no further kV pulses are enabled.
The DCB has an on-board millisecond timer that is used to time stamp all CAN messages that are
generated.
The DCB pulses the kV generator by sending a 1 ms trigger pulse over a co-axial link. The falling
edge of this pulse triggers the kV generator.
Even when kV radiation is not required, the DCB maintains an 40 ms delay between the readout
of each kV imaging frame. This makes sure that the frame time for kV image acquisition remains
constant, independent of kV exposure parameters.
4.11
Arm control board (ACB)
For non-Harmony, the ACB is behind the A-side cover of the arm base assembly. For Harmony, the
ACB is located in the A-side of chassis casting under base cover. The ACB controls the movements
system of the kV detector arm. It contains all input decoding, interlocks and power outputs.
The ACB has LEDs to help with the troubleshooting on the arm movement system. The LEDs are
divided into columns for each movement. They have the two modes of operation that follow:
•
NORMAL
•
EXTRA.
The modes of operation can be selected with a jumper that is moved to a different position.
4.11.1
Physical characteristics of the ACB
The ACB resides within the base assembly of the kV detector arm, behind the cover on the A side
of the arm assembly. The board is installed on insulating standoffs and an aluminum bar on the
left edge of the board. The aluminum bar also acts as a heat sink between the linear and PWM
based power devices to the shoulder casting. This provides adequate thermal mass, so forced air
cooling of the power devices on the ACB is not required.
The outline of the PCB and its fixing holes are defined by the shoulder casting and the heat sink
bar. Insulation is provided behind the ACB to minimize the occurrence of shorting leads on the
metallic parts behind the board.
For non-Harmony, the cover on the A side of the arm assembly provides physical and regulatory
protection. For Harmony, the base cover provides physical and regulatory protection. You can see
the ACB diagnostic LEDs through the cutout in the covers.
4.11.2
Machine interfaces
All the user interfaces necessary to operate the arm movements are filtered and authorized by
the ACB. These include the movement demand buttons of the XVI HHC, the HHC enable and the
manual brake release buttons, and illumination drive.
The ACB also contains an audible buzzer similar to devices used elsewhere on the host digital
accelerator, but pulsed for ease of identification.

4.11.4
Supplies and interlocks
Arm and host touchguard chains
A +24 V DC fused supply is connected in series to the detector touchguard chain and the middle
arm touchguard chain. The chain returns signal TGs_Healthy. The touchguard switches are
configured such that +24 V on TP13 signifies a healthy touchguard (that is, no collision indicated).
This makes sure that a fault such as a broken lead within the chains fails safe.
The TGs_Healthy signal closes the contacts of two relays (RL3 and RL1). The coils of these relays
are connected in parallel and the contacts are connected in series into the touchguard chain of
the host digital accelerator.

Field effect transistor TR6 makes sure that the relays are closed only if firmware output
Touchguard_Interlock is valid (logic 1). By using TR6, the firmware of the ACB can break the
touchguard chain of the digital accelerator - irrespective of the status of the detector or middle
arm touchguards.
For example if the kV detector arm is left between the open and closed positions, the touchguard
chain of the host digital accelerator is broken by TR6. This inhibits gantry rotation (unless the
touchguard override of the digital accelerator is used). The Touchguard_Interlock signal derives
from the interlocks_and_local_enable block within the firmware.
Note:
The example above is for non-Harmony only.
Supplies monitor
IC9 monitors the +5 V, +15 V, + 24 V, -15 V and -24 V supply rails. If any supply falls below a
threshold level, then the Supplies_OK output goes low (logic 0). This output is monitored by the
firmware and forms part of the interlocks_and_local_enable block within the firmware.
+10 V reference generation
A positive 10 V reference for positional feedback in the coarse and fine potentiometer
transducers is derived from the +15 V linearly regulated supply rail of the ACB. Current limiting is
provided by a current feedback circuit (R134, etc.). A test point and a discrete LED are provided
for measurement and visual indication.
Switched ±24 V generation
Depending on the status of the host digital accelerator, a nominal +26 V signal (motor drive
output) from the digital accelerator is used to drive relay RL2 on the ACB. The common 0 V
connection between the ACB and the digital accelerator is at the HHC, so RL2 makes sure that
signal Host_Movements_PSU_0V is isolated from the 0 V rail of the ACB. This arrangement
minimizes 0V/GND loops within the system.
The closure of relay RL2 closes two power relays (RL4 and RL5). The latter generate the switched
±24 V DC supplies that drive the pivot, longitudinal and lateral motors of the kV detector arm. The
closure of RL4 and RL5 depends upon the status of FETs TR9 and TR10. Transistor TR9 and its
associated driver circuitry make sure that RL4 and RL5 are not powered unless signal Config_Done
is valid. Therefore, until the field programmable gate array (FPGA) reports successful
configuration, the ±24 V DC supplies are not present. The FPGA is IC13 on the ACB.
Transistor TR10 is a similar interlock to TR6 in the touchguard circuitry, allowing the firmware to
remove the power drive to RL4 and RL5. Signal PWR_Relay_Interlock is generated within the
interlocks_and_local_enable block of the firmware. This enables the ACB to respond instantly to a
touchguard fault.
The TGs_Healthy signal is monitored within the firmware and, if the local touchguard chain is
broken, the supply to RL4 and RL5 is removed by means of TR10 for a nominal period of two
seconds. By removing the Host_Movements_PSU_+26V signal, this arrangement ensures a faster
response, of minimum duration, than that provided by the digital accelerator.
LED indication of the switched and unswitched ±24 V DC supplies is provided:
•
LED indication (and a test point) is provided for the Config_Done signal.
•
Indication of the logical status of the PWR_Relay_Interlock is provided by the bargraph
diagnostic LEDs.
Test points are also provided.
Local power rail generation
A positive 15 V supply is linearly generated from the +24 V dc supply to the ACB. The +5 V rail is
also linearly generated from +24 V. A power resistor (R1) is used to minimize the power dissipated
within the +5 V regulator. The 3V3 supply is generated from the +5 V supply and has current limit
protection and thermal shutdown.

4.11.5
Input conditioning
Digital inputs
All inputs are protected with a series 1KW 1W resistor, the output of which is connected through
a Schottky diode to the relevant power rail and GND. This protects the inputs from inadvertent
connection to the maximum on-board supply rail. The series resistor also provides RC filtering in
conjunction with a ceramic capacitor to GND.
With the exception of the filtered, buffered, movement potentiometer inputs, all inputs (after
filtering) are directly connected to the FPGA.
Some potential division is applied to the +24 V TGs_Healthy signal and the
Host_Movements_PSU_On signal.
Movement potentiometer inputs
The inputs from the analog movement potentiometers are buffered by an operational amplifier
after filtering to ensure a known output impedance to the next stage.
4.11.6
Altera
Oscillators
The oscillator is a single chip at an operating frequency of 10 MHz. The output enable pin (pin 1)
is pulled high by a discrete resistor to disable the output during production testing. The clock
output is connected directly to a dedicated input (DI1) on the FPGA. Within the FPGA, this signal
is clocked down for specific functions.
Watchdog
The watchdog device monitors the 3V3 supply rail and the presence of an indication of a clock on
the WDI input (pin 4). This signal is a direct output from the FPGA. Within the FPGA the Watchdog
output is connected to the clock input.
The watchdog acknowledges a fault by pulling the nReset input on pin 1 low (logic 0). This is
connected directly to the FPGA (the second dedicated input) - DI2 (pin 28). This is
“Watchdog_nReset” within the firmware and is used within the interlocks_and_local_enable
block.
EPROM
An EPC1 type EPROM (single shot programmable) is used.

4.11.7
Switched supplies monitors
+24 V switched supply monitor
A comparator is used to verify that the +24V switched supply is present. Hysteresis is provided by
R257. The output from the circuit, "+24VSW_Present", is monitored by the firmware. It provides
the firmware with the status of the power relay RL4. Therefore if the relay is 'stuck closed' it may

-24 V switched supply monitor
This circuit is similar to that used to monitor the +24V switched supply (described in the previous
section). The input is first inverted (unity gain inverter) before comparison. Diode D81 protects
the comparator input from -ve potentials. The output, "-24VSW_Present", is monitored by the
firmware.
+24 V switched brake supply monitor
This circuit is identical in configuration to that used to monitor the +24V switched supply. The
output, "+24VSwBrk_Present", is monitored by the firmware.
+24 V switched clutch supply monitor
This circuit is identical in configuration to that used to monitor the +24V switched supply. The
output, "+24VswClu_Present", is monitored by the firmware.
4.11.8
Longitudinal limits and imaging position
Longitudinal extension limit
The filtered and buffered longitudinal coarse potentiometer input is compared with an adjustable
threshold using a LM339 type comparator. Positive feedback is provided to ensure hysteresis. The
open collector output is pulled up to +5V and the output monitored by the firmware. The
'nLong_Coarse_Extend_Limit' output informs the firmware that the calibrated end of the
longitudinal travel in the T-direction (extension, that is, towards the Target).
Longitudinal isocenter
The imaging position of the kV detector arm is defined by a series of voltage thresholds. These
thresholds generate virtual windows of distance on the travel. Figure 4.33 shows the signal

The comparator circuits generate the logical inputs to the FPGA. Calibration is conducted by
means of adjusting the reference voltage. The adjustment is made by means of the 10 turn
vertical potentiometers on the ACB. Footprints have been provided to allow removal of the
potentiometer and 'fixing' of the threshold. Hysteresis is provided within the comparator stages.
The threshold level comparator input is pulled to either the +10V reference supply rail or GND to
ensure that failure of the reference deriving potentiometer wiper is controlled (that is, the input
is not left floating).
The movement potentiometer inputs increases linearly as the movement retracts (as shown by
the sloped line in the figure above. This follows the convention used within the NPSS movements
scheme and is hoped to minimize confusion.
Within the 'coarse window' the maximum speed is limited. Therefore approaching it at maximum
speed, the speed (voltage applied to the motor) is reduced. Upon reaching the 'fine window' the
movement stops for a nominal period of one second. After this time period the applied voltage to
the motor (proportional to speed) is ramped up to a reduced maximum value until the movement
exits the 'coarse window' when the speed is ramped up to a maximum speed again.
The speed is reduced on approaching the 'fine window' to optimise the positional accuracy by
reducing the stopping distance.
Note:
For non-Harmony, when using the 'auto close' function (Pivot Close HHC Button) the coarse and
fine window inputs are ignored to optimize the closure time.
Spare devices
The spare or unused device pins (IC12 pins 1,6 & 7) are connected to discrete resistors to enable
in-circuit testing of the comparator.

The principles and circuitry used for lateral movement limits are similar to those in the
longitudinal movements. Whereas only the fully extended position of the longitudinal drive is
interpreted using the coarse potentiometer, both motion drive limits are derived on the lateral
drive.
Full extension on the A side is signaled by the Lat_Coarse_Limit_A signal at logic 0: full extension
on the B side is signaled by the Lat_Coarse_Limit_B signal at logic 0. As implied by the
corresponding signal names, the coarse movement potentiometer is used to derive the limit
positions.
These output signals are direct FPGA inputs. Therefore drive is logically disabled upon reaching
the limit, and only the drive movement away from the limit is logically allowed. Hysteresis is
provided by positive feedback on the comparators, and calibration of the end limits is provided by
the on-board multi-turn potentiometers. The A limit is of lower potential than the B limit.

the longitudinal drive. Figure 4.34 shows the coarse and fine windows. Control of the motor

therefore the 'center' position is not dependent upon the correct calibration or correct

4.11.11
Locking solenoid (non-applicable for Harmony)
Solenoid driver
The solenoid driver source is the Burr-Brown DRV102T device. This is a controllable PWM (pulse
width modulation) device. This allows the solenoid to be driven at 100% duty cycle for a fixed
time period, and then at a lower duty cycle. This minimizes the power delivered to the solenoid
and therefore increases the system efficiency and minimizes the heat dissipated in the solenoid.
Note: the solenoid may be 'held' with a lower voltage once the pin has been withdrawn due to
the magnetic characteristics of such devices. The device is controlled by the FPGA. When the
FPGA output "Solenoid_Driver_input" is a logical one, the solenoid driver is 'on'. C20 allows
adjustment of the initial time period the device provides 100% duty cycle output. R9 adjusts the
output (for example, 50%) for the remaining period for which the output is applied (when the
"IN" input is logic one). The active low 'Flag' output indicates when the output is open circuit.
Note: this is seen to oscillate for such an inductive type load. The PWM output is filtered using L1
and C49.
For more information on this device refer to the manufacturer's datasheet.
Interlock
The filtered PWM output is switched using TR3, which is controlled by the FPGA. When the FPGA
output "ARM_Open" in a logic one, the FET TR3 in turned 'on'.
Logical conditions (firmware)
The logical conditions for the FPGA outputs may be seen in the two following sections.
Note:
The solenoid is released by a spring when the device is not energized.

4.11.12
Longitudinal motor drive
Demand control
The demand to the motor drive stage is an 8 bit digital word, an output from the FPGA. This byte
is the input to the DAC08, an eight bit DAC. The output of the convertor is a current output. The
device is used in a bipolar output configuration. When the MSB input is logical one and all other
inputs are logical zero, the output IOUT should be zero current. This has the effect of zero voltage
drive to the motor. When all the inputs are logical one, then the maximum current is sinked (-ve
current) by pin IOUT resulting in a positive output from the power operational amplifier. When all
the inputs are logical zero, then the maximum current is sourced (+ve current) by pin IOUT
resulting in a negative output from the power operational amplifier. The current output and
feedback resistor on the power operational amplifier are such that for inputs 11111111 and
00000000 the power operational amplifier output is pushed into saturation. This limits the power
dissipated for these two demand extremes and allows speed control (voltage output) to be
defined within the firmware.
Logical enable
The power operational amplifier has an enable pin (E/S). When the device is disabled, the output
may be compared with the 'tri-status' condition common in digital devices (refer to the BurrBrown datasheet for further information). The E/S pin is pulled low to disable. This pin is driven
low in it's 'default' condition by the n-p-n transistor TR28. The FPGA has control over the base
drive of this transistor and allows the transistor to be turned 'off', therefore the E/S pin is
released 'high' and the output is enabled.
Power operational amplifier
A number of the OPA549 device features have already been explained in this section. Other
features used are:
As well as acting as an enable pin, the E/S pin indicates the thermal shutdown status of the
device. The device pulls this pin low, indicating that the device is in thermal shutdown. This pin is
connected to the FPGA and indication of the status of this pin is provided by one of the red
bargraph diagnostic LEDs.
The ILIM pin this allows the current limit to be defined by a resistor to GND. A 10 nF parallel
capacitor minimizes the effect of noise. The current limit for the longitudinal axis is approximately
3 A.
4.11.13
Output monitoring
Hardware monitoring
The output voltage of the power operational amplifier is monitored by a series of comparator
circuits. Two active high outputs are generated. The signal Long_+VE_O/P indicates that the
motor drive output is positive, while the signal Long_-VE_O/P is negative. The threshold voltage is
nominally 1 volt, (+1VR). The output is potentially divided by R337, R334 combination. The BAS19
Schottky diode is used to minimize the voltage drop before monitoring by the LM339
comparators. The sensitivity threshold is therefore just over ±4 V on the motor drive output.
Firmware monitoring
The hardware outputs are monitored within firmware. This monitor has knowledge of the
expectation of the output (primarily a factor of the logical demand) and the hardware monitoring
feedback. If the feedback indicates an output with no demand or the monitor indicates no
feedback yet there is a valid demand an 'error' has occurred. During transient conditions (for
example, ramp up of the output) this 'error' is not valid. A counter is used to verify the validity of
the 'error'. This counter is allowed to count up and down, this repeated transient conditions do
not accumulate in the incorrect verification of such errors. Monitoring of the two conditions
provides dormant fault protection of the monitoring hardware.

Electrical power for the kV detector panel and arm movements is derived from the host digital

4.15
Image correction
4.15.1
Offset image corrections (black level)
While the XVI program is running, the DCB continually triggers the kV detector, with a pause of
182 ms between frames, and the software continually acquires images - even when the radiation
is off.
When the software detects that the radiation has been off for more than a specified number of
frames (AutoOffsetMinBeamOffFrames) and enough frames have been captured
(AutoOffsetMinFrames) to generate an offset image, a new offset image is created and
stored in memory. The offset is then applied to any subsequently acquired images.
The XVI program continually monitors the CAN messages from the DCB. A kV DCB inhibit appears,
if there is no communication to the kV DCB.
4.15.2
Gain correction
To optimize the image quality, a gain calibration is required at each energy. This corrects for the
differences in gain response of each of the pixels at different energies, and also calibrates the
image dose.
You can choose between Single Level Gain (SLG) and Multi Level Gain(MLG). You can do gain
calibration from the Service menu (Service > kV Service Functions > SLG and Filter calibration).
The number of energies required to be calibrated is set by the presets. When this is set, the
calibration procedure automatically takes the user through the gain calibration.
4.15.3
Filter correction
To improve the kV scatter correction and reconstruction uniformity, a filter calibration is
necessary at each energy. This corrects for the filter profile which is introduced in the image when
you use the filter. XVI calculates a normalization factor to correct for exposure.
4.15.4
Bad pixel map
A bad pixel map is used to identify image pixels that do not respond correctly and cannot be
corrected by using gain or offset. To overcome this condition, the value of the bad pixel is set to
the average value of the neighboring pixels.
For a new kV detector panel, a bad pixel map is supplied on an accompanying compact disc
(PerkinElmer Opto-electronics). This image is copied into the XVI directory during the installation
process. If the bad pixel map changes during the life of the kV detector panel, it can be updated
by using the XVI program.

another 10 seconds, the error message will be displayed again.

4.19
Extended Imaging Module (XIM)
The Extended Imaging Module (XIM) is installed in AREA 13 of the gantry. The XIM changes the
analogue voltages from the kV detector arm into digital CAN messages for interpretation by the
XVI control cabinet.
Refer also to XVI system diagrams.
Note:
The XIM communicates with the XVI control cabinet through the MV CAN bus, which is extended
from the iViewGT™ control cabinet to the XVI control cabinet.
The XIM takes various analogue and digital inputs from MV (Mega Volt) Arm Control Board, kV
(Kilo Volt) Arm Control Board and from collimator cassettes and filter cassettes. Five CAN
daughter boards change all these analogue inputs into useful CAN information.
In addition, the Daughter boards provide Digital IO to allow the system to generate key presses on
the hand held controllers (HHCs) from software on both the kV Arm and MV Arm. The Digital IO
also provides the facility to control the function key pad gantry ASU signal.
Finally the Digital IO provides a number of digital inputs. These are the kV gating signal from the
IBA and from the function key pad, a feedback signal from the gantry ASU signal, and finally a
signal from the IBA that indicates if there is a kV detector panel movement demand from either of
the kV detector arm hand held controllers.
There are also three local feedback signals from the isolated side of the XIM. A kV and an MV and
held controller output feedback signal are active when there is an active digital output on the MV
and kV digital outputs respectively. Finally there is local feedback of the Linac ASU output which
indicates if there is current flowing through the Linac ASU output transistor (indicating that the
relays which hold down the ASU and enable button within the FKP are active).
A socketed CPLD provides a host communication watchdog and gating function for the digital
outputs. If a failure mode occurs, all the digital outputs are disabled by the hardware. Outputs
may also all be disabled with a jumper link. In addition, if the microprocessor reset signal is
asserted, the digital outputs will be disabled.

4.20
Description of the Imaging Breakout Assembly
The Imaging Breakout Assembly is designed to support multiple functions in the system by
breaking into various signals and asserting some of them via relays.
It enables the Extended Imaging Module (XIM) to control MV and kV arm movements by breaking
into the HHC signals and routing them to the digital outputs of the XIM, allowing the XIM to
effectively press buttons on the HHC. Remote MV and kV arm movements can only occur when
authorized by both the function key pad via relays (FKP) and the XIM. If a button is pressed on the
HHC then XIM controlled movements are immediately disabled.
IBA supports remote panel retraction of the MV detector arm from the FKP. This is only supported
if the appropriate link plug is connected to SK60IBA1 instead of the XIM Digital IO connection
(1007653). It does this by asserting the MV and kV panel retract lines and the MV or kV user
enable lines. If a HHC demand button is pressed, remote movements are immediately disabled.
(See the iViewGT™ Corrective Maintenance Manual for more information).
It also routes the kV enable signal from the FKP to the kV generator footswitch input to let kV
radiation to be initiated from the FKP during a kV volume scan, to let the footswitch to be
removed.
In addition, the IBA supports kV gating from the FKP or external gating input, which sends a gating
request to the XVI control cabinet, through the XIM to the kV DCB (which will interrupt the trigger
pulses). Initiating a KV gate also switches off the kV room lamps. The gating signal path from the
external input to the kV DCB has a minimal delay to prevent unnecessary exposures.
The IBA also routes gantry speed relay signals from the gantry speed switch box to the gantry
speed module to allow variable speed for 4D image acquisition.

4.21.2
Changes to kV flexmap calibration for XVI R5.0 systems
The issue with the XVI systems before R5.0 is that these do not take account of Clockwise and
Counter Clockwise rotation directions so it is possible the best compensation is not necessarily
being applied. In XVI R5.0 it is necessary to have both Clockwise and Counter Clockwise flexmaps

•
CW and CCW flexmaps differ by more than 1mm from each other
If the flexmaps are older than 1 year a warning will appear or if older than 1.25 years an inhibit
will appear.

5.1
Important information before you start to do service work
on the XVI system
WARNING 5.1
Ionizing radiation is hazardous to health. Do not go into the treatment room while the radiation
warning lamp near the treatment room door is on (illuminated). If you ignore this warning, it
can cause fatal injury.
CAUTION 5.1
The X-ray tube can be damaged if it is used at continuous high power levels for long periods.
The kV generator monitors the temperature of the kV source and prohibits radiation if the
temperature exceeds approximately 85°C. But, the heat capacity of the kV housing is greater than
that of the anode of the X-ray tube. Consequently the anode may overheat before the maximum
temperature of the kV source reaches 85°C.
Instead of having an independent XVI HHC and an independent iViewGT HHC, the Harmony
machine has an integrated HHC which can control the extending, retracting and lateral (small and
large FOV) movement of the arm. The integrated HHC of Harmony cannot control the center
panel movement, the pivot open movement and the pivot close movement.
The table below shows the corresponding relationship between the buttons of the XVI HHC (nonHarmony) and the integrated HHC (Harmony). For example, the Open button on the XVI HHC
(non-Harmony) and the CENTER PANEL button on the integrated HHC (Harmony) have the same
function. In the following trouble shooting, instruction to press the Open button means press the
CENTER PANEL button on the integrated HHC.

5.14.3
Correcting the DICOM import failure
A parameter in sri.ini intended for diagnostic use can cause the DICOM import to fail with no
error messages reported on the third party system or in the XVI DICOM logs for the transfer. The
patient data is not imported into the XVI database. The DICOM data files are not transferred to
the Dicomtransitdb folder but the files can be found in another folder, for example c:\temp.
1 
Make sure that the parameter MsglogDirectory under the [Dicom] section in the sri.ini file
is empty (blank).
2 
Restart the XVIDicomSCP for the change to take effect.
Note:
The MsglogDirectory parameter is used to capture failed transfer messages to the XVIDicomSCP
and therefore should only be used as a temporary diagnostic setting. Setting a directory path for
the MsglogDirectory parameter will cause all DICOM data to be directed to the MsglogDirectory
irrespective of whether the transfer to the XVIDicomSCP was successful or not. The XVIDicomSCP
does not try to validate the messages and does nothing more with them.

To do a log file analysis:
1 
Examine three or four log files to find the cause of a problem. When an entry related to a

5.15.3.2
Examining the Context Manager.log
The ContextManager.log is generated by the program ContextMgr.exe. The Context
Manager examines that the inhibits are as expected and values are within tolerance for a
particular context. For example, the kV generator requires a number of conditions for a tube
warm-up. The context manager examines these values and instructs the Inhibit Manager whether
they are satisfactory or not.
1 
Look in this log for parameters going out of tolerance (OOT) that do not subsequently go in
tolerance (InTol).
The parameter name indicates the item that went out of tolerance, for example:
OOT[LateralTableShift]
5.15.3.3
Examining the InhibitManager.log
The InhibitManager is a software object residing in the program ContextMgr.exe. At XVI start
up, the InhibitManager.log lists a series of [...NodeNotOnline] messages. As each
node goes on line the InhibitManager.log reports the NotOnLine message as being
cleared. Many of these messages relate to CAN nodes that are not yet supported.
1 
Look in InhibitManager.log for inhibits that are Activated that are not
subsequently Cleared.

5.15.3.6
DicomSCPStatus.log
The DicomSCPStatus.log is generated by XVI DICOM SCP. It contains basic information
about the SCP activity and validation errors. This is a useful log to inspect if a DICOM transfer is

DicomSCP.log
The DicomSCP.log is generated by the programming tool kit used by XVI DICOM SCP when
some data is received. This log contains details of the DICOM transaction as well as the type of
data pushed to XVI SCP. The log can be difficult to read as many of the messages are not relevant
to the user.

The DICOMSCU.log is generated by the programming toolkit used by the XVI DICOM SCP when
data is sent. This log contains details of the DICOM transaction as well as the type of data pushed
from XVI. Because the log is generated by the toolkit used by the SCP it can be difficult to read as
it contains a lot of information, much of which is not relevant to the user.

(2148) 11-20 11:05:39.58 MC3 E: program title "DICOMAPP1" is not
configured

mergecom.app.

5.16.1
Correcting the workstation mismatch in the kV generator log file
If the message that follows is found in the kV generator log file:
ERROR: Workstation and Workingmode Mismatch [Workstation=PF(2),
Workingmode=Standard RF(4)] or similar [Workstation=PF(2),
Workingmode=Buckey 1(1)]
1 
If your kV generator is an SHF 435, do the procedure that follows (see Configuring the kV
generator to run in Workstation 2 - DSI mode (WS=2) for the Sedecal SHF 435 DSI Series).
Note:
The SHF 435 is not applicable for Harmony.
2 
If your kV generator is an SHFR 400, do the procedure that follows (see Configuring the kV
generator to run in Workstation 2 - DSI mode (WS=2) for the Sedecal SHFR 400 DSI Series).
5.16.1.1
Configuring the kV generator to run in Workstation 2 - DSI mode (WS=2) for the
Sedecal SHF 435 DSI Series (non-applicable for Harmony)
1 
Exit the XVI program and power off the generator.
2 
On the ATP controller board, make sure that the DIP switch ATPSW2-3 is set to the ON
position.
This puts the kV generator in Service mode.
3 
Switch on the kV generator and start the Sedecal Generator Service\Service Console
program.
4 
Select Configuration.
5 
Make sure that WS2 is selected as DSI and select WS2.
Note:
WS1 is selected by default when the Sedecal Generator Service window opens.
6 
Select Exit/OK to save the configuration and close the Sedecal Generator Service\Service
Consolewindow.
7 
De-energize the kV generator and set the DIP switch ATPSW2-3 to the OFF position.

5.18.9
Correcting a noisy or loose pivot movement (non-applicable for
Hamrony)
During the pivot movement of the kV detector arm, rollers at the ends of the latch pins give
smooth and stable movement. The rollers move along and apply a force to the metal track.
Adjustment screws let you adjust the rollers, and therefore the force they apply to the track.
1 
Set the gantry to 0°.
2 
Move the kV detector arm to the center of its range of rotation.
That is approximately 45°, between the fully open and fully closed positions.
3 
Adjust the pivot movement (see Figure 5.54).
a
Loosen the lock nuts.
b
If it is necessary, turn the adjustment screws clockwise to extend the latch pins to the
metal track.
CAUTION 5.2
Do not tighten the pivot adjustment screws too much. If the adjustment screws are too tight, it
is possible that the XVI system cannot move freely. If you ignore this caution, it can cause
damage to the equipment.
c
If it is necessary, turn the adjustment screws counterclockwise to retract the latch
pins away from the metal track.
d
When the movement is smooth and makes no noise, tighten the lock nuts.

5.23.2
Correcting the excessive error frame rate on the CAN card in the XVI
control cabinet
If the error frame rate becomes excessive on the CAN card in the XVI control cabinet, the card
automatically withdraws from the bus. The card therefore stops receiving and routing CAN
messages, so all proxies are starved and consequently time out 5 seconds later. Each proxy then
goes offline and causes an inhibit.
In XVI, only three proxies use the CAN bus, therefore three inhibits occur:
•
kV DCB (0x0001001)
•
gantry (0x0001004)
•
table (0x0001006).
This fault can occur when a new CAN device is added to the bus, or an existing CAN
device fails, therefore disturbing the bus termination.

5.31.1
Description of the image quality problems for an XVI system
This section gives information on problems related to the quality of kV images.
WARNING 5.6
Do not stand or sit on the kV source arms. If you ignore this warning, you can cause injury to
you, damage to the equipment and clinical mistreatment.
During the acquisition of kV images with the XVI system some quality problems can occur. Section
Correcting image symptoms- Spatial, contrast resolution and uniformity and section Correcting
image symptoms - Ring on images give possible causes on common types of bad quality kV
images and the applicable troubleshooting procedure.
Some of these problems cannot be resolved, because they are characteristic to the system (for
example radar artifacts, see Correcting image characteristics that cannot be resolved . In this
section we are trying to enhance your understanding of what can be resolved and what cannot.
As each individual bad quality problem is different, we can only give directions on how to do the
troubleshooting.
Troubleshooting
Diagnosing image quality problems
Document ID: 1522605_06
XVI R5.0x
Corrective Maintenance Manual
Page 248
© Elekta Group 2021. All rights reserved.

Cone-beam CT scanning is a two step process. The first step is the image acquisition followed by
the second step ‘reconstruction’. There are many parameters that can effect image quality. Some
of these are related to conditions in which the measurements are made to acquire the data.
Others are related to the computation and the mathematical process, other parameters concern
the display system itself.
An Artifact is a distortion that can occur in reconstructed images. Artifacts may have different
causes and appear in different ways. They may originate from the scanning system, the patient,
and the algorithm, or may be attributed to material outside the scanned field.
Movement artifacts are caused by movement of the patient or organs in the patient (breathing
and heart beating). These artifacts can be minimized by better immobilization of the patient and
by more rapid measurements (short bursts of radiation).
Movement artifacts cause blurring, if the motion is periodic and occur a large number of times
during the scan time.
Alignment artifacts are caused by the fact that the center of rotation of the imaging system is not
necessarily the same as the reconstruction matrix. The center of rotation produces a distortion in
the shape of the internal structures.
Ring artifacts appear as circles in the image. They are caused by a drift in the gain or offset, of
some of the detectors. The amplitude of the ring artifacts increases rapidly when the drifting
detector is close to the center of the array.
Noise and dose: If a homogenous material is scanned, it will be found that the CT numbers of a
given region are not all the same values, as would be expected. The attenuation values will be
randomly distributed around some average value. Noise is expressed in terms of standard
deviation, sigma, of attenuation coefficients. Noise depends on the size of the object, the kV, the
pixel size, the slice thickness and the skin dose.
Contrast resolution can be defined as the ability of a system to distinguish details from their
surrounding structures, while the relative contrast of those details to that of adjacent structures is
low. It is assumed in this definition, that the size of the details to be detected is large enough so
as not to constitute a limiting factor in the ability of the system to detect them.
Spatial resolution refers to the ability of a system to distinguish small details from their
surrounding structures. In this definition, it is assumed that the relative contrast of those details
to the surrounding structures is high enough so as not to constitute a limiting factor in the ability
of the system to detect them.
It is expected that the smallest object visible would be equal to the pixel size. In practice however
the smallest discernible detail is somewhat larger.
The following parameters can have a degrading effect on spatial resolution:
•
Artifacts
•
Non-adequate convolution filter
•
Scattered radiation.

This is a semi-circular shape in a CBCT scan which looks like a radar screen image. It is not
uniform, the brightness decays in the CBCT because of the acquisition time. It is a disk and not a

What is the cause of an radar artifact?
The cause of the radar artifact can be because of the panel lag. When an image is grabbed, the
image does not disappear from the panel instantaneously, it fades gradually and produces a ghost
image. The ghost image will be added to the next image acquisition.
The lag is caused by of the thickness of the scintillator and the trapped charges in the a-Si. The
panel will not flush the photodiode instantaneously.

Radar artifacts appear as a circular segment of decreased pixel values around a part of the edge
of the patient. Radar artifacts can be caused when a part of the kV detector panel is directly
exposed to high levels of radiation during a scan. This occurs for example when an image
acquisition laterally through a pelvis is done.
The necessary level of exposure for a thick region of the patient usually causes image saturation
or over-exposure of the kV detector panel where the X-rays go through air. The part of the kV
detector panel, that was exposed to the high levels of radiation shows high sensitivity for some
time.
When the XVI system rotates around the patient, and acquires images through anatomy, the high
sensitivity of the kV detector panel continues to have an effect on the projection images. This can
cause an apparent decrease in the reconstructed density for the region on the opposite side of
the patient to the ‘saturating’ projection angle.
5.31.7.2
Outline reduction effect
The outline reduction effect can occur in reconstructed VolumeView™ images, and causes a
decreased patient outline. Figure 5.78 shows an example of the outline reduction effect, seen
during image registration in green-purple mode. The reconstructed VolumeView™ image (green)
appears smaller than the reference CT volume (purple).
002686
©2011 Elekta Limited
Figure 5.78
Example of the ‘outline reduction’ effect
Projection rays that go through thinner or less dense areas of the patient anatomy, can cause
panel saturation because of their high transmitted intensity, and this can cause the outline
reduction effect. The reconstruction algorithm in XVI, identifies these saturated pixel values and
treats them as air in subsequent procedures.

pane, with the center along the axis of rotation (the linear accelerator G–T axis). In the Coronal or
Sagittal image panes, the same artifacts can also appear as lines, as they are cylindrical or conical

5.31.7.4
Streak artifacts in axial slices
In the VolumeView™ windows, streak artifacts are lines or bands of artificially lighter or darker
pixels across an image. Streak artifacts can occur if the cone-beam reconstruction procedure is
susceptible to discontinuities, or if there are inconsistencies between adjacent projection images
caused by sources, such as:

•
Edges in the image field that are inadequately sampled by the small number of
projections (that is, aliasing effects). Objects in the field-of-view (or included in a
subset of the projection set) that have hard high contrast edges can cause streaks in
the reconstructed slices. The ‘object’ is possibly a part of the patient (for example,
bony edges, teeth, metal inserts) or a part of the equipment (for example, the edge of
the table top or a part of an immobilization device). To find the cause of these artifacts,
try to follow the streaks back to the source, and if necessary, reconstruct a larger
volume.
•
Inconsistent beam hardening. As X-ray radiation goes through the patient, its spectral
profile changes as lower energy photons are absorbed (‘beam hardening’). Where
adjacent X-rays go through materials with different atomic numbers (Z), the degree of
the beam hardening of these X-rays can change. This can cause material in the
‘shadow’ of high-Z material to appear to have a different density to material that is the
same, but in a different area, this causes streaking. Figure 5.80 shows an example of
streak artifacts caused by beam hardening from spinal vertebrae.

©2011 Elekta Limited

•
Lag in the kV detector panel. This is a property of a-Si detectors. One sign of lag is that
the pixel response at the start of an exposure takes a few frames until it is at its
nominal value. When you do a 360° image acquisition, the first and last frames of the
projection sequence are acquired through the same patient anatomy, but, because of
lag, the last projection has a higher signal level than the first. This inconsistency can
cause a streak across the image at an orientation that is the same as the start/stop
angle of the scan.

5.31.8
Correction image symptoms - Rings on images
5.31.8.1
Description of the possible causes for rings to appear in images
Rings appear in images for different reasons:
•
Ghost (latency)
•
Problems with the badpixel map
•
Unwanted material that absorbs radiation on the collimator (lead swarf)
•
Problems during calibration with the water tank
•
Unwanted material that absorbs radiation on the detector touchguard.
There can be a combination of these effects, and the different problems must be isolated to find a
solution. Some of the problems are system characteristics and can not be resolved.

5.31.9
Ghost (latency) artifacts
Ghost (latency)artifacts occur when you can see some remaining signal from a previous
acquisition in the new images that you acquire. Latency is caused because incident radiation has
small temporary effects on the sensitivity of the CsI scintillator in the kV detector panel. This
change in sensitivity can have an effect on subsequent images. The latency effect is temporary
and its magnitude is related to the level of the earlier exposure to the kV detector panel.

artifact and also the type of ghost artifact.

XVI uses a three step procedure to warm up the X-ray tube. Each step changes the kV, mA, and ms
settings, which helps to prevent arcing of the X-ray tube. The arcing can cause an image
acquisition to terminate.
Note:
You can warm up the X-ray tube at all angles, with all collimator cassettes and filter cassettes, but
it is good procedure to use the smallest collimator cassette.
1 
Extend the kV source arm.
CAUTION 5.3
Do not warm up the X-ray tube if the kV detector panel is open. If the kV detector panel is not
retracted, you will possibly irradiate the detector panel electronics. If you ignore this caution,
you can cause damage to the equipment.
2 
Retract the kV detector panel.
3 
Make sure that there are no inhibits.
4 
On the menu bar, click Image > kV Acquisition > Tube Warmup.
Note:
All the other acquisition types are unavailable at this time, and appear dimmed.
The Tube Warm-up dialog box appears.
5 
On the FKP, press the kV START button.
Note:
If you press the kV INTERRUPT button before the X-ray tube warm up is completed, then you
cannot continue with that warm up beam. The subsequent warm up beam will start.
The radiation warning lamp comes on, the kV generator status changes to X-ray, and the

5.35.4
Finding the mechanical isocenter
1 
Rotate the gantry and BLD to 0°.
2 
Attach a mechanical pointer (for example a 1.5 mm ball end hex key fixed to the table)
approximately at isocenter.
3 
Center the ball end of the hex key on the cross wire.
4 
Rotate the gantry to +90°.
5 
Adjust the table height so that the ball is centered on the cross wire.
6 
Rotate the gantry to 0° and confirm the ball end is still on the cross wire.
7 
Rotate the gantry to 180°.
8 
Measure the error in the GT direction through the 180° rotation and position the
mechanical pointer so that it is positioned in the center of the movement (halve the error).
9 
Measure the error in the AB direction through the 180° rotation and position the
mechanical pointer so that it is positioned in the center of the movement (halve the error).
10 
Rotate the gantry from +180 to -180 and confirm that the deviation of the mechanical
pointer is less than 1 mm from the cross wires in any direction.
The ball end is now at the mechanical isocenter.

5.35.6
Aligning the sagittal laser
1 
Establish the rotational center of the gantry.
2 
Attach a piece of paper to the front gantry cover, project a shadow on to the cover
approximately 10 cm from the center using an external light source.
3 
Mark on the paper the position of this shadow for the cardinal angles 0, 90, 180 and 270°
gantry rotation.
4 
Join the marks with a ruler for 0 and 180 and 90 and 270.
The intersection is the mechanical center of rotation.
5 
Take a fine string from the rotational center of the gantry through the center of the ball
(mechanical isocenter) on to the sagittal wall.
6 
Mark the position of this string on the sagittal wall.
7 
Align the sagittal laser to the alignment string to within +/- 0.5 mm in the range 1 m from
isocenter.
8 
Hang a plumbline and confirm that the sagittal laser is within +/- 0.5 mm of the plumb line
in the range 1 m from the isocenter.
The lasers are now setup accurately enough to be used when checking or aligning the X-ray
tube and Imaging Panel.

6.1
Important information about service work on the XVI
system
Note:
Make sure that you replace fuses with the same type and rating or use an Elekta replacement
part.
Radiation warning lamp
WARNING 6.1
Ionizing radiation is hazardous to health. Do not go into the treatment room while the
RADIATION warning lamp near the treatment room door is on (illuminated). If you ignore this
warning, it can cause fatal injury.
Copying calibration factors to XVI after table or gantry recalibration
The table or gantry movements can be re-calibrated after work on the system, for example after a
potentiometer was changed. It is very important to then run the XVI DCB Utility and copy the
table and gantry calibration factors to the XVI system. These calibration factors are not copied to
XVI automatically. If this is not done then there could be a mismatch between where the table
actually is and where XVI thinks the table is, hence when the XVI calculates the table corrections
they may not be correct.
WARNING 6.2
If the gantry movements are re-calibrated, run the XVI DCB Utility and copy the gantry
calibration factors to XVI. If you ignore this warning, you can cause clinical mistreatment.
Overheating of the X-ray tube
CAUTION 6.1
The X-ray tube can be damaged if it is used at continuous high power levels for long periods.
The kV generator monitors the temperature of the kV source and prohibits radiation if the
temperature exceeds approximately 85°C. However, the heat capacity of the kV housing is greater
than that of the anode of the X-ray tube. Consequently the anode may overheat before the
maximum temperature of the kV source reaches 85°C.
Information for set up, test and calibration
WARNING 6.3
Replacing parts can have an effect on the calibration of the XVI system. Record all parts
replaced during the troubleshooting procedure. After the repair, do all test, set up and
calibration procedures that are given in the replacement procedures for those parts. If you
ignore this warning, you can cause clinical mistreatment.
Information for the administrator
If you are using XVI R5.0.6 with Mk6i control cabinet, the username of the administrator is elekta.

sense cables are installed correctly. If you ignore this caution, you can cause damage to the
equipment.

6.15.24
Environmental conditions for the XVI control cabinet
The XVI control cabinet has an internal operating temperature between 0°C to 60°C. The internal
parts give off a large quantity of heat and if this heat is not removed from the system the internal
temperature can increase.
To prevent the XVI control cabinet from getting too hot, make sure that the cooling fan inlets are
clear of any blockages (rear and front fans) and that filters are kept clean. If the control cabinet is
kept in a closed space, sufficient cooling must be given.
Note:
If the internal temperature of the XVI control cabinet rises above 60°C the XVI control cabinet will
give an audible indication, also the LED on the front panel labeled Temp will flash.
The switching on of the cooling fans and the temperature threshold - therefore the audible
alarms - are controlled by the DIP switches on the internal temperature monitoring board. These
DIP switches can be examined to make sure that they are set correctly.
Note:
The internal temperature monitoring board is located on the base of the inside of the XVI control
cabinet

1 
Extend the kV source arm to the imaging position.

small FOV.

FOV image.
7 
Put the mouse pointer on the vertical line of the cross (G-T axis).
8 
Make sure that the pointer is horizontally in the center, and on the line as accurate as
possible.
9 
Record the x coordinate value (x,y) in the bottom left corner of the XVI display.
10

If the coordinate value is satisfactory, calibrate the A-B position of the kV detector arm in
the large FOV.
12 
If the coordinate value is incorrect, do the steps that follow.
a
On the ACB, set jumper PL7 to the left position.
The system goes to LED Extra mode.
b
Move the kV detector arm until the sagittal laser aligns with the S mark.
c
If the kV detector arm stops before this position, on the ACB, set jumper PL9 to the
left position.
The system goes to override lateral limit.
d
Adjust potentiometer RV4 until LED 3.7 comes on.
e
On the ACB, set jumper PL7 to the right position.
The system goes to LED Normal mode.
f
Set jumper PL9 to the right position.
